collections.title: Europe's Ancient Oaks You Can Actually Visit
collections.intro: An oak does most of its living quietly, which is why so few of the truly old ones get noticed until someone measures the trunk. These eight, pedunculate and holm, span from a Tegel Forest giant that predates Berlin's first written mention to a Barcelona courtyard tree that neighbours spent three years fighting a developer to keep. None survived by being tended like museum pieces. One outlasted a Bavarian duchy. Another grew wider than its older neighbour simply by being left alone. What earns a place here is not age alone: a name, a fight, a naturalist's television campaign, a fence built to protect roots from foot traffic. Every entry is publicly accessible, every coordinate verified, and every page links onward with a map. Start with Berlin's oldest living thing, older than the city itself.

collections.title: Autumn Worth the Trip
collections.intro: Autumn is the one thing a tree does that you can put a date on. A yew looks much the same in April as in November, but a ginkgo drops a whole crown of gold in about a fortnight, and if you miss the fortnight you wait a year. This page ranks every tree we map that is worth going to see for its colour, grouped by the month it turns, so the question it answers is which weekend rather than which tree. The weeks move with the weather and with how far north you are: a Copenhagen beech and a Naples one do not turn together, and a warm October can hold the leaves three weeks longer than the average. Most of them sit in October. Each tree's own page says what it actually does.

collections.title: The Autumn Harvest
collections.intro: A tree at fruiting is a different kind of visit. There is nothing much to look at up in the crown and everything on the ground: acorns underfoot by the thousand in a mast year, sweet chestnuts split out of their cases, figs going soft on the paving, olives knocked down onto sheets. This page ranks every tree we map whose best moment is its crop, grouped by the month it comes, which in our data runs from August into November and peaks hard in September and October. Two things worth saying plainly. Most of these are protected trees and several are the only one of their kind in their city, so look at what has fallen and leave what is still on the branch. And not all of it is food, whatever it looks like: a yew's red arils sit around a seed that is poisonous.

collections.title: Europe's Best Tree City Trips
collections.intro: This list ranks the best afternoon, not the single best tree: cities where several ancient trees stand close enough for one honest walk rather than a taxi between highlights. Every distance and time below comes from the same walk planner every city page already uses, real streets allowed for, not straight lines, and it is a flat-ground number: a hillside city can cost more effort than the kilometres alone suggest, noted plainly where that applies. Order runs easiest first. Lisbon and Sintra are presented as one paired trip, a short train ride apart, so eleven cities carry ten rankings. Every fact here is drawn from this project's own verified research, nothing polled or scored by an algorithm.

collections.title: Europe's 10 Most Remarkable Ancient Trees
collections.intro: This is an opinionated list, and it says so up front. Europe holds tens of thousands of ancient trees; these ten are the most remarkable among the cities we have mapped and verified so far, and the list will shift as new cities join the map. What earns a place here is not age alone. A tree makes this list when it carries a story you can stand next to: a planting date from 1601 with the planter's name attached, a genus named after a family, a churchyard yew that predates the city around it. Every tree is publicly accessible, every location is verified, and every entry links to a full page with map and directions. Start in a London suburb, with the oldest living thing in the city.

collections.title: Europe's Most Remarkable Yews
collections.intro: A yew does not announce its age the way a wide-crowned oak does: the trunk hollows out from the inside, so the tree that looks modest from across a churchyard can be the oldest living thing for miles. These eight, across seven cities, range from a London yew that predates the Roman founding of the city to a Madrid specimen still under two centuries old but split into three fused trunks wide enough to need three separate girth measurements. Several stand guard at entrances, doorways and castle gates, a role yews have played in European gardens for centuries longer than most of the buildings beside them. Every entry is publicly accessible, every coordinate verified. Start with the oldest living thing in London, already ancient when the Romans arrived.

collections.title: Europe's Oldest City Trees Are Mostly Immigrants
collections.intro: Count the ancient trees on this map that stand in European cities and four in ten of them are not European. That is 271 trees out of 686, across 70 of the 79 cities, and the commonest species of the lot is a tree that exists nowhere in the wild: the London plane, a chance hybrid of an American and an Asian parent, which we map 62 times in 35 cities. The rest arrived the way anything else did, by ship and on purpose. A Mexican cypress came with Carmelite missionaries. A black locust arrived as seed posted from the Appalachians. A Californian sequoia was planted in a Paris quarry by an emperor with something to prove. These twelve are the arrivals worth the walk, oldest first.

collections.title: The Trees the World Has Written About
collections.intro: Fame and size have almost nothing to do with each other. Centurion, a mountain ash in Tasmania and one of the tallest living things on earth, has been written up in four languages. An oak in a Lithuanian village that most people outside the country could not place has been written up in nineteen. This page ranks every tree we map that at least two language Wikipedias thought worth an article, most languages first, with monthly reads breaking the ties. Two is the floor because one article usually means a local historian did their job, and a second language means the tree travelled. At the top is El Árbol del Tule outside Oaxaca, a cypress whose trunk has been written about in twenty-six languages and which stands in a church courtyard open every day of the year. The order changes as the articles do, and every tree here has a pin, a story and a way to get there.

collections.title: The Ginkgos Worth a November Trip
collections.intro: Ginkgo biloba is the oldest tree lineage on this site by tens of millions of years, a species that outlived the dinosaurs it grew alongside and, in a few documented cases near Hiroshima, outlived a nuclear blast. It also does something almost no other tree manages: every leaf turns the same uniform gold within days of its neighbours, then drops nearly all at once, rather than fading gradually like the rest of autumn. That trick is reason enough to plan a trip around, and these ten specimens, from a 750 year old survivor of the 1945 Tokyo firebombing to a pair planted the same year Milan's botanical garden opened, all perform it within weeks of each other. Most peak in November. Start with the oldest, in a Tokyo temple where a monk's walking staff is said to have taken root eight centuries ago.

collections.title: Japan's 10 Most Remarkable Ancient Trees
collections.intro: Japan keeps its oldest trees where it keeps its gods. Seven of these ten stand on shrine or temple ground, one in a World Heritage forest, and most were worshipped long before anybody measured them. That is why so many of the ages below are traditions rather than findings: a hollow cedar or camphor cannot be cored to the middle, so the number is what the shrine says, and each entry tells you which kind of number it is. What can be measured is the body, and here the figures are enormous: three trunks come close to twenty metres round or pass it. The order is ours, weighing age where a source gives one, girth and height where somebody has taped them, and how widely the tree is known. The last entry is the youngest by far, and it is here for a distance rather than an age.

collections.title: The Tallest Trees We Have Measured
collections.intro: Height is what people mean when they say a tree is big, and it is the measurement we hold least of, because it takes a surveyor rather than a tape. Every figure on this page comes from a register's own survey or from a plaque at the foot of the tree, never from our own prose: a sentence in a story about height is as often about the species in general, or the tree next to it, or how tall it stood before a storm took the top off. So this ranks the trees that have actually been measured at twenty-five metres or more, tallest first, and it grows as the measurements do. The building comparisons are rough. Start with a mountain ash in a Portuguese forest that is taller than most church towers around it.

collections.title: The Great Planes of Europe
collections.intro: A plane tree does not need to be the oldest thing in a city to be the most memorable. These ten, one per city, got their reputations from a bench eaten alive, a botanist's afternoon walks with Mozart, a bridge widening that moved two full-grown trunks by raft rather than fell them. None are ornamental additions to a park; each is the reason people know that particular corner at all. Start in Dublin, where a Victorian bench has been losing a very slow fight for decades.

collections.title: The Oldest Tree in Every City We Map
collections.intro:
Every place on this site has an oldest tree, and for a long while this page listed fifteen of them, because fifteen countries was all we mapped. It now names all 626, grouped by country, and it rebuilds itself: find an older tree in Kyoto tonight and Kyoto's line changes tomorrow.

Read it as a map of how differently the record is held. Sweden leads on a root system carbon dated to 9,550 years, with a spruce standing on top of it that is nobody's idea of ancient. Britain answers with two yews that have stood in churchyards since before the churches. Japan counts in camphors, Greece and Italy in olives, the Netherlands in lindens that were pollarded for centuries and came out thick rather than tall.

Where we do not know a tree's age the line says so rather than guessing.

collections.title: The Thickest Trunks We Have Measured
collections.intro: Girth is the honest measure of a big tree. Height depends on what the tree is competing with for light, and age is usually somebody's estimate, but a tape around a trunk at chest height is a fact, and it is the number every register in the world records. This page ranks every tree we map whose trunk passes four metres, thickest first, and it re-ranks itself whenever a new measurement arrives. What it cannot show is a tree nobody has measured, which is most of them: the ranking grows as the measurements do. The arm counts are a rough guide rather than a challenge, though the top of this list would take a school class. Start with the banyan in Hilo, which is wider round than most living rooms are long.

collections.title: The Oldest Trees We Have Mapped
collections.intro: Four hundred years is a useful threshold. Older than that and a tree predates nearly everything around it: the streets, the houses, usually the city's entire modern shape. This page ranks every tree we have mapped that clears it, oldest first, and it re-ranks itself the moment we add an older one. One rule keeps it honest, and it costs us entries: a tree qualifies on the LOW end of its estimate, so a tree recorded as one hundred to five hundred years old is not here, however tempting the upper number looks. Where the age is a range, the range is what you see, because that is what the sources say. Start at the top with olives that were already ancient when Rome was a village, and work down to oaks that were merely standing when the printing press arrived.

collections.title: Trees Planted by Kings and Their Gardeners
collections.intro: A monarch's word could put a tree in the ground and keep it there for centuries, and enough of them did that the result reads like an itinerary of vanished courts. A retired Japanese emperor carried his own camphor north in 1160 to plant it at a shrine he had just founded. A shogun kept his pine as a bonsai in a pot and only let it touch soil after his death. Henri IV's own herbalist raised Paris's oldest tree from an American seed, and his son planted the second inside the king's own medicinal garden. Queen Victoria planted a Californian sequoia on Irish soil in 1861 and started a habit every visiting head of state since has copied. None of these merely grow in a royal park. Someone with a crown, or a court appointment, specifically wanted each one exactly there.

collections.title: Trees That Outlived Their City
collections.intro: A tree does not know it is a monument until the buildings around it stop being ones. These six watched a temple burn to the ground, a palace flatten in an air raid, a revolution take the man who planted them, and kept growing anyway, the one part of the view that did not need rebuilding afterward. None of them survived by being protected: most were simply too far from the blast, the flame front, or the guillotine to matter to whoever was doing the destroying. What they share now is a strange kind of authority: ask one of these trees what a lost building looked like, and it is the only witness left standing. Start with a Tokyo ginkgo that took a direct hit and kept its scorch marks to prove it.

collections.title: Trees With a Known Planting Date
collections.intro: Almost every ancient tree on this site carries an estimate: a ring count, a girth measurement fed into a growth curve, a guess dressed up as a fact. These fourteen do not. Somewhere in a garden's own ledger, a shrine's dated tradition or a city's own peace festival records, someone wrote down the year a sapling went into the ground, and the record survived along with the tree. The span runs from a Medici garden in Florence, where the botanist who planted the yew in 1720 kept the books himself, to an Antwerp linden planted on a single named day in 1994. Between them: a plane tree that watched Napoleon abdicate, an oak planted for one dead soldier and all his comrades, and a fig gardeners put in the ground by mistake. Age by inference is common here. Age by paperwork is rare, and it changes what a visit means.

collections.title: Wisteria and Blossom Worth a Spring Trip
collections.intro: Spring is the one season no evergreen can compete with. These eleven trees, across nine cities, each have a real, documented peak between late February and the end of May: an orange grove that scents an entire cathedral courtyard, a wisteria a 19th century woodblock master painted from life, chestnut avenues that turn whole boulevards white with flower. None of these moments are guessed. Every one is sourced to the tree's own species and climate, not applied as decoration. Start in Seville, where the blossom comes earliest.

parks.name: The Arnold Arboretum
parks.intro: Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has been formally cataloguing every plant on its grounds since 1872, so its oldest trees come with a paper trail most cities can only guess at. A white oak on Peters Hill was already growing wild when the Arboretum absorbed the land, and it took until 2010 for anyone to accession it into the record and 2018 to core-sample it to a germination date in the early 1800s. Higher up the same hill, a Japanese black pine grown from seed E.H. Wilson bought in Yokohama in 1919 has spent a century twisting into the wind-shaped form Japanese gardeners spend decades training into a tree. A Franklin tree in the Explorers Garden descends from a species that has not grown wild anywhere on earth for roughly two hundred years, ever since John Bartram found it on a few acres of Georgia riverbank in 1765 and the wild population vanished within a generation. A dawn redwood by the Hunnewell Visitor Center grew from a 1948 seed shipment out of Hubei, China, sent after the species turned up alive in the Chinese interior having previously been known only from fossils. A paperbark maple in the Maple Collection is one of two seedlings a single plant collector dug out of a Chinese wood in 1907, the shared ancestor of nearly every paperbark maple now growing in America. And two katsura trees along Meadow Road began as seed mailed from Sapporo in 1878 by the college president who helped found what is now Hokkaido University. All are open to the public, free, every day of the year.

parks.name: Balboa Park
parks.intro:
Balboa Park's oldest tree is a Guadalupe Island cypress, planted around 1892 under Kate Sessions's lease of park land, the one that obliged her to plant a hundred trees a year here. It grows wild in exactly one place on Earth, a small island off Baja California where feral goats have long been the main threat to it, which makes a large mainland specimen unusual on its own. Nobody has published its height or girth.

The rest of the park's mapped trees are younger and stranger. A Moreton Bay fig outside the Natural History Museum, planted as a five-gallon sapling for the 1915 exposition's garden show, has grown twelve metres round; a second, younger fig over Palm Canyon pours buttress roots down the slope like a flying support. A kauri from New Zealand stands by the Mingei Museum with no age on record. And on the grounds of Marston House, an Australian tea tree grows sideways rather than up, its low trunks rooting again wherever they touch the ground, likely planted by Sessions herself around 1906.

All five are free to walk up to; only the museums beside them charge for what is inside.

parks.name: Castle Park
parks.intro:
Kasteel Helmond has stood in the middle of this town for nearly seven hundred years, a moated brick castle that is now the town hall and museum. Until the middle of the twentieth century it sat inside a much larger landscape park; the 1921 sale of the estate began the park's disappearance, and these seven trees are what survived it.

The oldest is a pedunculate oak, planted between 1880 and 1890 while the castle was still a private house, four decades before that sale. Its neighbour is stranger than it looks: the national register files it as a European beech, but its own description says otherwise, that it is a Chinese beech, Fagus engleriana, grafted onto ordinary rootstock because the species will not seed itself in Dutch soil, and as far as anyone knows the oldest and thickest of its kind in the country.

The rest of the grounds fill in around them. A silver maple and a silver lime span the decades either side of the 1921 sale. Two horse chestnuts stand about fifty metres apart, planted a decade apart, for the conkers as much as anything. And a common holly, an odd formality for a shrub, grows exactly where the register itself says it cannot be seen from any path, the one tree here you will have to go looking for.

All seven stand on open castle grounds in the centre of Helmond, free to walk to any day of the year.

parks.name: Central Park
parks.intro:
Central Park's oldest tree is probably the black tupelo in the Ramble, at about 168 years. Probably, because a multi-trunked London plane near the Reservoir may date to 1862, when the Reservoir itself was dug, and neither tree comes with proof: the tupelo has the better paperwork, the plane has more trunks than any ageing rule of thumb can handle, and they disagree by only four years.

That the contest is this close says something about the ground. The park opened in 1858 on swamp, rock and scattered farms with no old trees at all, so everything standing today was planted, and its oldest survivors are a record of what the park's own gardeners chose rather than what nature left behind.

Two of the seven trees here are American elms from the Mall's Literary Walk, one of the last major stands of the species anywhere after Dutch elm disease took most of the country's street elms from the 1930s on. A third elm, gnarled and wide-canopied at the East 97th Street entrance, is old enough that nobody wrote down its planting year. Between them stand a small grove of Lebanon cedars planted for a family's grandchildren, and 35 Yoshino cherries whose planting predates the more famous gift Washington received the same year, 1912. All free, every day, dawn to dusk.

parks.name: The City Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: Queensland's oldest public garden opened in 1855, and Walter Hill, its first curator, spent the next three decades filling it with plants brought in from across the world; the results are still standing. Thirteen of the trees we map grow here: the tree that started Australia's whole macadamia industry, a banyan with the finest aerial-root structure of its species in the country, the tallest tree in the gardens at forty-five metres, and a fig said to descend from the tree the Buddha sat under. All are free to walk past, a few minutes apart on paths in the middle of Brisbane's CBD.

parks.name: City Park
parks.intro:
Two hundred and forty nine live oaks in this park are registered with the Live Oak Society, which is more than any other place on earth holds, and the three oldest of them stand on the same strip of high ground. The Old Grove runs between City Park Avenue and the lagoon that was once Bayou Metairie, and the bayou is the reason the trees are there: centuries of it overflowing dropped silt and lifted that ground about a metre above the rest of the park. When the levees failed in 2005 and most of City Park went under water, the Old Grove stayed dry. The Old-Growth Forest Network added it in 2018 as the first site in Louisiana.

The McDonogh Oak is the biggest of them, a trunk over eight metres round under a crown held up on wooden crutches, and the Anseman Oak a few hundred metres west is given the same seven-to-nine-hundred-year range by some accounts and more by others. The Dueling Oak is the survivor of a pair that men shot at each other under, and the Suicide Oak out on Victory Avenue carries the darkest name in the park for reasons the page explains.

A century old rather than nine, and worth the walk anyway: an oak on the east side of Big Lake with seven sets of wind chimes hanging in it, tuned to a pentatonic scale so the wind cannot play a wrong note. And inside the Botanical Garden, the Enrique Alferez Oak grew the most of any tree on the park's own historic tour between 1983 and 1999, and is draped in blue lights every December for Celebration in the Oaks. The park itself is free and open daily; the Botanical Garden charges a small separate admission, and the walk from the museum to the Old Grove is about twenty minutes.

parks.name: Dominion Arboretum
parks.intro:
Wikipedia dates the founding of the Dominion Arboretum to 1889, the oldest arboretum in Canada, part of the Central Experimental Farm that has worked this ground in the middle of Ottawa ever since. The National Capital Commission's own register carries a bitternut hickory here planted between 1886 and 1890, close enough to that founding date that nobody can say whether it went in with the Arboretum's first plantings or a season or two before them. At roughly 136 to 140 years old, it is the oldest documented tree on these grounds.

A jack pine planted in 1921 is the one with the most famous portrait: this is the species Tom Thomson made recognisable, the leaning Algonquin Park silhouette that became one of the best known images in Canadian art, and the Friends of the Central Experimental Farm stop at this specimen on their CelebriTrees walk. Its cones stay sealed with resin until a fire's heat opens them, a trait built for ground this one has never had to survive.

Three more widen the range. A dawn redwood, a species known from fossils before living ones turned up in China in the 1940s, grows in the Arboretum's northern section and drops its needles every autumn like a conifer pretending to be deciduous; the register gives no age and the Friends' own tour lists three dawn redwoods nearby, so treat the pin as approximate rather than a match to one exact trunk. A swamp white oak stands where botanists once doubted the species grew this far north at all, tagged by the register for rarity. And a rock elm, a nursery-raised specimen of one of only three elms native to Canada, is young by this map's standards at 45 to 60 years, but its wild population was hit by the same Dutch elm disease that stripped the arching elms off North American streets, and Quebec listed the species as threatened in 2005.

All five stand inside the Central Experimental Farm, a National Historic Site open dawn to dusk year-round, free to enter, with free parking on site.

parks.name: Fort Canning Park
parks.intro: Fort Canning Hill was the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura before it was a British fort or a public park, and the five heritage trees mapped on it now sit on ground that has been fought over, planted over and walked over for seven centuries. A rain tree spreads its canopy directly above the public stairway that carries walkers out onto Hill Street, so most people pass beneath it without looking up. A Madras thorn beside the Service Reservoir is the largest of its species on Singapore's whole heritage register, its girth measured twice, eleven years apart, and grown wider both times. A tamalan on Fort Green is one of the last survivors of an ornamental planting scheme laid out across the hill in the early 1900s, when the old fort grounds became a colonial pleasure garden; NParks' own register notes that few of its neighbours from that planting are still alive. A terap nasi grows beside the hill's 14th Century Walk of History with plank buttresses broad enough to make its age feel physical rather than just recorded. And an earpod tree, named in both English and Spanish for seed pods coiled like a human ear, stands between the old fort wall and the hotel that now shares the hill with it. All five are NParks-registered heritage trees, free to see, on park ground open around the clock.

parks.name: Fota Arboretum
parks.intro: Fota Island sits at the same latitude as Newfoundland, and the only reason its arboretum can grow a Canary Island date palm and a camphor tree from southern China outdoors is the Gulf Stream, which keeps this stretch of Cork Harbour close to frost-free. The Smith-Barry family began building the collection here in the 1820s on what had been ordinary farmland, and the national heritage tree survey's oldest find, a holm oak banded to 200 to 300 years, predates that start and would have already been standing when they began. The rest of the collection is younger and stranger: a Campbell's magnolia that covers itself in dinner-plate pink flowers for about ten days each late winter before it leafs at all; a Japanese cedar cultivar whose every needle grows in a tight curl, a Victorian nursery mutation nicknamed Granny's Ringlets; a New Zealand conifer with no true leaves, its flattened stem tissue notched enough to look like celery; and a coast redwood that in its native California would be the tallest tree species on Earth, here still a child of 150 to 200 years next to the two-thousand-year specimens back home. Free to visit, on the same island as Fota Wildlife Park.

parks.name: The Giardini Montanelli
parks.intro: Milan's first public park, laid out in 1784, and the trees in it have been measured more carefully than almost anywhere else in the city. Six of them are on the monumental register. The largest plane in Milan grows here, spreading sideways rather than up; a bald cypress that gardeners called a metasequoia for years until somebody checked the genus properly; and the widest of Milan's three Caucasian wingnuts, five and a half metres round. One plane has become a research subject in its own right, with the city counting what lives on it.

parks.name: The Giardino dei Semplici
parks.intro: Cosimo I de' Medici founded this garden in 1545 to grow medicinal plants, which makes it the third oldest botanical garden in the world and older than most of what surrounds it. The name means the garden of the simples, simples being the single-ingredient herbs a physician worked from before pharmacy existed. Seven of the trees we map grow inside its walls, and several are the kind of specimen a botanical garden accumulates precisely because somebody was paid to keep them alive for four hundred years.

parks.name: The Giardino Inglese
parks.intro: Maria Carolina of Austria wanted an English garden and got one of the first in Italy, which is why the trees here are strange. She commissioned it in 1786 at the top of the Reggia's enormous formal park, and the English gardener John Andrew Graefer filled it with species the country had barely seen: a camphor tree from Japan, a cork oak, a Douglas fir from the American northwest, a sweet osmanthus. Seven of them are on the register today. The oldest is a yew by the Bath of Venus that was carried in fully grown, which makes it older than the garden it stands in.

parks.name: The Giardino Pubblico
parks.intro:
Muzio de Tommasini was a serious botanist who happened also to be the podesta of Trieste, and when the city bought land from Benedictine nuns in 1854 after a plan to build a church and housing there fell through, he laid out the garden and planted its avenue of planes himself. Three hectares now hold roughly 320 large trees from five continents, arranged along paths lined with the bronze heads of Triestine writers, and Italo Svevo walked here often enough that the garden turns up in what he wrote.

Nine of the garden's planes carry Italy's monumental designation, from the 542-centimetre giant whose root plate the city dug free of suffocating paving to a sibling seventeen centimetres short of its title. A pair of horse chestnuts, identical to the centimetre at 3.35 metres, stands with a valonia oak and a third chestnut whose own measurements two different registers cannot agree on. The garden is free and open daily.

parks.name: Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam
parks.intro: The Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam has been growing rare plants on the same corner of the Plantage since 1638. A Turkish hazel planted in 1795, the country's oldest and thickest according to the Dutch tree foundation, flowers with pollen-shedding catkins every January while the rest of the garden sits bare. A few paths over, a Turner's oak keeps its leathery leaves through the whole Dutch winter, evergreen in a garden that otherwise goes bare. Both stand a few minutes' walk apart, on the one Hortus ticket. Three more of the garden's monumental trees, a corkscrewing catalpa, a shellbark hickory and a ginkgo, are fully researched but currently held off this list because they sit behind that same ticket alongside a third of Amsterdam's other trees; they return the day the balance of paid to free trees allows it.

parks.name: The Hortus Botanicus
parks.intro: Leiden's Hortus Botanicus was founded in 1590, and ten of the city's remarkable trees stand inside it. The tulip tree by professor Herman Boerhaave's name came from a Virginia seed a London apothecary posted across the Channel in October 1716, eleven days before it reached Leiden's soil. The zelkovas came further: Philipp Franz von Siebold, a physician stationed on the Dutch trading post at Deshima in the 1820s, sent home more Japanese plants than any European before him, and the Hortus holds the first zelkovas that ever left the country. A ginkgo planted in 1785 spent a century and a half producing nothing but the small catkins of a male tree, until gardeners grafted female branches onto it in 1935 so it would finally bear seed. A date-plum, which children call the Halloween tree, has holes in its trunk left by a maple that seeded itself inside the older tree's wood in the late 19th century. A horse chestnut at the garden's edge is the thickest of its kind recorded anywhere in the Netherlands, 5.8 metres round by the national monumental tree register's own measurement, its roots reaching almost to the water of the Witte Singel. And a catalpa leaning toward the canal is kept from going in by cables tied to another tree on this same list. The garden is open to the public with an admission charge.

parks.name: The Jardi Botanic
parks.intro: Valencia's university botanic garden moved to this walled plot off Carrer Quart in 1802, and thirteen of the city's monumental trees now stand inside it, more than any other single place in Valencia. The Kashmir cypress is Bhutan's national tree, kept alive around Buddhist temples for centuries before Western botany even named it. The Caucasian elm grows nothing like an elm, its trunk breaking early into a sheaf of near-vertical branches that reads more like a bundle than a canopy. A Turkish pine went straight up for thirty metres without leaning or forking once, while a silk floss tree, a southern live oak, a Hartwiss oak, a London plane and a river she-oak fill out a collection assembled from four continents. Most of these carry no recorded planting date: the garden's own register measures trunks and crowns but keeps no year, so age here is mostly an open question left for whoever can read a ring count. The garden charges a small admission fee and is open to the public.

parks.name: Finch Arboretum
parks.intro: John A. Finch Arboretum grew from land a pioneer family gave the city, and six of Spokane's most remarkable trees now stand within a few hundred metres of each other inside it. Daniel H. Dwight's own family provided part of the original ground, and a Hungarian linden planted in his name still grows there. The state's largest white willow is here too, started as somebody's garden tree before the ground became a public arboretum, growing beside two of the first dawn redwoods ever brought to North America, seed-grown after a stand once known only from fossils turned up alive in China in 1943. A Miyabe maple, modest by its own species but the largest recorded in Washington, a Norway spruce the city calls its second tallest, and a broad Mexican pinyon pine round out the six. The arboretum is free, open daily, and every one of these trees sits inside a single short walk.

parks.name: Kalopa State Recreation Area
parks.intro:
Almost none of Hawaii's native lowland forest is still standing, and about a hundred acres of it are here. That is the whole reason this park holds trees like these: they are what an old forest produces when nobody interferes with it, and every species on this page grows nowhere else on earth.

Six of the trees we map stand on the marked Kalopa Nature Trail, a loop of just over a kilometre. The largest is an ohi'a lehua, 4.39 metres round and about 26 metres tall, rated in excellent health when the state last measured it. Beside it are two kopiko 'ula that make no sense for their species, a slim coffee relative that rarely clears 13 metres: one is 3.26 metres round, and we have found no larger one recorded anywhere. The park is free and open from seven in the morning until eight at night.

parks.name: The Kontumazgarten
parks.intro:
Six trees on 1.7 hectares each carry their own legal protection here, which is a great deal of attention for one small park. Nuremberg's 2020 natural monument ordinance lists them as ND-6 through ND-11: a horse chestnut, two European beeches and three London planes, each with its own number, coordinate and species. Two of the planes stand about five metres apart and the law counts them separately, so a visitor looking for six trees will find what reads as five sights.

The name says what the ground was. Kontumaz is the old German word for quarantine, and this is where the city held arriving travellers and goods until it was satisfied they carried nothing worse than themselves. It is a lawn with a playground now. The two beeches are the only trees here that would have grown in Franconia without anybody's help. Free, open daily.

parks.name: The gardens of La Granja
parks.intro:
Lightning hit the tallest tree in these gardens in 1991 and it is still growing. La Reina is a giant sequoia, measured at 42.5 metres by the regional register in 2006 and given 46 by Patrimonio Nacional now, which is what a healthy sequoia does with twenty years.

Five of the trees we map stand in the royal gardens, and four of them are foreign conifers planted as fashions arrived: the sequoias and a Douglas fir from the Pacific northwest, a cedar of Lebanon that reached western Europe around 1640 and is the one species Philip V's gardeners could in principle have known when they began the layout in the 1720s. The exception is a Spanish fir from 700 kilometres south, a tree that grows wild in three patches of mountain behind Ronda and nowhere else in Europe. The gardens are open to visitors; the palace is a separate ticket and the fountains run only on set days.

parks.name: Leijpark
parks.intro:
Leijpark's oldest trees were planted by men who needed the wages. Leonard Springer, the most sought-after garden architect in the Netherlands, drew the 30-hectare park in 1919, his last large design, and then nothing happened for fifteen years while the land was assembled. It was finally built between 1934 and 1939 as a work relief project in the depths of the Depression, in the English landscape manner along the little river Leij that gives it its name. A silver maple, the first tree in the park to do anything after winter, and a young pedunculate oak that will outlast every other tree here by centuries both went in with that original planting.

Tucked in the park's far northeast corner, in ground still locally called the Kloosterparkbos, stand three older trees the wider design absorbed rather than planted: an oak, a lime and a large-leaved holly, all named for a convent, home to the Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel from 1908, whose garden this land used to be before it was redeveloped and folded into Springer's park. The convent is gone; the trio it left behind, roughly 120 years old, makes an easy five-minute extension to the walk. All of it is free, open daily, no ticket.

parks.name: Margaret Island
parks.intro:
Three of these trees are older than the park they stand in. Margaret Island was laid out as a landscape park under Archduke Joseph in the nineteenth century, and a pedunculate oak, a yew and a black walnut on the higher ground are older than that work: remnants of the oak, ash and elm floodplain forest that covered the island before anybody designed anything.

The fourth is the one he planted himself. Joseph put a plane tree in the ground here in 1823, two years before the Hungarian Academy of Sciences was founded across the water, and the near-coincidence of dates is where its modern name comes from. The ages are FŐKERT's, from the city parks company's own 2020 dendrological survey of the island. All five stand on open public parkland, free, and the island is a twenty-minute walk end to end.

parks.name: Nara Park
parks.intro:
The oldest dated tree in Nara Park is a black pine at the corner of the block that holds Kofuku-ji's National Treasure Hall, about two hundred and fifty years old and three and a half metres round. Gardeners of the Edo period planted black pines through the park for no reason except that they looked right, and this one outgrew all the others. Flying squirrels still work its cone crop at night, stripping the seeds and leaving the cores scattered on the path beneath it in a shape locals compare to fried prawns.

Two more trees carry no recorded age but stand on ground that dates them anyway. A soapberry beside the approach to Kasuga Taisha has a bamboo growing up through its hollow trunk and out of the crown, so what looks like one tree is actually two, a plant nurses have described as a mother holding a child. Its black seeds strung prayer beads and filled the shuttlecocks of the New Year game hanetsuki. A chinaberry stands where Todai-ji's seven-storey east pagoda once rose above the park before it burned for the last time, planted, by tradition, because the species was believed to keep evil from ground where the dead were remembered.

The youngest tree here is also the one people mistake for a single giant: three camphors planted in 1908 on the spot where Emperor Meiji watched army manoeuvres have grown together into one unbroken dome, nearly five metres round at the thickest trunk and reaching twenty-six metres up. The park's deer graze right to the fence around them. A fifth tree, broad-canopied and mature beside a pond and a wooden rest pavilion somewhere between Todai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, arrived as a reader's photograph rather than a known record, and neither its species nor its exact pond has been settled yet. If you know the spot, tell us; that is how the fifth tree gets its name.

parks.name: The National Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: The Dublin Society founded the National Botanic Gardens at Glasnevin in 1795 to teach scientific agriculture, and the collecting habit that started then never stopped. A 2009 heritage survey by the Tree Council of Ireland recorded six of these seven trees as Exceptional Specimen Trees, gathered from three continents across two centuries of curators, all within 200 metres of each other: a dawn redwood grown from the seed that ended the species' presumed extinction in China, an Atlas cedar from a mountain range now losing its wild population to drought, a Caucasian elm so admired a County Offaly nurseryman propagated cuttings from it and sold the result as its own named cultivar, and a bald cypress built for Louisiana swampland doing its best in an Irish flower bed. The seventh and oldest, a formal double avenue of yew, carries the garden's separate Named Trees designation and is said, by tradition rather than record, to have been planted in memory of the essayist Joseph Addison before the gardens themselves existed. Entry is free, every day except Christmas Day, and all seven specimens sit an easy afternoon's walk from each other.

parks.name: The National Mall
parks.intro:
The Park Service keeps a register of trees that stood through documented history, and four of them are within a twenty minute walk of each other here. Each is on that list for a different reason.

The Jefferson Elm is the consequential one. It went into the ground around 1935 as one of roughly 600 American elms framing the central green, Dutch elm disease killed most of the rest over the next forty years, and this one did not die. Cuttings went to nurseries in 2005 as the 'Jefferson' cultivar, so American elms are going back into streets across the country on the strength of one tree beside Jefferson Drive.

The white mulberry on the Washington Monument grounds is the other kind of survivor. Days of rain loosened the ground under it in May 2019 and it went over, and instead of cutting it up the Park Service lifted it ten degrees and built it a steel crutch. It has been standing nearly horizontal ever since. Two hundred metres away a pair of catalpas flanks the Survey Lodge, a small building made of marble left over from the monument itself, and they were in the ground by 1902.

The fourth belongs to the Smithsonian rather than the Park Service, at the 9th Street end: an American elm five and a half metres round, accession number 1 in their tree collection, older than the museum behind it. All four are free, outdoors and unrestricted, and it is about a kilometre and a half from the first to the last.

parks.name: The Oosterplantsoen
parks.intro:
Two planes in this park are the same species and the older one is in worse shape, which comes down to where somebody put them. The plane on the Pakhuisstraat went in around 1870 and the town's register notes its base being squeezed by the pavement; the one a couple of hundred metres behind the aviary went in around 1890, out of the way of the street, and the register calls it a perfect tree. Both are over four metres round.

Seven of the trees we map stand here, along the Oosterpoortsgracht and around the Veliusbrug, most of them planted between 1860 and 1910 when the town laid out the strip. Several carry recorded problems, fungal infections at the root collar on two silver maples among them, which the register logs and the town keeps watching. Hoorn signposts its own tree route through the park. It is free and open daily.

parks.name: Orto Botanico di Lucca
parks.intro: Lucca's botanical garden was founded in 1820 by Maria Luisa di Borbone, Duchess of Lucca, and its early directors recorded exact planting dates for several of these trees. A cedar of Lebanon and a Corsican pine went in together in 1822; a redwood arrived around 1850, one of the first raised in Europe; a ginkgo, felled by lightning, regrew as three trunks from one root. By the pond, a pair of bald cypresses throw up woody knees from the water and turn rust orange each autumn, the garden's only conifer that behaves like a deciduous tree. Nearby, a seven-metre Balearic box grows to a size the species rarely reaches outside its native islands, next to the garden's youngest registered tree, a silver lime planted around 1900, and a fastigiate yew whose thickness belies how slowly the species grows. The garden charges standard admission.

parks.name: The Orto Botanico di Padova
parks.intro: The University of Padua founded this garden in 1545 to teach medical students which plants their patients were actually being given, the first botanical garden anywhere attached to a university and the model every later one copied. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1997, citing its continuous four-and-a-half centuries of scientific use rather than its age alone. Seven of the trees we map grow inside its circular walls, among them a dwarf palm Goethe wrote about, a ginkgo grafted to bear both pollen and fruit from one trunk, and Italy's first Himalayan cedar. Admission is a paid ticket, and worth it.

parks.name: The Real Orto Botanico
parks.intro: Founded by Napoleonic decree in 1807 and planted with things Naples had never seen, which is why most of these trees come from other continents. The widest trunk on Naples' entire national register stands here, a silk floss tree whose bulging green trunk looks less like timber than like something inflated. Beside it grows a Chilean wine palm, a species nearly drunk out of existence because its trunk is full of sweet sap that was tapped for wine. The exception is the ginkgo, which is not a novelty from far away but a survivor from far back.

parks.name: The Parc de la Ciutadella
parks.intro: This park is a fortress the city pulled down. The citadel that gave it its name was built to hold Barcelona after 1714, demolished in the 1870s, and the ground rebuilt as the city's first public park for the Universal Exposition of 1888, which is why almost everything old here dates from one fifteen year window. A Mexican white oak went in around 1887 and is the only one of its kind alive in Catalonia. A river she-oak followed beside the Cascada around 1894, its drooping grey green needles actually jointed twigs. A silk tree has flowered every July since about 1896, well past the age its species normally reaches. The stoutest black locust in Barcelona is here, 4.3 metres around on twelve metres of tree, and so is a plane nobody has ever cut back to knuckles, which is simply what the species does when left alone.

parks.name: The Parc d'Egmont
parks.intro: Brussels started its official inventory of remarkable trees in this park, with a squat evergreen oak that most people walk past. The Parc d'Egmont is small, hidden behind the shops of the Avenue Louise, and holds sixteen of the trees we map within a couple of minutes of each other, which makes it one of the densest pockets on the site. Among them is a ginkgo that is the seventh thickest recorded anywhere in the region and is being slowly damaged by the people who like it, and a tulip tree formally adopted by an art institute a few streets away.

parks.name: The Miramare park
parks.intro:
The man who planted these trees was shot by a firing squad in Mexico eleven years later. Archduke Maximilian of Habsburg began the Miramare park in the spring of 1856 on a limestone headland with almost no soil on it, and he ran the whole thing as an experiment: he wanted to know which foreign species would hold on to bare Adriatic rock. The soil was carted in.

The answer is still standing. Twelve of the trees we map grow here. A third of them are Californian: two coast redwoods over four metres round, a Monterey cypress of the same girth, and a ghost pine whose needles sit so thinly on the branch that you can see the sky through its crown. Six Aleppo pines, all individually registered as monumental, share the grounds with a holm oak whose 5.2 metre trunk two official surveys cannot agree is one stem or three. The park is free and open daily. Only the castle charges admission.

parks.name: The Parco del Valentino
parks.intro: Turin's oldest tree and Turin's tallest tree both stand in this park, a few hundred metres apart along the Po. The oldest is an oak behind the Castello del Valentino, past two hundred years by the regional register and the exception in a city where every other tree that old is a plane. The tallest is a plane by the Fontana dei Dodici Mesi at forty metres, and nothing in Turin beats it. A third plane, six metres round, is the widest trunk in the park, and a hackberry stands alone on open grass, which is why its crown is so even.

parks.name: Park Oliwski
parks.intro:
Park Oliwski's six protected trees cluster in the dendrological garden the park was laid out around, plus one elm by the pond, and between them they cover a stranger range of species than a Baltic park has any business holding. A cucumber tree magnolia from the forests of eastern North America has reached 19 metres and a trunk 271 centimetres round, well past two metres of girth, which the city's own survey of protected trees singles out as one of the collection's standouts. A katsura from Japan, a species no European garden could plant before 1865, has split into three trunks and carries a smell of burnt sugar through its leaves every October, strong enough that people look around for a bakery. A western red cedar from the Pacific coast of North America stands 23 metres tall in a group registered as a single object alongside two yews and a Nootka cypress.

The park's newest and oldest designations sit at opposite ends of the register. A pair of field maples was entered under one record on 26 February 2026, the most recent addition to Gdansk's roll of protected trees, named for the botanist Hugo Conwentz without any surviving explanation of why. The elm by the pond has been protected since 1 July 1988, its trunk 420 centimetres round, its Polish designation naming not the tree but the flowering ivy climbing it, ivy old enough to have reached the light it needs to bloom. Dutch elm disease killed most of the continent's big elms; this one, and the ivy on it, did not go.

Most of these trees carry no planting date, only a girth and a registration number from 15 March 1992 or thereabouts. What is documented is precise measurement without a birthday, which the pages say plainly rather than guessing one.

parks.name: Park Sonsbeek
parks.intro:
Park Sonsbeek's oldest claim stands beside a monument to a man who never saw it planted: a pedunculate oak dated to somewhere between 1750 and 1800, growing next to the 1931 memorial to physicist Hendrik Lorentz. The national register that puts an age on it is more taken with the shape than the years.

Three more pedunculate oaks share the park with it, and no two came by their trouble the same way. Two stand together at the edge of the Sonsbeek meadow, thick and tall enough that the register flags both for condition rather than just girth. A third grows alone in a grazed field where the corner meets Sonsbeekweg, and the electric fencing kept up for the livestock has also kept surveyors from getting a tape around it properly for years. A fourth, by the old Witte Watermolen, carries no name and no plaque, only a regular stop on the park ranger's own guided walk each Open Monument Day.

The other two trees break the pattern. A yew planted around 1850 has grown a waist over three metres round, genuinely rare for the species in the Netherlands. A copper beech, its purple leaves a colour mutation gardeners have propagated for centuries rather than a species of its own, was planted between the Sonsbeek villa and its pond sometime in the 1830s. All eight stand on open parkland, free to walk to any day of the year.

parks.name: The Parque de María Luisa
parks.intro:
Three of the biggest trees Seville has ever measured stand in this one park. The city's 2022 survey of its singular trees puts a Norfolk Island pine near the Torre Norte at 44 metres, second tallest in Seville; a bald cypress over the duck island at 35.7 metres, the tallest deciduous conifer it found anywhere; and a plane on the Avenida de Bécquer at 4.70 metres round, the widest of its kind in the catalogue.

Ten of the trees we map are here, spread across a park of glorietas and artificial hills where finding them takes an afternoon rather than a lap. One of them came first and the monument came later: the bald cypress at the centre of the Glorieta de Bécquer was already growing when the city built a marble monument to the poet around it in 1911. Entry is free.

parks.name: The Parque del Retiro
parks.intro: The Retiro was a royal private garden for two hundred years before Madrid was let in, and that is why its trees are old. Philip IV's court laid it out in the 1630s as the grounds of a palace that has since vanished, leaving the planting behind; the park only became public in 1868. Nine of the trees we map stand inside it, and they are spread wide enough that finding them is a proper afternoon rather than a lap of the pond. The oldest is a Montezuma cypress near the Paseo de Mexico, a species from central Mexico that arrived in Spain with the empire and outlived it.

parks.name: The Prinsentuin
parks.intro: Leeuwarden's Prinsentuin was laid out between 1822 and 1824 on the site of the city's former fortifications, making it close to the oldest public park in the Netherlands, and five of its oldest trees are old enough to remember that opening. Its horse chestnut, banded by the national monumental tree register to 1820 and 1830, is almost exactly as old as the park itself. A European beech stands by the Pier Pander Temple, a small classical building put up in 1924 to hold the work of the Frisian sculptor born in 1864 to a rag merchant's family and remembered here for the talent that got him out of it. A second beech grows behind Tresoar, the Frisian historical and literary archive, keeping company with a language that has spent centuries arguing over its own literature. An ash by the park's tea house carries a crown the register itself calls one-sided, the shape a tree gets when the trees standing next to it crowd out the light on one side and not the other. And a Canadian poplar nearby has a trunk so deeply grooved and studded with fist and head sized burrs that it reads more like rock than wood. All five stand in a park that has never charged admission.

parks.name: The Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens
parks.intro: Five of the six trees mapped here came from somewhere else, and the sixth is Australian without being Tasmanian. A Douglas fir out of the Pacific Northwest went into the ground in 1894, seven years before the Australian colonies federated, and measured 30 metres when the National Trust looked at it in 2014. Two giant sequoias planted together in 1879 still mark the entrance drive. A Queensland kauri, a rainforest tree from the warm wet coast far to the north, reaches 39 metres here at 42 degrees south and is listed on Hobart's register under four headings at once, where most trees carry one. A chir pine from the dry Himalayan foothills droops needles thirty centimetres long. The spotted gum is the local one, and even it grows wild in New South Wales rather than on this island.

parks.name: The Schlosspark
parks.intro:
Six trees in this park are worth stopping for, and the thickest is the one nobody has named. It is a plane about ten metres east of the second wingnut, 5.66 metres round, wider than the famous cedars beside the palace. It carries no plaque and appears in no register. It turned up in a dendrologist's survey of the park in 2021 and that is the whole of its paper trail.

The cedars are the pair everyone comes for, and they earn it. Sixteen seedlings arrived from Kew through Princess Elizabeth of Great Britain, who married Landgrave Friedrich VI Joseph in 1818 and kept her English botanical contacts; two went into the ground in front of the royal wing in 1822 and both still stand there. The larger runs 6.40 metres round and 21 metres tall, and by 2011 its crown measured more than 35 metres from east to west, so the tree is considerably wider than it is high.

Three big pedunculate oaks stand in the park: 5.39 metres round at the bridge, 4.94 by the lake, and the Schöne Eiche near the gate to the Altstadt, about five metres round and, by the estimate of a reader who knows the park trunk by trunk, some 36 metres tall. He named it for its crown, whole and vigorous without the dead limbs most old oaks carry. None of the three is dated or labelled. The fastest grower is the dawn redwood at the southern pond: about seventy years old, already 5.80 metres round and 28 metres tall, which is more girth than the cedar has managed in two centuries.

The ground has been garden since at least 1441, was laid out as a baroque garden from 1680 and remade as an English landscape park from the later eighteenth century, which is the style it still wears: grass, water, and single large trees given room. It is a Hessian state park, so walking through it costs nothing and passes no gate; the palace buildings themselves are ticketed.

parks.name: The Schlosspark Nymphenburg
parks.intro: Munich protects trees by law here for reasons written down in a city ordinance, and two of these five are protected for being odd rather than big. A large-leaved lime by the Badenburger See is listed as bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, which is an unusually honest thing for a legal document to say. There is also a weeping beech protected partly because people are fond of it, an oak in the Dorfchen, the part of a royal garden built to look undesigned, and a fern-leaved beech of a form that did not exist anywhere before about 1804.

parks.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: Singapore's Botanic Gardens opened in 1859 and earned a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2015, not for any single specimen but for grounds that have kept unusually good paperwork on the trees growing in them. A sausage tree arrived from Honolulu on 13 May 1931 and went into the ground that October, one of dozens of tropical trials from an era when a plant's usefulness decided its future. A cannon ball tree grew from a seed the assistant director E.J.H. Corner grabbed during a rushed eight-hour stop at the botanic garden in Peradeniya, Ceylon, the same year. A baobab, moved once in 1996 and only about forty years old, already carries five metres of girth, a fraction of the age a species that can pass a thousand years usually needs for that. A giant strangler fig by Swan Lake is registered as a Burmese banyan, though a 2024 study argues it is something else entirely, propagated here from cuttings for more than 150 years. A saga tree planted in the 1880s to smother weed grass now sits in the National Heritage Board's own art collection, photographed for a 2013 work mapping the island's saga trees. Two nutmeg trees near the old Economic Garden are what is left of the spice boom that gave Orchard Road its name. They all stand on garden ground, open daily and free to enter.

parks.name: Villa Borghese
parks.intro: Cardinal Scipione Borghese built this park in the early 1600s as a showcase for his art collection, and his gardener planted the trees to match: oriental planes brought in as a novelty, arranged in a valley that still carries their name. Adonis, the oldest of them, has stood here for over four centuries and outlived the villa's original owner by nearly as long. A cedar leans over the lake a few minutes' walk away, and past the boating lake stands what one conservation group calls the last survivor of the eighteen cypresses planted around Piazza di Siena in 1789, the arena that still hosts Rome's international horse show every year. Deeper into the park's holm oak wood, behind the museum that now holds a de Chirico and Warhol collection, a pair of hackberries with a four-metre girth waits on the official monumental status that roughly thirty of the park's other old trees are still queuing for.

parks.name: Villapark
parks.intro:
Villapark is not a park in the usual sense. It is a garden suburb, laid out from 1907 to house Philips executives, and its oldest trees stand on ordinary street verges rather than behind a gate. Whoever planted them reached past the default lime and plane for a small, deliberate collection: this is where you find a Caucasian wingnut on a residential street, its winged seed pods hanging in strings up to half a metre long by late summer, a species most visitors will never have seen anywhere else.

A pin oak on Prinsenhof carries the tightest date of the group, the national monumental tree register and the city's own separate street-tree survey landing within four metres and ten years of each other on 1890 to 1900, a rare case of two independent records agreeing this closely. Its neighbour a few doors down is a double-flowered horse chestnut, named specifically as a chosen cultivar in the municipality's own survey rather than whatever the nursery had spare that year. A second horse chestnut, the ordinary kind, stands 250 metres away on Palingstraat, easy to mistake for the first if you do not know there are two.

A southern catalpa on Julianastraat, the cigar tree with its heart-shaped leaves and orchid-like summer flowers, sits on one source rather than two: the register names it, the city's own inventory does not. It stands anyway, flagged honestly rather than left out.

All five grow on public verges and street corners, free to walk past any day, a five-minute loop through a district still recognisable as the plan that built it.

parks.name: Vosseparkje
parks.intro: Vosseparkje, officially Westerpark, exists because Leeuwarden needed a reservoir more than it needed a park. Garden architect Gerrit Vlaskamp landscaped the grounds around the city's drinking-water works in 1872, and the park he drew was redesigned once more in 1926, by which point most of its oldest trees were already decades in the ground. Seven of them sit on the Dutch national monument register today, all inside a few minutes' walk of each other. A Caucasian wingnut from the Caspian forests carries a trunk over a metre round and a scar from a 1987 ice storm. A black locust planted in 1924 has spent a century leaning and is now held up by a prop. Two feather elms of the same narrow cultivar stand at opposite ends of the park, told apart by which one is nearer the pond, and an oak by the south-east entrance has stumped the register itself: its own entry reads Caucasian or Persian oak, undecided, and nobody has settled which. Free, open, no ticket.

parks.name: Wilhelminapark
parks.intro: Leonard Springer laid out the Wilhelminapark in 1894, and its oldest tree already stood on that ground for thirty years before he arrived: a silver lime from the 1860s, its leaves felted silver underneath, planted near what is now a stone bench positioned to sit beneath it. Springer's own park brought the rest, all dated by the Dutch national monument register to the 1890s: a weeping beech at the pond's western edge whose lowest branches root back into the soil, a Caucasian wingnut on the Vijverstraat corner that strings its seeds in half-metre chains, and a plain green beech along Paul Withausenweg standing quietly among its more colourful, copper and weeping cousins. The fifth tree breaks from the register's dating entirely: a catalpa leaning so far out over the pond that the municipality now props its lowest limbs on columns, its age inferred from the park's own founding rather than any planting record. All five stand within a few minutes' walk of each other, free and open daily.

parks.name: Wilhelminapark
parks.intro: Leonard Springer drew the Wilhelminapark in the 1890s and opened it to the public in May 1898, and part of what makes it worth a visit is that he built around ground that already had trees on it rather than a blank field. Tilburg's oldest elm, on the Dutch national monument register, was standing here before Springer arrived, and a Canadian poplar nearby is older still, from a planting band of 1860 to 1870, decades before the park existed. Springer's own planting survives too: a weeping silver lime he put in himself in 1898, dated to the year in the register's own note, and a flowering ash from the northwest corner that the register admits you can barely see. The fifth tree breaks the pattern entirely. A Pontic oak from the 1970s, a species found wild only in one pocket of northeast Turkey and the Caucasus, is protected not for its age but for what it is, a rarity the register lists under a single word: dendrological. All five stand within a few minutes of each other, free and open daily.

parks.name: The York Museum Gardens
parks.intro: Ten acres of botanical garden laid over the ruins of a wrecked abbey, which is a strange thing to walk through and an excellent thing for trees. The Yorkshire Philosophical Society made these gardens in the 1830s around the remains of St Mary's Abbey, dissolved by Henry VIII three centuries earlier, and planted them as a scientific collection rather than a lawn. Six of the trees we map stand here, all within a few minutes of each other, which makes this the tightest cluster in the city and one of the tightest anywhere on the site.

parks.name: Zuiderpark
parks.intro:
The five oldest trees in Zuiderpark stand on an ordinary residential corner because they used to be a classroom. Between 1953 and 1967, evening students training as horticulturists and florists were examined here, on their feet, on the Latin and Dutch names of the trees around them, along a route locals nicknamed the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, for how it felt to be quizzed in front of an instructor. The trees they were tested on still ring the site of the municipal nursery that trained them.

A Caucasian wingnut misnamed 'Japanese' in its own register entry. An American yellowwood whose cut wood runs bright yellow. A pecan, a species that belongs to the warm river valleys of the American south, growing in Brabant since the 1950s. A Transcaucasian birch kept in its rare single-trunked tree form rather than the shrub shape the species usually takes. A golden beech that never really turns green at all. None of them are old by this project's usual standard, all roughly seventy years, and each one's only record is a single national register entry with no independent account. Their case for a page rests on what they were planted to do: give a generation of students something unfamiliar to learn. The school moved on in 1967. The trees, and the lesson, are still free to walk past.

countries.name: Australia
countries.intro: Australia's old trees keep two different kinds of time. Melbourne's elms have grown to a size and age Europe lost, because Dutch elm disease never crossed the water; its Osage orange on Yarra Boulevard is dated to the 1860s, among the oldest plantings the site maps here. Hobart's Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, founded in 1818 and the country's second-oldest, holds a Douglas fir older than Australian Federation itself, planted in 1894, alongside dawn redwoods of a species known only from fossils until a living stand was found in China in 1941. Brisbane's City Botanic Gardens, laid out from 1855, grew the tree that started the country's entire macadamia industry, dated from trials beginning 1858. Nothing mapped here is ancient by European or Japanese standards; almost everything is a nineteenth-century planting that got lucky with a climate and a curator who tried something unusual.

countries.name: Austria
countries.intro: Vienna keeps a tree register detailed enough to argue with itself. The oldest plane in front of the City Hall is dated 1783 by tradition and 1876 in the city's own records, ninety years apart with no way from here to settle it. The pagoda tree in the Stadtpark is on file as planted in 1860, in a park that did not open until August 1862. The friction is worth it: the register holds nearly nine hundred trees in the eighth district alone, which is why a girth or a planting year exists here where most cities have neither. Vienna also has one of the strangest trees on this site, a ginkgo at Schönbrunn carrying a grafted female branch, so a single tree is both sexes at once. Eighty-four trees are mapped so far, across Vienna, Graz, Salzburg, the lakeside cluster of protected yews around Hallstatt, and three single-tree destinations, a yew at Gutau, a mountain maple at Ramsau am Dachstein, and a disputed thousand-year oak at Bad Blumau.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.intro: Belgium keeps a national champion for each species, and one small Antwerp park hemmed in by three streets holds two of them: the thickest black locust recorded in the country at 4.10 metres, and a black mulberry at 1.28 metres, which is what a record looks like for a tree that never grows stout. Brussels runs an inventory of its own, and the first entry in it was a squat evergreen oak in the Parc d'Egmont that most people walk straight past. Six of the trees mapped here stand in that one park, within a couple of minutes of each other. The largest tree in Brussels by girth is not European at all: a giant sequoia in the Parc de Woluwe, measured at 8.66 metres around in 2017. 16 cities so far, 75 trees.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.intro: Brazil's most famous tree by international record is not its oldest. The Cajueiro de Pirangi, a single cashew whose branches root wherever they touch the ground, has spread across roughly 8,500 square metres near Natal and held the Guinness record for the largest cashew tree since 1994, at the modest age of about 138. The genuinely old trees keep quieter company: O Patriarca, a jequitiba-rosa in the cerrado of Vassununga State Park, is called the country's oldest by a press that cannot agree whether that means 600 years or more than 3,000. Rio de Janeiro supplies the range in between, a sumauma linked to Tom Jobim, a fig tree with a disputed two centuries behind it, a baobab that arrived on ships from Africa long before anyone thought to write its age down. Four cities mapped so far, nine trees, from a single record-holding cashew to a rainforest giant nobody can date.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.intro: Bulgaria's oldest tree is not its most impressive one to look at anymore. A 1982 core sample counted 1,637 rings in the Granit Oak, dating its germination to around 345 and giving Bulgaria a tree age nobody has to guess at, but a 1969 storm and falling groundwater have since reduced it to a single living branch. Higher up, in Pirin National Park above Bansko, Baikushev's Pine carries a gentler kind of age claim: tradition holds it was already standing when Khan Asparuh founded the First Bulgarian Empire around 681, a repeated figure of about 1,300 years rather than a measured one. Sofia supplies the political history in between, a mulberry linked to national hero Vasil Levski, an oak named for the poet Pencho Slaveykov, a spruce planted for Ivan Vazov. Four cities mapped so far, seven trees, from a dying record-holder to a living tradition.

countries.name: Canada
countries.intro: Canada's mapped trees keep circling one epidemic. Dutch elm disease killed roughly 22,000 of Montreal's American elms, and the Last Elm of Mont-Royal is one of the few left, a self-seeded survivor growing away from the streets where the disease moved fastest. Quebec City's Plains of Abraham lost most of its mature elms the same way and still keeps about 750 of them, monitored tree by tree against the fungus a century on, alongside wych elms, a European species growing beside the American ones. Toronto took a different route: in 2022 the city named an official tree for the first time, a 220-year-old red oak in Kew Gardens with a trunk 5.3 metres round. Montreal also holds a honey locust dated from a death recorded on the gravestone beside it, and a Japanese yew that grew fifteen metres wide instead of tall.

countries.name: China
countries.intro: China's oldest trees cluster around two kinds of ground: imperial temples and religious mountains. Beijing graded its ancient trees by class under the Qing and named ten "ancient tree kings" in 2018, five of which stand here, among them cypresses planted for state altars and a ginkgo that queues photographers every November. Further west, on the Tibetan plateau's edge, Bon tradition holds a giant cypress outside Nyingchi as the life tree of the religion's own founder, at up to 3,200 years the oldest tree this site maps anywhere. A ginkgo at Shaolin Temple carries a monks-training legend in the holes through its trunk, and a banyan on the Jinbao River near Yangshuo was a film location decades before anyone measured its age. Hong Kong's banyans are civic rather than sacred, rooted into a colonial trading port's walls and stairs.

countries.name: Croatia
countries.intro: Croatia's classified trees cluster around two very different kinds of site. Trsteno's arboretum on the coast near Dubrovnik still grows two Oriental planes a sea captain is said to have carried home from Constantinople five centuries ago, trunks over five metres round, alongside a run of 19th-century plantings, a ginkgo, a cedar of Lebanon, a yew, each with a planting date recorded to the year rather than estimated from growth rings. Inland, a single lime at Gornja Stubica marks a different history: tradition holds that Matija Gubec gathered his followers under its canopy in January 1573 before leading the Croatian-Slovene Peasant Revolt, an uprising that ended in his execution and has stayed central to Croatian memory since. Split's old town keeps its own smaller cluster, a mulberry, a cypress and a walnut, all a little over a century old.

countries.name: Czech Republic
countries.intro: The thickest protected tree in Prague measures seven and a half metres around, and the story everyone tells about it, that Beethoven sat beneath it, is almost certainly false. The city's register says as much rather than repeating it, which sets the tone for the rest. Prague dates its trees in ranges and admits where two records disagree by eighty years, as they do for the ginkgo in Stromovka. Brno keeps its own list: the Bystrc Lime, past 400 years old, survived a 1933 fire when a neighbour tried to smoke a marten out of its hollow trunk by setting it alight. Cesky Krumlov's oldest tree turns the usual pattern round: it is the free one, a village-square lime older than the paid monastery lindens nearby. Beyond the three cities, twenty single-tree villages carry the country's national Tree of the Year winners and its stranger stories: Teleci's hollow lime a person can stand inside, Rimov's pilgrimage linden that once held 51 people inside its trunk at once, an oak near Lukavice its own estate once tried to kill by stripping the soil from its roots, a beech at a mountain border crossing that is not the famous tree it replaced, a pine on a reservoir island near Vir that Europe voted its 2020 tree of the year, an oak in Viska that held back a flash flood in 2010, and the pear tree near Mrakotin that a folk song is named for. Twenty-four places, 66 trees mapped so far.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.intro: Copenhagen's remarkable trees come with tape measurements, which is rarer than it should be. The Danish dendrological society has surveyed them one by one and filed them under working names: a beech in Frederiksberg Have is registered as Bøgen ved Bådfarten, the beech by the boat trip, which makes it the easiest tree in the city to find. A honey locust has been on record since a gardening magazine featured it in 1941. Assistens cemetery holds five of the sixteen mapped here, and the thickest tree inside its walls is a sycamore, the least exotic species in it. The oldest is Skovfogedegen, a hollow oak 11 km north of the city at the edge of the royal deer park, which three Danish sources date to around the year 1200. The country's most famous oak is not in either city: Kongeegen stands propped and hollow in Jaegerspris Nordskov, the last of three named oaks in that wood, with Storkeegen dead in 1980 and Snoegen in 1991. Two single trees have their own places too: Ambrosius-egen on Tåsinge, redated from 700 to roughly 400 years by a 1997 core sample, and Svalebøgen in Gjerrild, a fused beech failing since a trunk came down in 2022. Twenty-six trees mapped so far, across five places.

countries.name: Estonia
countries.intro: Estonia put a tree on its money. The Tamme-Lauri Oak in Urvaste, 8.31 metres round at chest height and dated by a 1998 ring study to 1326, was printed on the back of the old 10 kroon note, and it is the country's thickest tree. The largest by volume is not an oak at all: the King's Pine in Järvselja, over 33 metres tall. Most of what you can walk to is in Tallinn, where the stories are small ones: a ginkgo that stopped a Soviet grandstand, an oak that moved a coastal road, and lindens planted in 1883 to mark two centuries of one family at one address. Tallinn's thickest, the Tammesalu Oak, was already sizeable when Peter the Great bought its land in 1714. Four places mapped so far, twelve trees, from a banknote oak in the south to a ginkgo on a city corner.

countries.name: Finland
countries.intro: This far north, cold winters and thin, rocky soil slow a tree down, so Finland's list runs on rarity more than raw age. Helsinki only became the capital in 1812 and most of its ten protected trees are Finnish size records, a thickest willow, a thickest park lime, rather than genuine veterans. Turku's Kalm's Oak earns its place differently: planted around 1750 in a garden the Great Fire of 1827 burned to the ground around it, and still called the city's oldest tree. Outside both cities stands Paavola's Oak on Lohjansaari, documented by the photographer I.K. Inha over a century ago and repeatedly called the most beautiful tree in the country since long before anyone here was searching the internet for it. Twelve trees mapped so far, across Helsinki, Turku and Lohja.

countries.name: France
countries.intro: France's oldest tree has a birth certificate rather than an estimate. The Robinier of Square Rene-Viviani in Paris was planted in 1601 by Jean Robin, herbalist to Henri IV, from seed the naturalist John Tradescant sent from the Appalachians, before the Mayflower sailed and before the genus that now carries Robin's name even existed. That precision runs through France's other oldest trees, most raised from seed by royal gardeners and university botanists rather than found growing wild: a Cedar of Lebanon that legend says crossed the Channel tucked inside a botanist's hat, a plane tree named for the naturalist Buffon who ran the garden that raised it.
