Seven cities carry that botanical lineage, Paris alongside Lyon's, Nice's, Bordeaux's, Strasbourg's, Toulouse's and Rouen's own plantings. The rest of the map is single-tree destinations of a different kind: a Norman oak with two working chapels built into its hollow trunk, a Breton oak on the edge of Broceliande, a hollow Calvados yew wide enough to hold thirty people, an oak in Ille-et-Vilaine covered in devotional offerings since 1792, a Weppes lime cited to a 1490 deed that outlasted a chateau and a world war, a solitary Lot-et-Garonne oak that survived a 2022 trunk fissure the year after being named the country's Tree of the Year. French ancient trees tend to come with an actual planting year rather than a growth-ring guess, because someone with a reputation to protect wrote the date down. 35 places mapped so far, 125 trees.

countries.name: Germany
countries.intro: Germany protects individual trees the way other countries protect buildings. A Naturdenkmal is a legal designation attached to one named object, and the reason for it gets written down: Munich's 2021 ordinance protects a lime by the Badenburger See for bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, and an ash on Leinthalerstrasse for an extremely wide spreading crown, with no age, no measurement and nothing else on file. Nuremberg fits six separately protected trees onto 1.7 hectares of one small park that used to be a quarantine station. Berlin supplies the age: Dicke Marie, in the Tegel Forest, had probably been growing for a long time before the city got its first written mention in 1237. Bamberg supplies the opposite case, five trees with no age recorded for any of them, a pattern that repeats in Stuttgart, Freiburg and Heidelberg, whose registers name and protect a tree without ever measuring it. 66 cities and 303 trees are mapped so far, and the paperwork here is usually better than the dating.

countries.name: Greece
countries.intro: The three Greek places mapped here answer the age question in different ways. Thessaloniki took core samples from four plane trees in 2019: 828 years for the one below the Byzantine walls, then 310, 235 and 205 for the others. Athens works in inheritance: the olive beside the Erechtheion is tied by Herodotus to the Persian sack of 480 BC, though the wood standing today is only 70 to 110 years old, since an olive regrows from its base and a trunk is never the tree's age. Another Athens olive carries an estimate spanning 300 to 2,500 years. Crete claims outright: the Olive Tree of Vouves is put at 2,000 to 4,000 years and still bears fruit, and a second, at Azoria, carries 3,000 to 3,400 years from pottery buried in its roots. All three say so plainly, which is more than most places manage. Twenty trees so far.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.intro: Budapest argues about its trees in public and keeps the evidence. The Old Acacia of Szechenyi Square is celebrated as 227 years old, planted in 1789, and a historian has taken that number apart using photographs of the square. The Taban Mulberry is credited to Ottoman occupiers by popular legend and, in the better sourced version, to Maria Theresa's eighteenth century push for a domestic silk industry, which put mulberry orchards across the district specifically to feed silkworms. Some dates are firm. Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary, planted the Tree of Science with his own hands in 1823, on what was then his private island. Others come with a warning attached: the Seven Chieftains Plane is not the tree the name first belonged to. Twelve trees, one city so far.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.intro: Ireland's oldest trees are yews on old church ground, and nearly everything else worth the walk was shipped in by Victorians. Cork's Witch's Yew is put at more than 600 years and was voted the country's Tree of the Year in 2019, then backed by 11,372 people across Europe for the continental title; Dublin's Dean's Tree matches it for age. The rest of Dublin reads as a nineteenth century plant collection: Glasnevin's Atlas cedar, dawn redwood and Caucasian elm, the last of which a nurseryman propagated into a cultivar sold under the garden's own name, and a giant sequoia Queen Victoria planted on what is now presidential ground in 1861. Trinity College has the one nobody forgets, a plane slowly swallowing a cast iron bench. Two cities so far, 30 trees.

countries.name: Italy
countries.intro: Padua's botanical garden opened in 1545 and one of its founding plants is still alive: a dwarf fan palm that Goethe wrote an entire essay about in 1786, using it to illustrate his theory of how plants grow. That tree sets Italy's pattern. Its oldest survivors stand less in open woodland than behind walls someone built on purpose, villa gardens, monastery cloisters, university botanical collections kept for study rather than shade. Rome's own oldest confirmed tree, a 425-year-old oriental plane, grows in a garden laid out for a cardinal. Italy's national tree register lists more monumental specimens than any other country mapped here, but carries no age field at all, so most of the dates on this site come from regional catalogues and city archives instead, the same close reading that first put a number on Goethe's palm.

countries.name: Japan
countries.intro: Japan is the one country on this map where the oldest trees are older than the buildings by design. Shrines are rebuilt, sometimes every twenty years as a matter of ritual, while the tree in the courtyard is left alone and wrapped in a straw rope to mark it as sacred. A camphor at a shrine gate is not decoration, it is the thing the shrine was built around. The state has protected trees as Natural Monuments since 1919, and the Environment Ministry keeps a record of every tree in the country over three metres in girth, which is why ages and measurements here are firmer than almost anywhere else in Europe. Be careful with the biggest numbers all the same: a thousand years is usually tradition rather than measurement, and the sources say so. Some places here hold one tree, which was the whole reason to travel.

countries.name: Latvia
countries.intro: Latvia's old trees are mostly oaks and limes, and several are hollow. The Elku linden in Valdemārpils is the thickest lime in the Baltic states, and visitors read owls, hedgehogs, turtles and snakes in the shapes inside its trunk. The Kaņepju Oak at Jērcēni, split by lightning, is said to hold eight people. The Sēja Oak carries a story of chieftains meeting beneath it that at least one Latvian source calls a recent invention; the tree, roughly 500 years old, needs no such claim. Riga is the easiest place to go on foot, and its trees carry the city's own record-keeping: a linden with a rowan growing from its fork, an oak patched for decades with metal plates, and a maple that went from four metres round in 1975 to 5.34 by 2009. Three places mapped so far, eight trees, most of them oaks and limes with damage they have outlived.

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.intro: Ancient Trees maps 8 places and 28 trees across Lithuania, most of them protected by a single Environment Ministry order rather than a city ordinance: one order, issued on one day in April 2018, designated five trees at once around the small town of Priekulė. The country's oldest confirmed tree, the Peace Hill Oak above the Kaunas reservoir, carries a name and role handed down from an earlier 800-year-old oak that a 2007 arson attack finally destroyed; Trainiškis does the same for a tree lost to a 2016 storm, mapping the honest young clone planted at its stump rather than pretending it is what it replaced. Braziūkai's Motinėlė, the country's thickest recorded lime trunk, sheltered insurgents against Russian rule in 1863, and Raudonė's seven-trunked lime was voted Lithuania's Tree of the Year in 2018. Lithuania protects its trees by decree; it does not always know how old they are.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.intro: Mexico's classified trees keep returning to one species: the ahuehuete, Taxodium mucronatum, sacred to the Aztecs and now the country's national tree. El Arbol del Tule outside Oaxaca carries the widest trunk of any tree on Earth, so wide that botanists once assumed it had to be several trunks fused together, until DNA testing in the 1990s proved it a single individual. Seven more ahuehuetes stand scattered across Mexico City's older parks and squares, planted in colonial-era courtyards and still growing wherever the water table lets them. Chiapa de Corzo's town square was built around a different giant, a kapok already standing when the Spanish founded the settlement in 1528. Between them, a country whose oldest trees were mostly there first, with the cities built to fit around them.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.intro: The Netherlands is the wrong country for ancient trees and has them anyway. Half of it was seabed, peat bog or open water within the last thousand years, the soil is young, the water table sits close under the roots, and North Sea storms arrive with nothing in the way to slow them down. What survived did so under shelter, and that shapes the entire list: a pear tree inside an almshouse courtyard, a cycad potted in a botanical garden in 1704 and never repotted since, lindens pollarded for three centuries because a village square needed its shade. Dutch ancient trees are tended survivors rather than forest giants, which is why so many stand behind a gate you have to find rather than out in open parkland. It also explains the oldest one on this list: a fruit tree.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.intro: New Zealand's old trees split across two entirely different timescales. Deep in Waipoua Forest stands Tane Mahuta, the largest known kauri alive, estimated at somewhere between 1,250 and 2,500 years old, a single tree that predates New Zealand's human settlement by more than a thousand years and is protected today by a boardwalk that never lets a boot touch its roots. Everything else mapped here is comparatively young and imported. Christchurch's oldest surviving oak went into the ground in 1863 to mark a royal wedding, and outlived the 2011 earthquake that flattened the buildings around its neighbours in Cranmer and Latimer Squares. Auckland's coronation oaks, planted for Edward VII and George V, and its Moreton Bay figs brought over from Australia, are barely a century old beside the kauri: a colony's civic ceremonies and a forest's own patience running on entirely different clocks.

countries.name: Poland
countries.intro: Poland names some of its oldest trees after people, not always the ones you might expect. Krakow's Henryk Oak is named for a man who lived beside it from 1923 to 2010 and saved it from a wartime felling order, though the tree predates him by a century, the last survivor of a forest the village grew up around. Warsaw's oldest carries a grander name and an honest gap: Dab Mieszko I, six hundred to six hundred forty years old, is named for the ruler who brought Poland into recorded history, though it began growing centuries after his death. It survived a 2019 arson attack and stands propped and cabled, one of the last fragments of wild forest inside the city. Beyond the five original cities, a dozen national and continental champion trees each stand as their own destination, from a disputed 800-year-old yew at Ksiaz castle to Lodz's 2023 European Tree of the Year. Seventeen places are mapped so far, running centuries younger than equivalents further west, less for lack of old ground than a twentieth century that spared little of it.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.intro: Portugal has been putting individual trees on a legal register since 1938, and the habit shows. A tree of public interest here comes with a file: species, girth, height, the year it was classified, and often the year it was last measured, all published by the forestry institute. That makes Portuguese ages more reliable than most, and it makes the disagreements visible when they happen. The trees themselves are a record of the voyages, as in Spain but more so: jacarandas from Brazil, dragon trees from Madeira, Moreton Bay figs whose aerial roots turn a Lisbon garden into something that looks borrowed from another continent. Lisbon holds more classified trees than any other municipality in the country, which is unusual for a capital and says something about what the city chose to keep.

countries.name: Romania
countries.intro: Romania's best-known tree stands in front of a village church. In 2011 the lime of Leliceni, in the Szekler hills of Transylvania, won European Tree of the Year with 23,298 votes, after winning the national contest first. It has company in the north, where the town of Cajvana keeps a live camera on its oak, reckoned at roughly 810 years, and in the Cibin gorge near Sibiu, where a silver fir called the Guardian of Cibin rises about 42 metres. Bucharest adds a different kind of tree: a mulberry with a legend on a plaque in its church porch, a plane in Cișmigiu whose roots were cut by a lighting trench in 2018, a Turkish hazel that is one of only two officially protected in the country, and four ginkgos in the Botanical Garden. Five places mapped so far, eight trees, from mountain fir to city park.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.intro: Slovakia's most-told tree story belongs to Bojnice, where a linden behind the castle is tied by tradition to a visit from King Matthias Corvinus and put at over 700 years, no measurement behind the round number. The better-documented tree is a plainer oak in Dubinné, near Bardejov, hollow enough that the wood which would date it has rotted away, leaving a working estimate of at least 800 years and the country's own claim to its oldest oak. Most of the rest of the oldest trees here are lindens, which is not a coincidence: the lime has been Slovakia's national tree since the 13th century. Hronsek's stand in the yard of a UNESCO wooden church; Uzovská Panica keeps something rarer, a 250-year-old service tree that once marked a property line. Bratislava's own collection reads almost as an inventory of other continents: a Japanese pagoda tree on the Danube embankment, an Empress tree from China, a paper birch that belongs in Canada. 27 trees across 18 places now, and the plainest one, not the castle linden, is the oldest.

countries.name: South Korea
countries.intro: South Korea's Cultural Heritage Administration keeps close enough tabs on its old trees to catch a legend in the act: an oak in Sillim-dong said to have grown from a general's walking stick in 1019 measured out, on survey, to about 250 years, a successor standing near where the legend took root. Seoul carries eight of the eleven trees mapped so far, among them the Siheung-dong ginkgos, two or three trees at the center of a traffic circle marking a vanished royal way station, and a Changdeokgung juniper the palace itself is built around. Busan holds a fortress pine and a stand of crape myrtles, eight hundred years old by tradition. An hour east in Yangpyeong, a ginkgo King Sejong is said to have granted a court rank turns the mountain road gold each autumn, and by most measurements is the tallest of its kind in the country.

countries.name: Spain
countries.intro: Spain's great native trees are out in the countryside, in the dehesas where holm oaks stand a hundred paces apart over grazing pigs. What grows in its cities came back on ships. The ombu in Seville is from the Argentine pampas, the dragon trees are Canarian, the Moreton Bay figs are Australian and the ahuehuetes are Mexican, and they are here because Seville and Cadiz held the monopoly on trade with the Americas and captains brought seedlings home the way other people bring back souvenirs. The result is that a Spanish city garden is a record of where its ships went. It also explains the ages: most of these trees arrived with the botanical fashion of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, so two hundred years is old here and five hundred is exceptional.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.intro: Sweden's old trees survived on paperwork. Five of the ten mapped here are boundary oaks, oaks that marked where one property ended and the next began, which made felling one a legal problem rather than a morning's work. Four of them stand in Orgryte in Gothenburg and were declared nature monuments on the same day, 14 October 2025, after a citizens' group spent years pointing out that a crash barrier was growing into the largest one. That tree, Granseken, is over six metres round and at least five hundred years old. Stockholm's are royal rather than legal: Birger Jarl's Oak at around eight hundred years, Prince Eugen's on the Waldemarsudde grounds, and the elms of Kungstradgarden, which are only two centuries old and famous anyway, because in 1971 people sat in them to stop a metro entrance and won. The oldest thing on this page is not an oak at all. Old Tjikko is a thin, wind-bent spruce on the Fulufjallet plateau whose visible trunk is a few centuries old and whose root system has been carbon dated at roughly 9,550 years. Fifteen trees so far, across Gothenburg, Stockholm and Fulufjallet.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.intro: Geneva has recorded the date a chestnut tree opens its first leaf every spring since 1818, one of the longest continuous records of its kind anywhere, and the tree currently doing the job is about eleven years old. The sautier of the cantonal parliament walks to the designated tree, checks it, and reports the date to the press. Age here tends to arrive with that sort of paperwork: five planes in the botanical garden were already mature enough to appear on a cantonal map in 1728, and the cedars of Parc Beaulieu, around 290 years old, grew from seed a French naturalist carried out of an English garden. Zurich adds four more, and Robenhausen contributes a single oak on the shore where a 19th-century dig gave a whole period of European prehistory its name. Twenty-six trees, three cities.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.intro:
Taiwan's oldest trees are almost all conifers found deep in mountain forest rather than in a city park, on slopes too steep for the logging that cleared most of the island's lowland giants. The Bilu Sacred Tree, a Taiwan fir put at over 3,000 years, and the Sianglin Sacred Tree, a red cypress whose age is disputed between a newly measured 626 years and a long-quoted 2,300, both stand alone in remote reserve forest rather than beside any town.

Chishang's contribution is deliberately different: a fifty-year-old Bishop wood known not for its age but for a shampoo advertisement filmed beneath it in 2001, which turned an ordinary field tree into one of the island's most visited photo stops. Taipei holds the rest of what is mapped so far: a three-hundred-year-old camphor at Zhishan Rock, a stand of Ryukyu pines known as the Common Three Pines, junipers planted at the Confucius Temple in 1962, and a ginkgo on a university campus. Between them they cover most of what an ancient tree can be here, from a shrine-grove giant nobody has fully aged to a tree made famous by something that happened to it decades after it was already grown.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.intro: Istanbul's oldest living thing is an oriental plane put at 1,300 to 1,400 years, which predates the city's Ottoman name by seven centuries. It stands inside a university forestry station at Bahcekoy, and a stranger one grows nearby: the Ahtapot Cinar, whose lowest branches touched the ground centuries ago, thickened where they landed, and now read as seven trunks sharing a single root system. Turkey keeps a national Monument Tree register that carries ages, so the numbers here are firmer than in most of Europe. The famous exception is Topkapi's plane in the First Courtyard, the one said to have witnessed the conquest of 1453, which has been dead for about a century. Fifteen trees mapped, all in Istanbul, and eight of them are planes.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.intro: Britain's oldest trees are yews, and it is churches, not palaces, that kept most of them standing. London's Totteridge Yew is put at two thousand years old, roughly a millennium and a half older than the church built beside it, one of many British yews reckoned to predate Christianity in these islands. Oaks tell a different story: a mild, fire-free climate let them stand long enough to earn names tied to real dates, a Domesday Oak already growing when the Conquest was surveyed in 1086, a Royal Oak enclosed inside a park wall in 1637 because it was already centuries old. Age here survives less through law than inheritance, a landed estate, a cathedral close, a royal park that changed hands but never changed use. Twenty-four places are mapped so far, from Edinburgh's botanic garden to Oxford's college quadrangles, and wherever a yew appears it tends to win on age. The extreme case is Fortingall, a Perthshire village of a few houses whose churchyard yew is dated at anywhere between two thousand and five thousand years, because the heartwood rotted away centuries ago and there is nothing left to count.

countries.name: United States
countries.intro: America's most famous trees are destinations rather than city sights. People drive to the Angel Oak outside Charleston and to the Hundred-Horse Chestnut's American cousins the way they drive to a canyon, and that is how this country reads on a map of old trees. The registers behind them are patchy in a way that surprised us: Portland keeps a genuine Heritage Tree list and Hawaii designates individual Exceptional Trees by county ordinance. San Francisco keeps a numbered Landmark Tree list on ordinary webpages, and most other cities either protect any tree over a set trunk size automatically or publish every street tree they own and nothing in between. So the good American trees are found one at a time, by name, and that is how we map them.

species.name: Aleppo Pine
species.intro: An Aleppo pine keeps its cones locked shut on the branch for years and opens them with heat, so the fire that kills the tree sows the next generation of it. It is the pine of the Mediterranean's dry hillsides, and the old ones mostly stand where somebody decided to keep them. Nice owes a whole forest to it: when the city became French in 1860 the slopes of Mont Boron were bare rock, and the replanting begun in 1862 is the pine wood you walk through today. Trieste's Miramare park protects six within three hundred metres of each other. Bari's Pine of Carrassi is close to six metres round, though one botanical survey calls it a stone pine. And in Canberra the Lone Pine of the Australian War Memorial grew from a cone a sergeant picked up at Gallipoli in 1915 and carried home.

species.name: American Elm
species.intro: American elm once shaded street after street in the cities of North America, until Dutch elm disease arrived and killed the great majority of them. That is why every old survivor now reads as an event. Montreal once had about 22,000, and the Last Elm of Mont-Royal is one of the few still standing. Central Park's western edge carried about 500; a 1985 survey counted 23, and the Great Elm of Central Park West is on that shortlist. In Washington the Smithsonian lists its Witness Elm as accession number 1 of its living collection, five and a half metres round and somewhere between 175 and 210 years old, depending on whose account you take. In Oklahoma City the Survivor Tree lost most of its branches to the 1995 bombing, came into bloom again about a year later, and was kept at the centre of the memorial.

species.name: American Sycamore
species.intro: Platanus occidentalis is the sycamore of the eastern United States and the American parent of the London plane, the hybrid that lines half the streets in Europe. At home, on wet river ground, it gets enormous. The Pinchot Sycamore in Simsbury, on the flood plain of the Farmington River, is the national champion of its species: 884 centimetres round and wider than it is tall. The Sunderland Buttonball Tree, on the verge of North Main Street, is traditionally dated before 1665 and widely called the largest tree in Massachusetts; buttonball is the New England name, after the seed balls that hang on the bare winter limbs. In Europe a full grown specimen standing in its own right is unusual. Ljubljana keeps two, the last of an avenue drawn on a map of the city in 1744, and Como's is the tallest tree on its lakefront walk.

species.name: Amur Cork Tree
species.intro: You can press a thumb into the bark of this tree and it gives. The Amur cork tree carries a thick, soft, deeply ridged corky layer that dents under a hand and springs back, and Munich's natural monument ordinance protects its specimen for exactly that, an interesting bark pattern, while calling the species extremely rare in the city. Under the cork the inner bark is a startling sulphur yellow, and it is one of the fundamental herbs of Chinese medicine. Paris's went into a small garden opposite the Collège de France in 1925 and wears a lightning scar down the trunk. Washington's stand inside the Roosevelt Memorial with no provenance at all: in 1962 the Park Service went looking for a planting record, found none, and kept the trees on the grounds that they were, in its own words, very attractive old trees.

species.name: Atlas Cedar
species.intro: An Atlas cedar in a European park is safer than one at home. Cedrus atlantica grows wild in a narrow band of mountains in Morocco and Algeria, and the IUCN now lists the species as endangered there, squeezed by drought, logging and a warming climate its range cannot outrun. In a nineteenth century garden it has none of those problems, which is why the old ones in European parks are mostly enormous and mostly untroubled. Lyon's is the reason its park has the shape it does, with the lawn and paths arranged to give the tree room rather than the other way round. Perugia's took the weight of a trumpeter and an accordionist playing a concert twelve metres up in its crown in 2020. Lucca's, seven metres round, carries the name of a priest who from 1943 hid Jews and partisans in his community's house.

species.name: Austrian Pine
species.intro: Austrian pine, Pinus nigra, is a Mediterranean and Balkan species that nineteenth-century cities across two continents planted for exactly what it does best: shrug off compacted, disturbed ground that would stunt almost anything else. The oldest here grows in the chateau park of Velke Opatovice in Moravia, about 250 years old, its trunk splitting into five stems just above the ground and one of those into three more, which is why locals call it the six-headed dragon. Montreal's, just inside the gate of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges cemetery, took its tolerance sideways instead of up, spreading eighteen metres wide on a trunk barely half as tall. Portland's grows out of a street planter a florist put in before the street existed and has reached 31 metres. Vienna's has been a protected natural monument since 1942 with no age ever recorded.

species.name: Avocado
species.intro: Persea americana is native to central Mexico and grown almost everywhere in Europe for its fruit rather than its shade, which makes a mature specimen remarkable rather than ordinary. It wants heat, water and no frost, and a tree grown from a stone takes a decade or more to fruit and then usually disappoints whoever planted it. Barcelona has catalogued two for their size instead. The one on Placa de Can Bruixa in Les Corts went into the ground in 1945 and, unpruned for picking, simply went up: 17 metres on a trunk only 80 centimetres round. The other stands in front of the Teatre Lliure, planted around 1946 beside a building that has been an exposition pavilion, a flower market and finally a theatre, with a canopy 15 metres across. Nobody has recorded whether it still fruits.

species.name: Bald Cypress
species.intro: Bald cypress grows with its feet in standing water in the swamps of the American South, pushing woody knees up out of the mud around its trunk, and it is a conifer that drops its needles every autumn. At home it lives for centuries. Old Baldy, on Onion Creek in Austin, was already old when Father Antonio Olivares wrote about it in 1716, and Texas puts it past five hundred years. Abroad, nineteenth century gardeners wanted the shape and took the swamp tree without the swamp. Berlin's has stood for two centuries in the Charlottenburg palace garden. Seville built its monument to the poet Becquer around one that was growing on the spot first. Miyazaki Shrine holds the largest in Japan, and Milan's was filed under the wrong genus for years until somebody checked properly.

species.name: Baobab
species.intro: Adansonia digitata belongs to the dry savannah of Africa, where it stores water in a swollen trunk and can live a thousand years. Carried across oceans, it puts on girth astonishingly fast. Honolulu's Foster Garden tree, nicknamed the Dead Rat Tree for its grey, furred seed pods, reached close to thirteen metres round in around ninety years. On the University of Hawaii's Manoa campus, the university built its new Art Building around a baobab in 1973 rather than move it. Brazil has the older ones. Maria Gorda, on the island of Paquetá in Rio de Janeiro, is ten metres round and probably centuries old, though its age is disputed, and a sign in front offers eternal luck to whoever kisses it. In Fortaleza, the city's Candomblé community venerates the baobab of the Passeio Público as sacred.

species.name: Bishop Wood
species.intro: Bischofia javanica is planted as an ordinary street and avenue tree across the tropics, which makes an old one unusual simply for how long it has been allowed to stand. Okinawa calls the species akagi and has treated old specimens as sacred for generations. At Uchima a single akagi of about 400 years stands over the village well, which is why it became a god tree. The grove at Shuri Kinjo was designated a national natural monument on 15 May 1972, the day Okinawa returned to Japan. Porto keeps three of the oldest in Portugal together in its botanical garden. And in Taiwan a farmer planted one in his rice paddy in the 1970s to tie his cattle to; an airline commercial with the actor Takeshi Kaneshiro made it famous, and when a typhoon pushed it over in 2014 it was righted and replanted.

species.name: Bitter Orange
species.intro: Citrus aurantium is too sour to eat off the tree, which is exactly why it survived where sweeter oranges would have been picked bare: it was planted for shade, symmetry and scent rather than fruit. Its home in this data is the ablutions courtyards of Andalusia's great mosques, later absorbed whole into the cathedrals built over them. Cordoba's Patio de los Naranjos is the grove that gives the type its name here, ninety-eight trees in rows lined up with the prayer hall's columns, watered by channels that trace back to a tenth-century cistern; oranges are recorded growing in it since at least 1512, replanted tree by tree ever since, so the grid is ancient and no single trunk is. Seville Cathedral's own Patio de los Naranjos looks the same age but is not: a twentieth-century restoration replanted it, whatever grew there before did not survive. And in the Real Alcázar a single stunted bitter orange carries the name of Pedro the Cruel with no record of when it was planted or why, which the page states plainly rather than guessing.

species.name: Black Locust
species.intro: The oldest tree in Paris is a black locust planted in 1601, and the second oldest is its son. Jean Robin, herbalist to Henri IV, raised the first from seed sent out of the Appalachians; in 1636 his son Vespasien took a cutting and planted it in the new royal medicinal garden two kilometres away. Both are still standing, and the genus Robinia carries the family name. The species is otherwise the opposite of distinguished. It arrived from North America in the eighteenth century, spread across Europe's sandy ground so successfully that it is now valued mainly for holding loose banks together, and it typically runs up thin and fast and then falls over. Which is what makes the exceptions worth the walk: Barcelona's went sideways to 4.3 metres on twelve metres of tree, and Antwerp's is the thickest recorded anywhere in Belgium.

species.name: Black Mulberry
species.intro: Britain's silk industry failed on a species error and left the trees behind. In 1608 James I ordered mulberries planted across the country to feed silkworms, but silkworms eat white mulberry and mostly refuse black, and black was what went into the ground. Charlton House got one of them and it is still fruiting four centuries later. Christ's College in Cambridge planted another in 1608 or 1609, the year after John Milton was born. The oldest here is older than the scheme: Adam Winthrop planted the Groton mulberry in Suffolk around 1550, on the ground where his grandson grew up before leading the Puritan fleet to Massachusetts. Its trunk collapsed decades ago and the fallen wood rooted again, which is how old mulberries keep going. Breda's public library was designed around three of them rather than the other way round.

species.name: Black Poplar
species.intro: Europe's native black poplar has been quietly bred out of its own landscape. Almost every poplar planted along a European road or river for the last two centuries has been a hybrid with an American species, so the wild form is now one of the continent's more threatened natives, and it is fast, soft and short lived on top of that. Very few reach real size. Bordeaux's has the biggest waistline in the city's entire register at 741 centimetres, three trunks fused near the ground. Helena, on a street corner in Hel, is about 220 years old; when her twin fell in a windstorm the town's woodcarvers turned its trunk into a sculpture of fishermen, and since winning Poland's Tree of the Year in 2017 she gets a name-day party every 22 May. Venice's grows alone in a wood that took over a former military firing range on the Certosa.

species.name: Black Walnut
species.intro: Budapest's biggest black walnut is also its frailest, and both findings come out of the same survey. The city's parks company dated the tree on Margaret Island to around 213 years in 2020 and measured its trunk as the thickest black walnut there by a wide margin, with the runner-up 119 centimetres smaller around; a national database ranks it second in Hungary on girth. Portland's is what is left of a fourteen acre estate, a single walnut on a school lawn, and its own plaque and the city's field guide disagree about the planting date by roughly fifteen years. Split's is a curiosity for a different reason: Juglans nigra is an eastern North American forest tree, and the city's botanical survey grades it a rarity precisely because it has no business making a living this far down the Adriatic.

species.name: Blue Jacaranda
species.intro: For a few weeks a year a jacaranda stops looking like any other tree, its whole crown turning violet-blue and the ground beneath carpeting in the same colour when the flowers drop, which is why cities from Pretoria to Sydney planted it far outside its native Argentina and Bolivia. Cagliari's specimen in the Giardini Pubblici does this every May among trees chosen for shade rather than spectacle. Cordoba's grew inside a walled garden that belonged first to a Dominican convent and then to a Renaissance palace, invisible from the street until the gate finally opened to the public in 2004. Sydney's is the odd one out: the jacaranda that made the University of Sydney's Quadrangle famous fell in 2016 after 88 years, and the tree standing there now is a clone planted the following year, carrying the same genetics and almost none of the age.

species.name: Boab
species.intro: Australia's boab is the only baobab outside Africa and Madagascar, a swollen bottle-trunked tree that drops its leaves for the dry season and photosynthesises through its bark. Its scientific name, Adansonia gregorii, comes from Ferdinand von Mueller naming it after Augustus Gregory, whose 1855 expedition camped beside the Timber Creek tree that still carries the party's carved arrival and departure dates. Derby's so-called Boab Prison Tree carries a legend, colonial prisoners held inside it, that historians have traced to a 1948 newspaper caption rather than any record; what is documented is its real use by the Nyikina and Warrwa people as shelter and burial ground. And Perth's Gija Jumulu, over 750 years old, made the longest recorded road journey of any living tree its size: 3,200km from the Kimberley in 2008, given its name by the Gija people who once stood beside it at home.

species.name: Bodhi Tree
species.intro: Most of these trees have a planting date, because with a bodhi the lineage is the point. Cuttings are carried from tree to tree back toward Bodh Gaya, and Thai temples record the year one arrived the way they record a relic. Wat Saket's went in in 1818, brought home by two monks sent abroad by King Rama II who came back after three years with cuttings instead of the relics they were sent for. Wat Phra Kaew's dates from 1864 and grows inside the most photographed temple complex in Thailand, where almost nobody photographs it. Wat Benchamabophit's was planted in 1900, nine years after Thailand received its first direct cutting from Bodh Gaya itself. The fourth in Bangkok is Lan Pho on the lawn at Thammasat University, where the protest that brought down a dictatorship began in October 1973. Singapore's stands on Pearl's Hill.

species.name: Bottle Tree
species.intro: Brachychiton populneus carries a name it barely earns. Kurrajong is what Australians call it at home; the English "bottle tree" nickname borrows from Brachychiton rupestris, its barrel-trunked cousin, but this species keeps a slimmer, upright shape its whole life. Three planted specimens map here, all in old botanic and garden collections rather than in the wild. Caserta's, in a Bourbon queen's English Garden, has reached thirty-five metres, roughly twice the height the species usually manages. Barcelona's grows half-hidden in the wooded part of the Torre Girona gardens, the one tree here a visitor actually has to go looking for. Valencia's is a garden's second bottle tree by name only, sharing a nickname with an unrelated species and nothing else.

species.name: Box Elder
species.intro: Box elder has a bad reputation. It seeds itself into alleys and vacant lots, drops limbs without warning, hosts the boxelder bugs that swarm into houses every autumn, and rarely gets the chance to grow old before someone cuts it down as a weed. It is also, unusually for a maple, compound-leafed, so people routinely mistake it for an ash. The old ones are the exceptions that outlasted the reputation. Setubal's, about 117 years old, stands in the Jardim do Bonfim on ground that was open country when it went in. Eindhoven's, planted in a parish churchyard in the 1920s, has outlived the congregation that put it there. Chicago's, on a public golf course in Edgebrook, is Illinois's state champion. And Krasnystaw's is famous for its shape: the trunk kneels almost to the ground before curving back up, beside the town hall on the market square.

species.name: Buddhist Pine
species.intro: The Buddhist pine is not a pine. Podocarpus macrophyllus is a broad-leaved conifer from Japan and southern China, and the trees mapped here show how differently the same species ends up living. At Kakuonji in Kamakura, past where the tourist route gives up, one grows as a City Natural Monument in the quiet inner precinct of a temple most visitors never reach. In Naples, Piazza Cavour holds a pair: the register only recognises the upright one, 25 metres tall, because its twin toppled years ago and kept growing horizontally, struck from the official list for lying down rather than for dying. In Las Vegas it turns up as ordinary landscaping, pressed flat against a wall on the UNLV campus, and happens to be the state's largest recorded specimen anyway. A temple guardian, a survivor lying on its side, and a state record hiding as a hedge plant.

species.name: Bunya Pine
species.intro: The bunya pine drops the heaviest cone of any conifer on earth: up to ten kilograms, roughly a bowling ball, from a crown that can be twenty-eight metres up. In southeast Queensland, the only place it grows wild, the trees fruit heavily every few years, and Aboriginal groups travelled hundreds of kilometres for the gatherings that followed. Australian parks now sign and fence them for the obvious reason. Europe planted them for the silhouette instead: a straight column with branches in flat symmetrical whorls and leaves stiff enough to draw blood. Porto's is the tallest thing in the Jardim da Cordoaria at roughly 40 metres. Bucaco's is five metres round beside a hotel that was still a Carmelite convent when it was planted. Barcelona's has been in the Teatre Grec gardens since about 1920.

species.name: Bur Oak
species.intro: The bur oak is the prairie oak, its bark thick enough to survive the grass fires that once kept the American Midwest open, so the old ones are survivors of the savanna that cities were built across. The Big Tree in the Missouri river bottoms near McBaine was already about two hundred years old when Lewis and Clark came up the river in 1804; it is 7.3 metres round and the national champion of its species. In Indianapolis, Mae Kile refused to sell her house to anyone who would not promise to keep the oak. Chicago keeps several. One in the grove on Wooded Island blew down around 2016 and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730, and the oak on the Midway Plaisance was the one tree left standing when the ground was cleared for the 1893 World's Fair.

species.name: California Fan Palm
species.intro: Everyone in Athens will tell you Queen Amalia planted the palms at the National Garden entrance. The calendar disagrees. Amalia laid the garden out between 1838 and 1840 and left Greece for good in 1862, and Washingtonia filifera did not reach European cultivation until seed arrived at a Belgian nursery around 1876, three years before the genus was even named. The row went in later, and her name attached itself the way a founder's name does. None of that makes the palms less worth the walk. Nice's stand at the corners of three formal flowerbeds at the Villa Masséna, designed by Édouard André and opened to the public in 1921 on a condition attached to the bequest. Barcelona's four have been in the courtyard of a former orphanage since about 1904. The species itself comes from desert oases in the American Southwest and northern Mexico.

species.name: Camperdown Elm
species.intro: Every Camperdown elm alive is the same tree. Around 1835 a forester on the Earl of Camperdown's estate near Dundee found a young elm growing contorted and weeping instead of upright, and because the mutation will not come from seed, every specimen since has been a cutting grafted onto a straight trunked host. Brooklyn has two of them. The famous one went in behind Prospect Park's Boathouse in 1872 and had declined so badly by the 1960s that the poet Marianne Moore wrote in its defence; the second stands two miles south in Green-Wood, and nobody recorded when. Edinburgh's grows by the main door of St Cuthbert's, a parish site far older than the 1894 building on it. None of them has a straight branch anywhere.

species.name: Camphor Tree
species.intro: Crush a camphor leaf and the tree explains itself: the sharp medicinal scent is camphor, distilled for centuries from its wood, and it is one reason the species lives so long, discouraging the insects and fungi that hollow out other trees. In Japan the kusunoki is the great shrine tree, wrapped in sacred rope, its canopy sometimes wider than the buildings it shelters; several of the country's largest and oldest trees are camphors, and city districts have been rerouted around them. The species is evergreen, so a thousand-year camphor in January looks as alive as it does in June. The camphor trees mapped so far are listed oldest first, shrine giants leading.

species.name: Canadian Poplar
species.intro: Canadian poplar is a hybrid of Europe's black poplar and an American cottonwood, bred for timber and shelter belts: fast, soft, and usually felled within decades rather than left for centuries. The old ones are the trees somebody forgot to take out. The oldest poplar in the Netherlands grows behind a concert hall in Arnhem, on the last stretch of moat the city never filled in, and has stood since somewhere between 1750 and 1800. Amsterdam's in the Vondelpark has reached about 38 metres on the edge of a bicycle path. Leeuwarden's Marilandica, a named clone, has a trunk so covered in burrs that it reads closer to rock than bark. Warsaw's was already mature when the ground it stands on became a transit camp in 1944, and Antwerp's runs six metres of clear trunk before the crown starts.

species.name: Canary Island Date Palm
species.intro: Every Canary Island date palm on the French Riviera arguably descends from one garden on Nice's eastern port, where Baron Vigier is said to have acclimatised the species in France for the first time in 1864. That rests on the garden's own preservation society rather than on any independent record, so take it as the claim it is. The species is easy to admire and impossible to date, because a palm lays down no growth rings to count. Valencia's Palacio de Pineda has a construction date to the year, 1728 to 1731, and its palm has nothing at all; you can order a coffee under it. Barcelona's double row along the Vil.la Amelia avenue produces its own small disagreement, since the city register counts fourteen palms and the garden's chronicler counts fifteen. Valencia's other three stand in a row so recognisable that a bar took their nickname.

species.name: Canary Pine
species.intro: Pinus canariensis is endemic to the Canary Islands and about as fire-adapted as a pine gets: a mature tree can resprout new needles directly from a trunk that fire has scorched black, a trick almost no other pine in the world manages, which is how specimens survive centuries on slopes that burn periodically. The two most extreme examples stand 150 metres apart above the town of Vilaflor de Chasna on Tenerife, on the same short marked trail off the TF-21. Pino Gordo is on the town's own coat of arms, 9.36 metres round at the trunk and the thickest native tree in Spain, estimated at 700 to 800 years old, already a substantial pine when Castile finished conquering the island in 1496. Pino de las Dos Pernadas, the taller and slimmer half of the pair at 56 metres, is the tallest native tree in Spain, its trunk splitting about ten metres up into two near-identical limbs, which is what its name literally describes. Both carry visible fire scars and both are free to reach on foot from the same car park. The third, in Seville, is a different kind of specimen entirely: an undated pine on the open grounds of the university's engineering campus, rated in optimal health by the city's 2022 survey of singular trees, standing 26 metres tall a very long way from the volcanic slopes the species calls home.

species.name: Cannon Ball Tree
species.intro: Couroupita guianensis grows its fruit and flowers straight out of the trunk rather than the branches, a habit botanists call cauliflory and gardens call a hazard: ripe cannonball-sized fruit falls from height and splits open with a smell that carries, and Honolulu's Foster Garden has posted a sign warning visitors under its specimen. Three trees on this site share the trick. Singapore's, in the Ginger Garden, grew from seed E.J.H. Corner carried aboard ship in 1931 during an eight-hour stop in Ceylon. Its flowers make no nectar; the sterile pollen at their centre exists only to bring carpenter bees in for the fertile kind elsewhere on the bloom. Oahu's second specimen, on the UH Manoa campus, carries a trunk 314 centimetres round and an unconfirmed campus legend that the playwright Thornton Wilder planted it in 1933. All three flower and fruit from bark most trees keep bare.

species.name: Cappadocian Maple
species.intro: Acer cappadocicum takes its name from Cappadocia, the region of central Anatolia where it grows wild in the mountains, though its native range continues north into the Caucasus, which is why it is sometimes called Colchis maple instead, after the kingdom Jason sailed for in the story of the Golden Fleece. Snap a leaf stalk on any of them and the sap that beads up is milky white rather than clear, the same trick its close relative the Norway maple plays. What gardeners actually plant it for is the autumn show: rather than the mixed reds and oranges of most maples, this one turns a uniform, saturated gold and holds the colour for weeks. Cork's grows in the gardens at Blarney Castle, dated to somewhere between one and one and a half centuries old by a 2009 heritage survey that never recorded who planted it. Utrecht's stands at the west entrance to Wilhelminapark, one of the park's original 1880s plantings according to the Dutch national monumental tree register. Lyon's, in the Tête d'Or's arboretum since the garden was founded in 1857, has been measured at 3.20 metres round and 26 metres tall, mature rather than record-breaking. None of the three carries a confirmed planting date, which for a tree grown as a specimen rather than a landmark is the ordinary state of things.

species.name: Caucasian Elm
species.intro: Europe lost most of its large elms to a fungus in the twentieth century, and these survived by not quite being elms. Zelkova carpinifolia is an elm relative from the mountain forests between the Black Sea and the Caspian, far less susceptible to Dutch elm disease, which is why trees this size still stand in the Latin Quarter and along the Avenue Foch. The shape gives it away: a short trunk breaking into a dense sheaf of near vertical stems, so the crown reads as a bundle held upright rather than a spreading canopy. Oxford's is the tallest recorded anywhere in Britain at around 33 metres. Dublin's was propagated into a named cultivar sold under the garden's own name. Florence's lost roughly two thirds of its height to surgery in the 1980s and is still on the national register.

species.name: Caucasian Wingnut
species.intro: The Caucasian wingnut is a walnut relative from the humid forests between the Black and Caspian Seas, and Amsterdam has more remarkable ones than almost any city outside its native range. It reached Europe around 1782 and thrives in exactly the wet, soft ground that much of the Dutch capital is built on. In summer it hangs curtains of green winged seeds, the catkins that give it its name, sometimes half a metre long. Left alone it suckers into a small grove from a single tree, which is why several of the city's specimens read as thickets rather than trunks. Amsterdammers have gone to court to keep them: one felling permit fight over a pair of wingnuts ran all the way to the Raad van State, the country's highest administrative court. These are the wingnuts mapped on the site so far.

species.name: Cedar of Lebanon
species.intro: This is the only tree on a national flag, and the only one whose timber built both Solomon's temple and the ships of the Phoenicians, at least according to the sources those builders left behind. When seeds reached Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries the Cedar of Lebanon became the ultimate estate status symbol: an aristocrat planted one knowing only his grandchildren would see the famous silhouette, the enormous level layers of dark foliage held out flat as trays. That slow flat-topped shape is the tree's signature and takes a century to appear, so every convincing cedar crown you see is old almost by definition. The cedars mapped so far stand in parks and former estates, oldest first.

species.name: Cherry
species.intro: Most cherry trees are finished inside a century, which makes every old one an exception rather than the rule; the trees here carry only their genus, Prunus, because no source names the species. Uda's Sen'nen-zakura is reckoned at over 900 years old and stands beside the stone steps up to the temple Butsuryuji. In Iida a weeping cherry of about 350 years, 3.8 metres round, hangs down the embankment of the old Enshu Kaido and is lit at night in blossom season. Fukuoka's Seicho-zakura was lifted whole by crane in January 2008, an eight-metre tree of roughly three and a half tonnes, and set down thirty metres from where it had grown. Kyoto's carriage-turning cherry is a roughly 80-year-old successor of the original. If you know which of Japan's many flowering cherries any of these are, tell us.

species.name: Chilean Wine Palm
species.intro: The Chilean wine palm carries one of the thickest trunks in the palm family, a grey column that can run past three and a half metres round, and that trunk is why the species barely survives in the wild. Jubaea chilensis stores its sugar as sap, and for two centuries Chilean producers got at it by felling a mature palm and draining the stump for palm honey, a tapped tree never growing back. Central Chile's valleys once filled with these palms; a handful of protected stands are what is left. The tree found a second life in nineteenth-century Europe instead, where its rare cold-hardiness for a palm made it a prize for villa gardens built to look exotic in a climate that kills most others. The old ones still stand in exactly that ground, in Italian villa parks from Genoa to Florence.

species.name: Chinaberry
species.intro: Three cities, three uses for the same tree. Cordoba grew one to twenty-four and a half metres beside the Puerta de Almodovar, casting four hundred square metres of shade from a species that usually stops at ten; its hard seed stones, strung as rosary beads, gave the tree its other name, bead tree. Nara planted its specimen on the burned platform of Todai-ji's east pagoda, because chinaberry was believed to drive off evil spirits and was traditionally set at sites where the dead were remembered; for two weeks each May it covers itself in pale purple flowers. Paris keeps one in Square Boucicaut, where the French call it lilas de Perse, Persian lilac, and where its pale yellow berries stay on the bare branches through December and January, a Mediterranean tree fruiting through a cold it was never bred for.

species.name: Chinese Hackberry
species.intro: In Japan this tree is enoki, and for two and a half centuries it did a job before it did anything ornamental: the Tokugawa shogunate planted one, or a red pine, at every ichirizuka, the paired earthen mounds that marked each ri of the great highways out of Edo, so a traveller had shade to rest in as well as a distance to measure. Shrines took to it for the same reasons: it grows fast, broad and long-lived. The Enoki of Wakamiya in Nara, below Kasuga Taisha, is five metres round and only seventeen tall, put at two to three centuries by the national survey. Kyoto's at the Demizu-guchi gate of the Imperial Palace has a crown ten metres wider than the tree is tall, and a Hiroshima shrine's stands taller than the celebrated wife camphor beside it and has never been given a name.

species.name: Chinese Juniper
species.intro: The Chinese juniper is best known in the West as a bonsai subject, trained small in a tray. Left alone for centuries beside a temple or a palace, it does the opposite: it grows into a slow, twisting giant whose bark spirals hard enough that people read dragons into it. Court records describe the coiled eastern branch at Seoul's Changdeokgung as a dragon ascending to heaven, and Beijing's Nine Dragon Cypress is a juniper misnamed by generations who never doubted the resemblance. The oldest, in Nanjing, is reckoned at about 1,500 years and is still called a pine. Kamakura's pair at Kenchoji have stood since the temple's founding in 1253, on a site once known as Hell Valley. Courts and monasteries protected what everyone else would have shaped smaller, which is why the old ones are almost all on sacred or royal ground.

species.name: Chir Pine
species.intro: The chir pine belongs to the dry outer foothills of the Himalaya, the resin belt running from Pakistan through northern India into Nepal, where it is tapped for turpentine the way other trees are tapped for rubber. Its needles run up to thirty centimetres in bundles of three and hang rather than bristle, so a mature crown looks like a loose green waterfall rather than the stiff cone most people picture at the word pine. Every old one here is a long way from that range. Rome's monumental register lists exactly two, one of them on Colle Oppio, grown from a seed the Tibetologist Giuseppe Tucci carried back from an expedition and planted directly above Nero's buried Domus Aurea. Caserta's, about 150 years old, grows in the English Garden of a Bourbon palace, and Hobart's in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens' pinetum.

species.name: Coast Redwood
species.intro: The tallest tree species on earth takes a serious share of its water straight out of sea mist, which is why it belongs to the fog belt of the northern Californian coast. There it gets very old: Colonel Armstrong, in the grove a lumberman set aside near Guerneville, is roughly 1,400 years old, and the Parson Jones Tree beside it runs past 94 metres. Europe hands it the rainless summer and none of the fog. So the redwood on Rome's Pincio has stopped at thirty metres, a good height for a Roman tree and a failure for this species, and has gone thick instead. Where the air stays damp the answer is different: Lucca's clears every tower inside the walls except the two you can climb. Most of Europe's went in within a few decades, because seed reached the continent in the 1840s and every ambitious garden wanted one.

species.name: Common Camellia
species.intro: A camellia is supposed to drop its flower whole, head and all, which is why samurai were said to dislike them. The four hundred year old tree at Byakugo-ji in Nara does not: it sheds petal by petal, and it opens red, white, peach, striped and variegated blossoms on the same plant. Japan's thickest wild camellia stands in a village burial ground at the end of a dead-end valley in Himi, three trunks grown back into each other and 3.89 metres round; its age is put at 500 years by the city and 700 to 800 by an older survey. Portugal is the other home of old camellias. The mild wet north suited Camellia japonica so well that Portuguese growers ended up exporting it back to the rest of Europe, and the pair in front of the church at Paranhos in Porto are six and a half metres tall.

species.name: Common Fig
species.intro: A common fig is a Mediterranean shrub that most gardens this far north keep low and trained flat against a warm wall. Three of these refused. Paris's, in the Square Georges Cain beside the Musee Carnavalet, stands ten metres tall in the open with a trunk 145 centimetres round, which a fig this far from the Mediterranean has no real business doing. London's Amwell Street fig went the other way, sprawling low across the front of a former parochial school in Clerkenwell on several stems from one rootstock, propped up where its own limbs outgrew their strength, and it may have been planted as a teaching aid rather than an ornament. Seville's is the oldest of the three at over 300 years, growing in the Huerto del Rey Moro, a walled plot on Calle Enladrillada that neighbours occupied in 2004 rather than watch it get built over, and have run themselves ever since. One species, three trees that each broke the pattern in a different way.

species.name: Common Lime
species.intro: Common lime is a hybrid of Europe's two wild limes, and it took over the north as the tree you plant on purpose: along canals, up drives, around squares, and in the middle of villages where decisions were made. Hilvarenbeek's aldermen read out the local decrees under theirs before the village had a noticeboard. The Linde van Sambeek is the thickest lime in the Netherlands at 7.97 metres round, hollow, with a second stem grown up inside the shell after storms took its crown in 1884 and 1901. Groningen's oldest tree is one, about 340 years old at a farmhouse called De Rollen. On a bare dike near Utrecht, boatmen on the Lek used to steer by a single lime. In Tallinn, one of the Skoone Bastion lindens was already decades old when work began on the bastion it now crowns.

species.name: Cook Pine
species.intro: Cook pine comes from one stretch of the Pacific, New Caledonia's Isle of Pines, where eighteenth-century sailors mistook its narrow, leaning columns for stone and named the island after the mistake. Planted as an ornamental far from home, it tends to end up the tallest thing around: Brisbane's, one of two set out by Prince Albert, Duke of Edinburgh, in 1868, is now the tallest tree in the City Botanic Gardens at forty-five metres. Lima's stands inside a seventeenth-century Spanish olive grove and has already outgrown trees three centuries older than it. Palermo's rises thirty-eight metres over Villa Tasca's swan lake, the pine on one shore answering a fig tree's shade on the other.

species.name: Copper Beech
species.intro: Every copper beech in Europe descends from an accident. The purple leaf is a mutation that turns up at random in wild green beech forests, and it is a handicap rather than an advantage: the pigment masks the chlorophyll underneath and cuts the light the leaf can put to work, so purple seedlings are outgrown by green ones and vanish. The tree exists in numbers only because gardeners in German and Swiss forests kept the freak and propagated it, usually by grafting, since it does not come true from seed. Leiden's was grafted low onto a green rootstock, and two centuries of mismatched growth rates have left it with a broad gnarled base that looks nothing like a beech. Boston's is the only living Historic Landmark in Cambridge, designated in 1985 to stop a building. In 2024 a grafted Silesian beech was voted Europe's tree of the year.

species.name: Cork Oak
species.intro: A working cork oak gets stripped to the bare wood every nine years or so, its bark peeled off in slabs for wine corks and flooring. The Whistler at Aguas de Moura in Portugal has been harvested more than twenty times since around 1820; a single stripping in 1991 gave more than 1,200 kilos, and in 2018 it won European Tree of the Year. The ones in gardens were never harvested, so they carry what the industry takes away: an outer bark up to thirty centimetres thick, spongy enough that pressing a thumb into it is half the reason to go. Sintra's is the Sobreira dos Fetos, the Fern Cork Oak, because ferns grow straight out of its bark; Portugal's register puts it at 350 years. The oak in Rome's orangery was measured twice in three years and grew from 5.00 metres around to 5.30 in between.

species.name: Crimean Linden
species.intro: Tilia x euchlora is not a tree anyone found in the wild. It is a hybrid raised in cultivation around 1860, small-leaved lime crossed with a Caucasian relative, chosen for glossy dark leaves and a tolerance of compacted, polluted city ground that its parents do not share, which is why it turns up on streets and in parks rather than in forests. Rotterdam's stands on the Parklaan, one of a small planting spree that followed Queen Wilhelmina's 1898 coronation. Manchester's is a cluster in a Didsbury park that the Collins Tree Guide's own author called of national importance, though nobody has measured or dated it in print. In Leeuwarden you walk past one, planted in 1954, on the way into the public library through the gate of the old prison. Heidelberg's has been protected since 1986 for reasons its register never explains.

species.name: Crows Ash / Australian Teak
species.intro: Flindersia australis is a Queensland rainforest hardwood, milled and sold commercially as Australian teak, named for the navigator Matthew Flinders. The Brisbane trees carry an honesty gap rather than a measured age. The oldest by claim stands in Brisbane City Botanic Gardens, planted in 1884 to replace an older crows ash felled in 1826 to clear the ground for the settlement's first government garden, no relation between the two. A second, in Newstead Park, is dated only by inference: a television gardening segment judged it older than the 1846 house it stands beside and called that over 160 years, a floor rather than a figure. The third lives worse than either, a memorial tree planted in Toowong in September 1924 inside a sandstone planter box, stunted by its own container ever since, dedicated to a town council abolished thirteen months after the planting.

species.name: Daimyo Oak
species.intro: Kashiwa, the daimyo oak, is a slow tree of poor ground and cold slopes that rarely puts on real bulk, which makes every specimen here worth the detour on size alone. Its broad leaves are the reason most people in Japan know the species without knowing they do: they wrap the rice cakes eaten at Children's Day, chosen because the old leaves cling on through winter and let go only when new buds push them off, read as a family line that never breaks. Sapporo's stands on the path to Hokkaido Shrine's worship hall, probably the largest of several big kashiwa on those grounds. Hiroshima's carries the same three-century age band as the giant cedar it grows beside. The oldest and strangest is Shogen-in's Sakasa Gashiwa in Shiwa, its trunk splitting into four limbs at ground level that run outward before turning up, so the branches read as roots that changed their minds; the only daimyo oak under national protection in Japan.

species.name: Date Palm
species.intro: A date palm belongs to an oasis, not a city square, yet a handful have made themselves at home in European parks and gardens. Lisbon's, in the Ninth of April Garden, is the most argued over: the city calls it the tallest tree in the capital at 38 metres, the national register measured it at 26.7, and nobody has climbed up to settle it. Palermo's stands over a Roman mosaic of Alexander the Great hunting a lion, unearthed by accident under Villa Bonanno and left where it was found. A date palm is meant to grow as a single trunk, and two of these refuse. Seville's forks into a cluster in the Parque de Maria Luisa. Valencia's La Carcasa, in the university's botanic garden, grows more than 35 trunks from one base and is named for the spent casing of a firework shell.

species.name: Dawn Redwood
species.intro: Every dawn redwood on this page descends from one valley in central China. The species was known only from imprints in stone and filed under extinct until living trees were found there in the 1940s, and seed collected in 1947 and 1948 went out by post to botanical gardens around the world, which is where these came from. The rediscovery gets dated to 1941 and to 1944 depending on which step is being counted, and both dates turn up in the records behind these trees. They are young, most between sixty and eighty years old, and worth the walk anyway, because a conifer that turns rust orange and drops its needles every winter is an odd thing to meet. Portland's coned in 1952, the first any dawn redwood had done in the Western Hemisphere since the species vanished from it.

species.name: Douglas Fir
species.intro: Douglas fir grows wild down the Pacific coast of North America, and at home it is enormous and old. Seward Park's Big Tree in Seattle, put at 400 to 500 years, still carries the scars of fires in 1508 and 1701. Sylvia, across Lake Washington, is about eight metres round; a windstorm took her top off in 1993 and she has been growing a candelabra of new ones since. The Doerner Fir near Coos Bay is 84 metres tall, and Portland's Balch Creek fir 74. Everywhere else it is an import with a hard start date, since seed only left the Pacific Northwest for Europe in 1827, and it still outgrows the locals. Germany's tallest tree is Waldtraut vom Mühlwald, a Douglas fir planted near Freiburg in 1913 and measured at 67.85 metres in 2024. Hobart's went into the botanical gardens in 1894.

species.name: Downy Oak
species.intro: Downy oak is the tree dry limestone hillsides are made of, usually a modest, crooked field-edge oak that loses out to better species on good ground, so a big one is worth the detour. The most famous stands on Orbán Hill above the wine town of Bátaszék in southern Hungary, hollow, 4.7 metres round and put at 300 to 400 years. In 2016 it was voted Europe's Tree of the Year, and every 25 May locals pour wine over its trunk for a good harvest. Umbria grows the species on every slope. Outside Assisi, the oak of Via di Valecchie went onto Italy's national register in July 2026 as the tallest monumental tree in the region, thirty metres up. Near Perugia two grow 150 metres apart within eight centimetres of the same girth, on ground the species shares with truffles.

species.name: Dragon Tree
species.intro: Nobody can date a dragon tree, and that is the species rather than sloppy record keeping. Dracaena draco lays down no annual rings, so every age here is an estimate and some are wide open: Tenerife's Drago Milenario is put near 700 years by a modern study and at a thousand or more by tradition, and the tree in the Parque Genoves in Cadiz anywhere between 100 and 200. The name comes from the sap. Cut into the bark and the resin that runs out is dark red, sold across Europe for centuries as dragon's blood, a dye and a medicine. Shape is the other reason to go. An old dragon tree spreads into a low dome of blunt branch tips, and the one at the Quinta Conde dos Arcos in Lisbon is more than twice as wide as it is tall.

species.name: Dutch Elm
species.intro: Dutch elm disease is named for the country that first identified it, which makes every mapped tree of this hybrid a small act of defiance. Amsterdam's Oudemanhuispoort elm has turned a brick-walled courtyard into an advantage, reaching 35 metres because the only direction open to it was up, and a second Amsterdam elm is the last of roughly thirty planted outside Centraal station in 1889, the rest lost to the epidemic decades ago. The Hague's Malieveld elm dates to the 1830s and has now outlived two separate waves of the disease, the second and worse one arriving in the 1970s. In Portland, the Rockey elm survived a 1963 demolition order only because an architect parked his car where the removal crew needed to stand. Each of these is a tree the fungus could have taken and did not.

species.name: English Elm
species.intro: Dutch elm disease took the mature English elm almost everywhere in England, so most of the old ones now stand somewhere else. Brighton is the exception: it has cut infected wood out of its elms since the early 1970s, and the surviving Preston Twin, planted around 1613 in what was probably a hedgerow, is 6.38 metres round; its felled twin was carved and raised again on the same ground. Melbourne kept its elms too. In Boston, Saint-Gaudens built his memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th around a pair planted between 1772 and 1812, on a vault designed to spare their roots. New York's Hangman's Elm on Washington Square is put at 300 years or more, with a nickname no court or newspaper record supports. Portland's was the only elm left on its block after the Columbus Day Storm of 1962.

species.name: European Ash
species.intro: Ash is the tree Europe is losing right now. A fungus from east Asia, harmless to the ashes it evolved alongside, was first noticed in Poland in the early 1990s and has since worked its way west across the continent, which puts a different weight on every old one still standing. Lithuania's thickest, the Witch's Ash at Plateliai, is 7.41 metres round and looks like four trees knotted together, which local legend says it once was. In Stockholm, Carl Linnaeus wrote down Valkasken, the burl ash, in the 1740s, and it is still there on Langholmen. Gdansk's Ash of King Jan is 6.1 metres round. Prague's grows to 37 metres in the one corner of Strahov Monastery the monks left open to the public. And in Giethoorn an ash has heaved the ground under a farmhouse into a mound.

species.name: European Beech
species.intro: Almost nothing grows under a beech, and the tree is doing it deliberately. The leaves sit in dense overlapping layers that let very little light through, which is why a beech wood feels like a room rather than a thicket, and why left alone most of northern Europe would return to beech forest within two centuries. So a beech in a city park is often the one tree that would have been there anyway, which is what Nuremberg says of its two. The ones worth crossing town for are beeches given open ground, which keep their lower limbs and bring the crown down in a skirt you have to duck under. Prague's Twin Beech reaches 45 metres on a 1620 battlefield. Haarlem's carries a crowned monogram an exiled king cut into it around 1809. Denmark's Svalebøgen, said to have sprouted from a mouse's buried larder, is 12.5 metres round.

species.name: European Larch
species.intro: A larch drops its needles every winter, which is unusual for a conifer and part of why the ones that get noticed tend to stand out. Lithuania's State Protected Areas Service records one in the forest near Degsne at 49 metres, the tallest tree of any kind in the country, grown from a stand planted in 1849. Krakow's grows on a slope that was fenced off as woodland between 1902 and 1909 and kept shut to walkers for roughly half a century before the park finally let people in. Reykjavik's stands in Holavallagardur, the city's oldest cemetery, where conifers generally struggle against Iceland's wind and thin soil badly enough that the national forestry society singled this one out in 2011 for having managed it anyway.

species.name: European Pear
species.intro: Nobody planted these to be looked at. A pear is an orchard tree, grown for fruit and grubbed out when it stops paying, so an old one is something somebody chose not to replace. The oldest is in The Hague, planted in 1638 in the courtyard of an almshouse for women of unblemished character, and the residents have been turning its hard little juttepeers into jelly for close to four centuries. Helsinki's is the last survivor of a manor orchard and is reckoned the tallest and oldest pear in Finland. Two have won national votes. Slovakia's pink-fleshed pear at Bošáca, about 200 years old, took the country's Tree of the Year in 2015, and the Czech Republic elected a lone pear in a field near Mrákotín in 2023, the one a folk song says stands in the open field.

species.name: European White Elm
species.intro: This is the elm that likes wet feet. Ulmus laevis is a floodplain tree, and Berlin's Great Elm of Treptower Park takes that literally: its roots run straight into the Spree, which foresters credit for a vigour unusual at 250 years. It was added to Germany's national heritage list on 25 September 2025. The damp ground it favours is also why it mostly escaped Dutch elm disease, which took nearly every other big elm in Europe. Gdansk's stands by the pond in Park Oliwski, 4.2 metres round and 30 metres tall, protected together with the ivy that flowers up its trunk in October. The Dutch register calls the Elm of Heure, on an estate near Borculo, the thickest elm in the Netherlands and records no girth to back it. Munich's register says no older elms are known anywhere in the city than its twin trees in the Englischer Garten.

species.name: European Yew
species.intro: No tree in Europe grows older than the yew, and no tree is harder to date: the trunk hollows out with age, taking its own tree rings with it, so the oldest yews keep their exact age a permanent secret. Estimates for the great churchyard yews of Britain and Ireland run from several centuries to several thousand years, and in many cases the tree is provably older than the medieval church beside it, because early Christians built next to yews that were already sacred. Every part of the tree except the red flesh of its berries is poisonous, which kept cattle away and longbows supplied. The yews mapped so far, castle gardens and churchyards included, are listed oldest first.

species.name: Fern-leaved Beech
species.intro: Genoa's city hall has a beech in its courtyard and its leaves are wrong. They come out narrow and deeply slashed, closer to a fern frond than to the broad oval a beech is supposed to carry, which is the whole of the fern-leaved beech and the only reason anyone notices one. None can be very old. The form was not around before about 1804 and cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every specimen is a cutting off another one. Leiden's, planted in the Hortus in 1818, is the oldest in the Netherlands and has grown outward into one enormous low dome. Vienna's, planted in 1873, is six metres round, the thickest of the 449 trees registered in the Rathauspark. Munich registers its two not for size or age but for how rarely the form turns up anywhere in the city.

species.name: Field Elm
species.intro: Ulmus minor was the species Dutch elm disease hit hardest, so every big field elm still standing has outlived nearly all of its kind. Sliven's Old Elm, beside the town hall, is put at about a thousand years by tradition, won European Tree of the Year in 2014 and is on a Bulgarian coin; the disease reached it too, and specialists are keeping two low branches alive. The Olmo de Navajas in Valencia province was planted in 1636 by a settler named Roque Pastor and is still the centre of the village square. In Romania, the elm of Căpeni is 7.3 metres round. French has a phrase for being kept waiting, wait for me under the elm, and the elm in question stands in front of Saint-Gervais in Paris: the present one was planted in 1935, on a spot that has carried an elm since the Middle Ages.

species.name: Field Maple
species.intro: Field maple is the tree that fills gaps between hedgerows rather than anchoring a park, usually clipped into a hedge long before it can become anything, so a big one stands out from its own species. Copenhagen's in Hans Tavsens Park has 4.03 metres of trunk, and the Danish register ranks it third thickest in the country. In Gdansk, the city council protected a pair in Park Oliwski in February 2026 and named them after Hugo Conwentz, the botanist credited with founding the world's first state conservation office. Utrecht's, on the Bartholomeibrug, is the only maple native to the Netherlands among all the city's maples. Prague's, in the Seminary Garden above a pond, carries a careful estimate of 160 to 170 years, and Graz has protected one in the Augarten since 1979, after a 1956 survey had already called it worth keeping.

species.name: Fig
species.intro: A fig this size stops being a single trunk and becomes a structure. Nago's Hinpun Gajumaru is the clearest case: its aerial roots fused into a mass nearly 12 metres around, old enough to have gradually swallowed a pine growing beside it. The Philippine balete is a strangler fig that starts in another tree's branches and replaces it; the Millennium Tree in Maria Aurora is a cage of fused roots around a hollow you can stand inside, and on Siquijor a spring rises at the roots of the Enchanted Balete of Lazi. Rio de Janeiro's fig on Rua Faro became the city's first landmarked tree in 1980, after neighbours stood under it to stop a construction crew. Alicante's is wrapped in fireproof tarps every June before the plaza around it is set alight for the Fogueres festival. None has been keyed to an exact species.

species.name: Giant Sequoia
