species.intro: The heaviest living things on earth reached Europe only in 1853, and the timing shaped everything: Victorian Britain was at peak plant mania, and a tree that could outweigh a blue whale sold itself. Nurserymen shipped seeds by the ton, aristocrats raced to plant avenues of them, and the British even named the species Wellingtonia after the recently dead duke, a name Californians never accepted. Every sequoia outside America is therefore young, barely 170 years at most, yet many already dominate their skylines, because the species grows fast and simply does not stop. At home in the Sierra Nevada it passes 3,000 years: the President is reckoned at about 3,200, the Grizzly Giant has lost four fifths of its bark to fire and is still alive, and General Sherman stands 83.6 metres tall.

species.name: Ginkgo
species.intro: The ginkgo has no living relatives. Its family goes back over 200 million years, so far that when the first botanists examined one they were looking at a tree older than flowers; everything else in its lineage is fossil. It nearly vanished too, surviving in Chinese temple grounds until monks and then Dutch traders carried it around the world. It is almost comically hard to kill: six ginkgos stood within two kilometres of the Hiroshima blast and all six leafed the following spring. Cities love it for that same stubbornness, and every November it pays them back, dropping all its golden fan-shaped leaves at once, sometimes in a single day. The ginkgos mapped so far run from Tokyo's shrine giants to the first European imports, oldest first.

species.name: Gray Poplar
species.intro: Gray poplar is a natural cross between white poplar and aspen, and it grows fast enough that a thick trunk is no proof of great age the way it would be on an oak. Ferrara's, over 150 years old and 4.44 metres round, grew for most of that time screening a private courtyard at the Palazzo dei Diamanti, one of the Italian Renaissance's most recognisable buildings, until a 2023 restoration opened the garden to visitors. Sofia's is the oldest tree in the Doctors' Garden, planted in 1892, four years before the garden formally opened as one of the city's first botanical collections. Warsaw's, on a pavement corner in Mokotow, holds an entry in Poland's national register at 21 metres tall. In Hoorn, storms have torn into one's crown and inspectors still rate it in good condition.

species.name: Handkerchief Tree
species.intro: The white handkerchiefs are not flowers. Davidia involucrata makes a small dark flower head of no interest whatever and wraps it in two oversized white bracts, modified leaves that hang below it and turn in any breeze. For roughly ten days to a fortnight in May a mature tree carries hundreds of them at once, which is where handkerchief tree, dove tree and ghost tree all come from, and outside those two weeks it is an ordinary looking thing. Western botany did not know the species existed until the French missionary Armand David documented it in the mountains of central China in 1869, and it stayed rare in cultivation because the seed can sit for two winters before it does anything. Copenhagen, Edinburgh and Utrecht each keep one, and only Edinburgh's has a date: an accession number that opens 1928.

species.name: Himalayan Cedar
species.intro: Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through to Nepal, where deodar means timber of the gods and a tree can pass a thousand years. Every one here grows a very long way from those mountains. It reached Europe in 1822, and six years later Padua's Orto Botanico planted one that is still standing. The continent's park builders took to it at once: Florence's specimen was on the botanical garden's books by 1880, and Bergamo's stands alone in the middle of a lawn with its own lightning conductor, because it is the tallest thing for some distance. Austin's went in beside George Littlefield's house in 1893, and Tokyo's in Yanaka started as a pot plant at a bakery door around 1926. The drooping branch tips are the field mark that separates a deodar from the stiffer cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas.

species.name: Hinoki Cypress
species.intro: Hinoki is the most valued softwood in Japan, the timber the Ise shrines are rebuilt in every twenty years and the smell people mean when they say a Japanese bath smells of wood. A working forest fells a cypress long before it reaches real girth, so the big ones stand almost entirely on shrine and temple ground, where somebody decided long ago they were not for cutting. The Japanese ones fit that pattern: one beside a bathhouse in the mountains outside Hiroshima, the other in a prefectural monument grove near a hall where sacred dances are performed, both over three metres round and undocumented beyond one government measurement. The third breaks the pattern entirely. Boston's Larz Anderson hinoki has spent all 289 of its years in a pot, started in 1737 and shipped from Yokohama to Brookline in 1913, now rotated through a pavilion at the Arnold Arboretum a few weeks at a time.

species.name: Holm Oak
species.intro: The holm oak is the oak most northern visitors fail to recognise: evergreen, with small dark leathery leaves closer to an olive's than to the lobed oak leaf on every pub sign, holly-like enough that holm is simply the old English word for holly. Around the Mediterranean it is the landscape itself, the dark domed canopy of Spanish dehesas where pigs fatten on its acorns for jamon iberico, and it shrugs off drought, salt wind and poor soil that would kill its deciduous cousins. Planted north of its range it grows slowly into dense, near-black domes that read as older than they are. The holm oaks mapped so far are listed oldest first.

species.name: Honey Locust
species.intro: A wild honey locust is armed. Branched thorns up to fifteen centimetres long grow straight out of the trunk and the older wood, generally read as a defence against browsing animals that no longer exist in North America. Street plantings use thornless varieties, which is part of why old specimens look so different from one another. Zaragoza's had three main branches taken out of it at some point and came out the far side as a parasol, a flat horizontal crown on a short trunk. Florence's has never been bred for anything: over five metres round, standing alone at a residential junction, and known locally as Spino di Giuda, which people regularly confuse with the pink flowered tree of the same legend. Copenhagen's has been surveyed and remeasured since 1941, twelve metres then and sixteen in 2019.

species.name: Hornbeam
species.intro: Carpinus betulus is Europe's shear-proof hedge tree, planted by the thousand for its density and its patience under a blade, which is why a hornbeam left alone to grow into its full, fluted-trunked shape reads as a surprise. Salzburg's, outside the old biology institute on Freisaalweg, is put at more than 200 years and carries a strikingly round, globe-shaped crown on several stems. York's cut-leaved hornbeam is hollow and curls into itself, its canopy low enough to brush the grass. Copenhagen's in Frederiksberg Have is the Pacifier Tree, harvested bare every November of the dummies local toddlers tie to it. And Enschede shows what the hedge habit can do at scale: the Beukenberceau of Van Heekpark, the beech arbour, is about a hundred hornbeams clipped into a green tunnel for about a century, and contains no beech at all.

species.name: Horse Chestnut
species.intro: Every conker in Europe descends from a handful of mountain ravines in northern Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, the only places the horse chestnut still grows wild and where it is now classed as vulnerable. Everywhere else it is a planted tree, and cities planted it hard. Vienna lined its grandest avenue with chestnuts from 1840. Munich's brewers put them over their beer cellars, because the species throws heavy shade from shallow roots that will not force their way into a vault, and the beer garden followed from there. Geneva went further than anyone: since 1818 an official has walked to a designated chestnut each spring, recorded the date its first leaf opens and reported it to the press, which makes one of the longest continuous records of its kind anywhere. None of the old ones here is anywhere near the wild population.

species.name: Hungarian Oak
species.intro: Quercus frainetto is a large-leaved oak native to the Balkans and southeast Europe, reaching parks and streets further north only because someone planted it there on purpose. Its leaf is the giveaway, among the largest of any European oak and cut into many narrow lobes. Glasgow's grew from a single afternoon in April 1918: days after some British women won the vote, Louisa Lumsden planted it in Kelvingrove Park on behalf of four rival suffrage groups that agreed, for once, to plant a tree together. Krakow's, in Poland's oldest botanical garden, is 4.62 metres round. The Dutch register calls Arnhem's, in Park Zijpendaal, the tallest Hungarian oak measured in the Netherlands, leaning east from beeches that crowded it for a century. Warsaw's stands at the corner where Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage until 1942, and carries his name.

species.name: Indian Banyan
species.intro: An Indian banyan does not grow a single trunk so much as recruit one. Aerial roots drop from its limbs, thicken into props where they reach the ground, and fuse with their neighbours into a mass that a tape measure reads as one continuous trunk, which is why the girth can run to absurd lengths without the tree being especially old. Brisbane's, in the City Botanic Gardens since the 1870s, measures 49 metres round. Singapore's in Tiong Bahru Park reached 22.8 metres of girth in under sixty years. Hawaii planted them in every town square. The Lahaina Banyan, set out in 1873 to mark fifty years of the town's first Protestant mission, grew sixteen trunks under a crown covering two thirds of an acre; the 2023 fire that destroyed the courthouse beside it scorched the tree and took much of its canopy, and it is still standing.

species.name: Indian Laurel Fig
species.intro: Hong Kong keeps a category of tree that almost nowhere else bothers with. A stone wall tree grows straight out of a masonry retaining wall, roots threaded down through the joints, and the department responsible for several of them is not the one that runs the parks but the one that looks after government masonry. Twenty-seven of them line three walls on Forbes Street, and when engineers planned to extend the MTR through Kennedy Town the station was rerouted rather than the wall removed. The species is common enough that the city plants it by the thousand and almost never lets one grow old. The exception is the King Banyan in Kowloon Park, put at four hundred years and still the largest urban tree in the city after a 2007 typhoon took a third of its trunk. In Okinawa, a whole village carried one banyan to where it stands now.

species.name: Japanese Bay Tree
species.intro: Tabunoki, the Japanese bay tree, is the backbone of the evergreen laurel forest that once covered lowland western Japan before farmland replaced it. What survives mostly survives on shrine ground, soil nobody ploughed, built on or sold, and several stand in exactly that condition: hamlet shrines in the hills north of Hiroshima, each past three metres round and not one line published about it beyond a government surveyor's bare measurement. The record thins further from any city. Kanazawa's Hongakuji tabunoki, 8.4 metres round in a graveyard behind the hall, is the biggest tree in its quarter and one of the least visited. Kamakura's stands beside one of the most photographed level crossings in Japan, where the Enoden train passes within a couple of metres of the torii. Ground bark from this species was once the standard binder in Japanese incense.

species.name: Japanese Black Pine
species.intro: Pinus thunbergii is the pine of the Japanese coast, tough enough for salt spray and heavy snow, and gardeners have spent centuries training it into shapes weather alone never would. The Yogo Pine at Zenyoji in Tokyo, said to be over six hundred years old, is eight metres tall and spreads over more than eight hundred square metres on eighty-two wooden props; in 1980 a sumo referee was called in to settle whether it or a rival in Kagawa was Japan's finest pine, and ruled them joint champions. Kanazawa strings ropes from a pole above its Karasaki pine every November so wet snow cannot break the limbs, the rigging that has become the picture of the city in winter. Tokyo's Hamarikyu pine grows in a garden the bay still floods on purpose, and Nara's is the fattest survivor of centuries of planting for looks.

species.name: Japanese Cedar
species.intro: A picture scroll donated to Kasuga Taisha in 1309 shows this shrine's great cedar as a sapling. Seven centuries on it is roughly eight metres round and twenty five tall, and it is the same organism, which makes it one of very few ancient trees anywhere that can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. A second tree took root in its base and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof; the hole is still there. Fukuoka's cedar at Kashii Shrine is traditionally dated at about 1,800 years, from a legend that Empress Jingu pushed a branch from her armour into the ground here. Kyoto's stands in the old imperial timber forest and layers under heavy snow, rooting where the trunk is pinned down.

species.name: Japanese Chinquapin
species.intro: Sudajii, the Japanese chinquapin, was the dominant tree of the evergreen broadleaf forest that once covered lowland western Japan, before it was cleared for rice, timber and capital cities, so a mature one standing inside a city today is a leftover of the landscape the city replaced. Kyoto's grows at the Omiya gate of Kyoto Gyoen, on ground that outlasted the forest around it. Kanazawa's pair flank the entrance of the old Ishikawa prefectural office, made a National Natural Monument in 1943, built low and broad rather than tall. Tokyo's, roughly four hundred years old and eight metres round, grows on the former Hosokawa estate where Oishi Kuranosuke is said to have been held after the Ako Incident of 1701.

species.name: Japanese Fir / Momi
species.intro: Momi, the Japanese fir, is a warm-temperate species of Honshu and Kyushu that favours cool upland shrine groves and dislikes heat. The old ones here grow within a few kilometres of each other in the hills around Higashi-Hiroshima, and none carries a recorded age: Japan's giant-tree register measures girth, not years. Uneyama Shrine's fir, at 3.4 metres, stands in a grove the prefecture designated in 1987 and later lost trees to a typhoon; written accounts of the grove name five other species and never this one. Hongu Hachiman's, also 3.4 metres, shares its hilltop with cedars by the dozen and a 1701 hall the city protects as an important cultural property. Ashuku Hachiman's matches them, and the one behind Morimasa Shrine measured exactly three metres in the 2000 survey, which is to say it qualified for the register by nothing at all.

species.name: Japanese Maple
species.intro: Japanese maples are usually shrubs, small enough to see over, so a specimen that clears a metre round and earns a place on an official monumental-tree register is genuinely unusual. The Netherlands has two on this site: one in Arnhem's Park Angerenstein, dated to the 1920s and protected on dendrological grounds alone, nothing historical attached, the tree itself being the whole reason; and one in Maastricht's Waldeckpark, whose register band of 1910 to 1920 sits oddly early against the park's own 1921 layout, a discrepancy nobody has resolved. Japan's own entry needs no register to prove itself: a temple maple in Iwaki whose age nobody will state, but whose autumn colour the city government tracks and publishes year by year, which is a different, more useful kind of record than an age nobody can verify.

species.name: Japanese Nutmeg-yew
species.intro: Torreya nucifera, called kaya in Japan, is a slow evergreen conifer that looks the same in February as in August, which is part of why its oldest specimens went unnoticed for centuries; its wood is what every serious go player wants a board cut from. Japan names three great kaya trees. The one at Yokomuro in Maebashi earns its place on girth, 8.1 metres round, and the one at Kitahama stands alone behind a white fence on farmland near Hamamatsu, viewed from the road. Yono no Okaya in Saitama City is traditionally dated to the 1030s. The kaya at Nagoya Castle carries a stranger claim: the first Owari lord ate its nuts before marching on Osaka in 1615, and his successors kept eating them every New Year after. None gives up its age easily; surveys and temple tradition disagree, sometimes by centuries.

species.name: Japanese Pagoda Tree
species.intro: This tree flowers cream in August, when almost nothing else in a city is doing anything at all, and that habit is most of the reason it was ever planted. Despite the name it is Chinese rather than Japanese, where it is the scholar tree, and it reached European gardens in the eighteenth century. The oldest are in Asia. Beijing's Tang Scholar Tree in Beihai Park is traditionally dated to about 1,200 years, and the Qianlong Emperor built a pavilion so he could sit and look at it. In the courtyard of Jogyesa in Seoul, one put at 400 to 450 years disappears under thousands of paper lanterns every Buddha's Birthday. Kew's, planted in 1762, is one of the five veterans the garden's first curator nicknamed the Old Lions, and Hamburg's, six metres round, was named a German national heritage tree in 2026.

species.name: Japanese Red Pine
species.intro: Pinus densiflora is the red pine of Japan, called akamatsu for the orange-red plates its bark breaks into higher up the trunk, brighter the further you look. Matsutake, the country's most expensive mushroom, forms almost exclusively on its roots, which is one reason old red pine groves like the one at Hongu Hachiman Shrine in Higashi-Hiroshima have been tended for centuries. In the mountains above Shokawa, a single red pine forks two metres up into three trunks reaching the same height, a shape the surveyor who recorded it compared to Neptune's trident; the marker beside it, dated 1971, still calls it Mumaya Sanbonmatsu, the name three pines for a tree that is only one. In Seattle's Kubota Garden, a Japanese immigrant gardener planted an avenue of about twenty in the 1920s; a century of storms has left exactly one standing.

species.name: Japanese White Pine
species.intro: Three of these pines have been shaped by hand for six centuries or more, and all three are in Kyoto. The one beside the pond at Kinkaku-ji was a bonsai in a pot belonging to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the shogun who built the Golden Pavilion; after his death in 1408 it was planted out and clipped, generation after generation, into a sailing ship with its bow pointed west toward the Pure Land. Yoshimine-dera's grows almost flat instead of upward, named the playing dragon in 1857 and once fifty metres end to end, until bark beetles in 1994 cost it fifteen. Hosen-in's is the subject of a picture frame garden: you sit on a red felt cushion in a wooden hall and look at it through a doorway. In Seattle's Kubota Garden, one was the favourite tree of the gardener who spent his life making the place.

species.name: Japanese Wisteria
species.intro: Japanese wisteria is a vine, and it can outlive almost any tree around it. The Great Wisteria of Ushijima, near Kasukabe, is put at roughly 1,200 years, four metres round at the base and trained across a trellis of 600 to 700 square metres; it is the only wisteria Japan protects as a Special Natural Monument, and the garden around it opens for about three weeks a year. At Yama-jinja, near Mount Fuji, two vines seeded themselves and climbed unassisted, granted national monument status in 1928. Ichinohe's vine, several hundred years old by local account, is untrained too. Tokyo's Kameido Tenjin wisteria has a claim stranger than its age: art historians trace a line from Hiroshige's 1856 print of it, arched drum bridge and all, to the wisteria Monet later planted at Giverny.

species.name: Judas Tree
species.intro: The flowers come straight out of the bark. Cercis siliquastrum is cauliflorous, so in spring, before a single leaf opens, rosy purple blossom breaks directly from the trunk and the old wood, and the tree looks briefly upholstered rather than in bloom. The name is old and unkind, from the tradition that Judas hanged himself from one. It is usually a small tree that goes sideways: the one on Placa Joanic in Barcelona is five metres tall under a crown ten metres across. Seville's in the Alcázar's English Garden has done what the species rarely bothers to, reaching sixteen metres. The oldest stands on the cold north side of a church on the Great Hungarian Plain at Mélykút, about 250 years old, a long way from the warm hillsides it belongs to. Go in spring, before the leaves.

species.name: Kapok
species.intro: Kapok is a rainforest giant, native to tropical lowland forest where it pushes its crown above the canopy on wide buttress roots. Chiapa de Corzo in Mexico was built around one: when the town was founded on the Grijalva river in 1528, La Pochota already stood where the plaza now sits, and its position was used to lay out the original street grid. A neighbour irritated by its fluff set part of it alight in 1945, and the scorched limb kept growing. Singapore's, at the foot of Mount Faber, has an 11.55 metre girth, among the largest trunks on the city's heritage register. Honolulu's was planted around 1851 by the physician William Hillebrand on his own homestead and is now the oldest tree in the botanical garden later built around it. Lima's holds on in a coastal desert city of grey sea fog.

species.name: Katsura
species.intro: Katsura grows wild in the old forests of Japan, and its oldest trees rarely keep their first trunk. The Great Katsura of Itoi, in a gorge near Asago, is a hollow stump ringed by roughly eighty root suckers, over 18 metres round together and put at more than a thousand years; a travelling priest is said to have draped his robe over it and prayed for rain. At the Koganeyu hot spring in Sapporo, a katsura became a god, worshipped as Fudo Myoo standing in tree form. The species travels well. The Sapporo Katsuras in Boston grew from seed William S. Clark sent from Japan to the Arnold Arboretum in 1878. Every October the yellowing leaves give off maltol, and the ground under a katsura from Gdansk to Pittsburgh smells of burnt sugar.

species.name: Kauri
species.intro: A kauri does not look like other big trees, because it throws away the parts that would make it look like one. It sheds its lower branches as it grows and flakes off its lower bark in plates, which keeps climbers and epiphytes off the trunk, so what you walk up to is a bare grey column with the crown a long way overhead. Tāne Mahuta in the Waipoua Forest is 45 metres tall and most of that is column. Te Matua Ngahere, in the same forest, went the other way: shorter, squatter, and thicker round than anything else standing in New Zealand. Both are protected from their visitors as much as for them, because kauri dieback travels on the mud in a shoe tread. On the Coromandel, loggers left the Square Kauri standing because its angular trunk was the wrong shape to mill.

species.name: Kentucky Coffeetree
species.intro: The genus this tree belongs to has exactly two species in the world, this one and a Chinese cousin, and it survives mostly because people kept planting it. The Kentucky coffeetree takes its English name from settlers who roasted and ground its seeds as a coffee substitute, a recipe not worth reviving since the raw seeds and pods are toxic. What gives it away is timing: it leafs out later than almost anything nearby, often not before late May, then drops early and spends the rest of the year as bare, blunt grey branches, so stark that the Dutch call it the dead men's bones tree and the French call it chicot, stump. Bordeaux's, over 130 years old, is fenced and pruned around cavities in its trunk. Ottawa's went in near Queen Elizabeth Driveway around the turn of the twentieth century, and Idaho's largest stands in Boise's Julia Davis Park.

species.name: Kurogane Holly
species.intro: Kurogane holly is a glossy-leaved evergreen of warm southern Japan that rarely gets large: Japan's giant-tree register will not count a trunk under three metres. Two of the three the site maps clear that easily. Kagoshima's Terukuni Park holly is thickest at 4.85 metres, multi-stemmed, standing at the crossroads where four national highways end; the city made it preserved tree number 6 in 1974, its first batch of designations. A second Kagoshima tree, in Gionnosu Park on land reclaimed from the Inari river mouth, has reached 2.4 metres since roughly the 1890s and now shares its ground with three nineteenth-century stone bridges moved there after a 1993 flood destroyed their originals. Higashi-Hiroshima's, on the temple mountain of Fukujo-ji, measures 3.1 metres and is the only one of the three with no recorded age.

species.name: Lacebark Pine
species.intro: Most pines are planted for their needles or their shape. This one is planted for its bark, which sheds in irregular plates of olive, grey-green and chalk white until an old trunk looks close to ivory, a trait so distinctive the species barely needs its Latin name to identify it. Pinus bungeana is native to China, and every specimen mapped here arrived somewhere else as a deliberate transplant. Lyon's, in the Parc de la Tête d'Or arboretum, was probably planted in 1856 and is known locally as the Pin de Napoléon. Pittsburgh's stands in Mellon Park, named to the city's own official Remarkable Trees list in 2023 for its bark alone, with no age on record. Seoul's, beside the Constitutional Court in Jae-dong, carries a six-century legend that a Ming dynasty envoy brought it as a gift, unproven but attached to the tree for generations. Three cities so far.

species.name: Large-leaved Lime
species.intro: A lime has marked the exact spot where three Brussels communes meet since at least 1777, and that is the sort of job this species keeps getting: boundary post, landmark, court, dance floor, the tree a place organises itself around. Schenklengsfeld held its court under its lime from 1557 to 1796; at 17.91 metres round it has the largest trunk circumference of any tree in Germany, and in the 2018 heatwave the village fire brigade pumped 100,000 litres of water onto it. Heede's is widely reported as the thickest lime in Europe and sits on the village coat of arms. Prague has one a president refused to lose, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk having had a castle terrace built around it. Telling a large-leaved lime from a small-leaved one is harder than it sounds, and under Nuremberg's 400 year old tree the sign and the botanists still disagree.

species.name: Lime
species.intro: These are the limes nobody has narrowed to a single species, planted or grown before anyone thought to record which Tilia they were, which is common enough with a genus this widely hybridised that the honest label is simply Tilia sp. Amsterdam's Wilhelminalinde went into the ground on the Kalverstraat to mark Queen Wilhelmina's 1898 coronation and is a tidy, dateable 128 years old. Nuremberg's gnarled lime at the Hallerwiese has taken lightning and storm damage across some three and a half centuries and is still putting on growth, damaged and healthy in the same trunk. Frankfurt's eight-stemmed linden in Grüneburgpark is not one tree that happened to fork; it is a deliberate bundle planting, several saplings set into one hole so they would fuse into a single crown, rare enough to be a protected natural monument in its own right.

species.name: Lombardy Poplar
species.intro: Lombardy poplar is the columnar form of black poplar, propagated only from cuttings of a single line, so every one traces back to the same origin tree and none of them set seed. It is also famously short-lived: usually rotten by fifty, gone by seventy, planted by the million and protected almost nowhere. The old ones here are the exceptions. Amsterdam's stands as a living pilaster in the Rijksmuseum's garden of salvaged doorways, planted within a few decades of the museum's 1885 opening. Seattle's grew up beside the temporary Fine Arts Palace built for the 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition and has now outlasted the building it was planted to frame. Portland's, out on the eastern edge of the city, carries the widest trunk on the entire heritage tree register at 9.75 metres round, an absurd measurement for a tree built to be thin.

species.name: London Plane
species.intro: The London plane is a tree that a city adopted and then named after itself. It is a hybrid, a cross between the American sycamore and the Oriental plane that appeared in Europe in the 1600s and turned out to be almost indestructible in a dirty city: it shrugs off soot, tolerates brutal pruning, and sheds its bark in patches to slough off pollution. That made it the default street tree of industrial London, and from there of Paris, Amsterdam and half the capitals of Europe. The oldest specimens are now three centuries old and enormous, and because the tree was planted everywhere, the remarkable ones hide in plain sight: a churchyard in the City of London, a Mayfair square, a riverside suburb. These are the London planes mapped on the site so far, oldest first.

species.name: Maple
species.intro: These are maples recorded at genus level, either because nobody has settled the species or because the sources disagree. The best of them are a pair of hananoki, Acer pycnanthum, in two hamlets of Higashiomi in Shiga, 600 metres apart and named National Natural Monuments on the same day in March 1921 as the westernmost wild specimens known. Hananoki means flower tree, and in early spring red flowers crowd the bare twigs before a single leaf opens. The southern one, 5.2 metres round, lost its main trunk in 2010; the northern one has lost two trunks to storms, in 1866 and 1950, and stands on six limbs. In Žilina, the national register calls a street maple a sugar maple and Slovak Wikipedia calls it a silver maple. If you know your maples and walk past, look up and tell us.

species.name: Mastic Tree
species.intro: Pistacia lentiscus spends most of its life as a shrub, a low, dense presence across Mediterranean scrubland that most walkers step past without a glance. Left standing for long enough, on the right ground, it does something else: pushes up a real trunk and takes on the shape and size of a proper tree. The species is best known for mastic resin, tapped for millennia on the Greek island of Chios. The oldest here is U Listincu on the Gattone plain in eastern Corsica, reckoned at 700 to 1,000 years and rooted in the stonework of a Roman-era structure; it was France's Tree of the Year in 2011. Istanbul's Florya mastic is put at roughly 500 years. Catalonia protects a mastic at Torrent by law, and Barcelona and Palma each keep one that grew up instead of out.

species.name: Mediterranean Cypress
species.intro: The Mediterranean cypress is the most recognisable punctuation mark in landscape: a dark green exclamation point that Van Gogh painted obsessively and that Greeks, Romans and Persians planted at graves for three thousand years before him. The mourning association is practical as much as poetic, because the tree is close to immortal by garden standards, evergreen, drought-proof and content on thin stony soil, exactly the qualities you want from something meant to outlast grief. Its species name sempervirens simply means always alive. Individual cypresses in Iran are credibly claimed at four thousand years. The cypresses mapped so far stand in cemeteries, monastery courtyards and old gardens, oldest first.

species.name: Mediterranean Hackberry
species.intro: Italians call this tree spaccasassi, the stone splitter, because its roots get into paving and open it, and cities across southern Europe plant it in their squares regardless, because little else gives that much shade on that little water. Celtis australis is deep rooted, drought hardy and indifferent to heat, with a smooth grey trunk closer to a beech than an oak and small dark berries that taste faintly of dates. Mostly it is treated as background, which is why the exceptions stand out. Istanbul protects one by name. Munich registers a group of eight as an extremely rare species, five hundred kilometres north of where the tree grows wild. Varedo's, near Milan, is five metres round and 27 metres tall. And a hackberry in Zaragoza came third in Spain's national tree of the year vote in December 2025, put forward by five neighbourhood associations.

species.name: Mexican Cypress
species.intro: A Mexican tree carries the name lusitanica, meaning Portuguese, and the tree responsible for the mistake is still standing. When Philip Miller described the species in 1768 he was working from cypresses growing at Bucaco, where Carmelite monks had planted them, and named it for where he found it rather than where it came from. The Cedro de Sao Jose, about 380 years old, is one of those trees, and a second stands further along the Via Sacra beside the station marking Christ's first fall. Portugal has called the species cedro-do-Bucaco ever since, which compounds the error, since it is a cypress and no kind of cedar. Lisbon's first legally protected tree, presiding over the Praca do Principe Real, goes by that name too. The oldest is in Granada at roughly 440 years, named for San Juan de la Cruz.

species.name: Mexican Fan Palm
species.intro: The building these palms were planted for was demolished in 1951 and the palms are still standing: seven Mexican fan palms in a line at the Palacio de Cristal in Porto, roughly 160 years old, outliving the glass hall they were meant to frame. That is the pattern with this species in Europe, which arrives as instant architecture and then outlasts it. Granada's four went up over the Plaza de Gracia in 1923, the year the palace behind them was finished. Palermo's line an avenue in the Villa Giulia, which opened in 1778 and is generally counted as Italy's first public garden. Valencia has two from the early twentieth century, one of them the result of a gardener's error that left it standing where it should not have been, taller and thinner than every palm around it.

species.name: Mexican White Oak
species.intro: Quercus polymorpha barely counts as an American oak. Its native range runs through Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras, crossing into the United States only once, in a single wild stand north of the Rio Grande in Texas. Everywhere else it grows on purpose: gardeners value it for holding leathery, plain-edged leaves through most of a mild winter and for shrugging off heat that would stress most oaks. Houston's own specimen, in a Bellaire park, is the nearest thing to a native tree the site maps for the species, broader than it is tall at nearly 20 metres across. Cross the Atlantic and it turns rare: Barcelona's Ciutadella park holds the only one in Catalonia, leaning over the sand since about 1887, and Valencia's Botanic Garden keeps a second, 3.44 metres round. One species, and almost nobody outside its home range plants it.

species.name: Monkey Puzzle
species.intro: Every branch of a monkey puzzle is sheathed in thick, overlapping, scale-like leaves that stay sharp for decades, an armour scientists think evolved to keep long-necked herbivorous dinosaurs from stripping the crown, tens of millions of years before Araucaria araucana ever left the volcanic slopes of central Chile and Argentina. A Cornish gardener supposedly coined the English name in the 1830s, remarking that climbing one would puzzle a monkey; Victorian Britain then planted it obsessively, which is why a grove of them can still be found guarding a Scottish castle. It is Chile's national tree and endangered in the wild, felled for timber and burned in forest fires faster than it regrows. These are the monkey puzzles mapped on the site so far, oldest first.

species.name: Monterey Cypress
species.intro: In the wild this tree grows on two headlands near Monterey in California and nowhere else on earth, together covering less than a square kilometre. The Lone Cypress grows out of a granite headland above Carmel Bay by itself, propped by a retaining wall and steel cables since the 1940s; it was probably seeded around 1750, close to the ceiling for its species, and the Pebble Beach Company has held a trademark on its drawing since 1919. The Old Veteran at Point Lobos has been painted since 1879. Give the species a mild wet winter anywhere and it grows fast and enormous, which is how it reached Italian and Portuguese gardens within a few decades of being described. Trieste's stands at Miramare, put in after 1856, and Lucca's on the San Regolo bastion of the city's Renaissance walls.

species.name: Montezuma Cypress
species.intro: Taxodium mucronatum is Mexico's national tree, the ahuehuete, planted at springs by the Aztecs, and it holds the stoutest trunk on earth. El Árbol del Tule, in a church courtyard in Oaxaca, measured 42 metres round in a 2005 laser survey; its trunk is so lobed that botanists long assumed it was several trees fused together until DNA work in the 1990s showed it is one. Its age is put at 1,400 to 1,600 years on growth-rate grounds. Mexico City began protecting its ahuehuetes by name in 2025: El Sabino de San Juan is 18.5 metres round. In Europe, Florence's is seven metres around and was hit by lightning barely a decade ago, Naples has nicknamed its own the Tree of Thule, and Madrid's in the Retiro's parterre comes with two origin stories that cannot both be true.

species.name: Moreton Bay Fig
species.intro: A Moreton Bay fig announces itself at ground level first: buttress roots the height of a person come snaking across the earth like walls, and the trunk they support looks less grown than poured. In its native eastern Australia the species often starts life as a strangler high in another tree, sends roots down, and eventually stands on its own; planted in the mild coastal cities of Europe and beyond in the 19th century, it skipped the strangling and went straight to the monumental, single trees shading entire plazas within a human lifetime. It needs frost-free air, which is why every great specimen marks a mild microclimate. The Moreton Bay figs mapped so far are listed largest and oldest first.

species.name: Muku Tree
species.intro: Muku is a tree most of Japan has walked past without learning its name. Its leaves dry rough enough that woodworkers once used them to sand wood, horn and lacquer, and in autumn it drops small dark fruit that birds strip and people once ate straight off the ground. It seeds easily and grows fast on undisturbed soil, which is why it turns up old on shrine land: nobody there had a reason to cut it. Two stand on hamlet shrine ground north of Hiroshima, at Kirihata and Furosaki, each measured once by a government survey and never written about since. The third, at Kyoto's Omiya Gate in Kyoto Gyoen, has not even been formally identified: its bark and leaves suggest muku, but nobody has taped its girth or entered it on a register.

species.name: Narrow-Leaved Ash
species.intro: Fraxinus angustifolia is the ash of southern Europe, a riverside species that follows watercourses through country too dry for its northern cousin, and for centuries it was pollarded for fodder and tool handles rather than left to grow free. That habit shapes the old ones differently. Girona's, at L'Aulet in Vidreres, carries a 5.90 metre trunk built from decades of repeated cutting, a short massive base under a crown that is all regrowth. Barcelona's grew the opposite way, straight up a Montjuic quarry pit whose damp, sheltered air let it reach 29 metres, the tallest of its species recorded anywhere in Catalonia. Leiden's was planted in a Dutch botanical garden around 1818 and grafted, the swelling from that graft still visible after two centuries. York's willow-leaved form is a Yorkshire champion at twenty-four metres.

species.name: Norfolk Island Hibiscus
species.intro: Lagunaria patersonii comes from one small island in the Tasman Sea, Norfolk Island, a native range of about thirty-five square kilometres that makes almost anywhere else it grows a transplant by definition. Coastal cities plant it for a practical reason: it tolerates salt wind and poor soil better than most ornamental trees, and it flowers in summer in pale pink cups that pass for a small hibiscus. The seed pods carry the species' other reputation, packed with fine hairs that itch for hours if opened carelessly, which is why English speakers call it the itchy bomb tree and Catalans the pica-pica. Barcelona's in the Teatre Grec gardens is about 103 years old, and Seville's in the Jardines de la Madrina has reached 22 metres.

species.name: Norfolk Island Pine
species.intro: The entire species comes from one Pacific island eight kilometres long, and it now stands over port cities from Hobart to the Atlantic coast of Portugal. Araucaria heterophylla grows in regular tiers, a candelabra of horizontal branches on a dead straight stem, which is why it reads as a tree drawn by a child and why nineteenth century gardeners could not resist it. Height is usually the point. The Malaga specimen, around 200 years old, is the tallest in its province; Barcelona's clears 27 metres above one of the most densely built neighbourhoods in Europe; Sintra's is the tallest tree at Monserrate. Setubal has six of them at 26 metres, standing in a ring around one old circular stone tank with a fountain in the middle. Hobart's is the one nearest home, and a local nurseryman asked in 2025 to name his favourite tree in the city picked it.

species.name: Northern Red Oak
species.intro: Northern red oak is the oak of eastern North America, and Europe planted it for one thing: nothing native turns that colour in autumn. Brussels Environment's own walking route through the Parc d'Egmont gives up on describing its red oak and tells you to come back in autumn instead. At home the old ones are older. In 2020 Toronto's city council bought a private house on Coral Gable Drive and tore it down to save Zhelevo, an oak of roughly 300 years left from the savannah along the old Carrying Place trail. Toronto's official tree, in Kew Gardens, is 5.3 metres round with one limb sagging to the grass. In Europe, Prague's stands on the island where the city's archers used to practise, and the Baarn oak, roughly 175 years old, wears a ring carrying words the municipality asked its residents to write in 2021.

species.name: Norway Maple
species.intro: Norway maple is one of the most planted street trees in northern Europe, valued for tolerating road salt, compacted soil and bad air, and just as routinely cut back once it outgrows its spot, so an old one is what a city decided to keep. Riga's Zasulauks maple, beside a wooden tenement in the Kalnciema Quarter, measured four metres round in 1975 and 5.34 by 2009, a third of its waistline added in thirty-four years. One in Den Bosch stands on a two-metre-thick fortress bastion built in 1634. Munich protects two under a 2021 natural monument ordinance: one on Mondstrasse defines its square, the other on Herrnstrasse survives for being rare at its size among inner-city courtyards. Snap a leaf stalk and it bleeds white sap, the surest way to tell a Norway maple from the sycamore it is otherwise mistaken for.

species.name: Norway Spruce
species.intro: Norway spruce belongs to the mountain forests of Scandinavia and central Europe, and on a Swedish fell it may hold the oldest living thing on this site. Old Tjikko, on Fulufjället, is a scrappy spruce about five metres tall whose visible trunk is only a few centuries old; the root system beneath it has been carbon-dated to about 9,550 years, sending up a new trunk each time the last one dies. Lithuania's Witch's Spruce breaks at knee height into eighteen stems that climb together to 32 metres, a habit specialists know of nowhere else in Europe. In cities it is always somebody's choice. Sofia's tallest was planted in 1885 by the writer Ivan Vazov and has outgrown the bust raised to him later, and Helsinki's Independence Spruce was sown on 6 December 1917, the day the Finnish Parliament accepted the declaration of independence.

species.name: Oak
species.intro: These oaks carry only their genus, Quercus, because nobody has yet taken a leaf or an acorn stalk close enough to say which species each one is. That gap does not make them less worth the walk. The oak on the Hrádek at Lukavice, put at nearly 800 years, survived an estate manager stripping cartloads of soil from its roots and was voted Czech Tree of the Year in 2024. Belfast's Belvoir Oak got down to six acorns one winter and is still standing. Ypres's Christusboom has been cut to nothing by two wars and grown back from the stump both times. Austin's Auction Oaks shaded the 1839 sale of town lots before the city existed. Hainich's Betteleiche is hollow because medieval friars are said to have carved it out to keep alms dry. If you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile oak at a glance, tell us.

species.name: Ohatsuki Ginkgo
species.intro: Most ginkgos hang their seeds on a stalk, apart from the branch. This mutation grows them straight out of the leaf blade itself, first described to Japanese science in July 1891 from a specimen in Minobu, Yamanashi. Only seven trees of the kind hold National Natural Monument status, and an unexplained three of them stand within two kilometres of each other in that one district: one toppled by Typhoon Trami in 2018 and still fruiting from its fallen trunk, another the sole male of the seven, its single fertile branch discovered only in 2011 after decades of nothing, and a third that local legend has the monk Nichiren planting himself in 1282. None has a documented planting date; all three ages here stay broad estimates rather than measurements.

species.name: Olive
species.intro: No tree has been in continuous employment longer than the olive. Humans have cultivated it for at least six thousand years, and individual trees stay on the payroll for a thousand or more, still setting fruit on trunks so twisted and split they look geological rather than botanical. That endurance is built in: an olive regrows from its base after fire, frost or felling, so the gnarled base can be many centuries older than every branch above it. The ancient world treated the tree accordingly, as the literal embodiment of peace, victory and civic pride; Athens named itself over one. The olives mapped so far, some relocated into city squares, some in their original groves, are listed oldest first.

species.name: Ombu
species.intro: The ombu is not wood at all. Phytolacca dioica is a giant herb that behaves like a tree, a soft stemmed relative of spinach whose swollen base is water storing tissue you could dent with a thumbnail, laid down for the dry seasons of the Argentine pampas it comes from. It grows fast and cannot be aged by counting rings, which is why the one in Cadiz is undated. What it does instead is get very wide. Two in a single Lisbon garden came out at 10.45 and 10.4 metres around, and the one at Largo do Limoeiro is wider than the house fronts on the street. Seville's is credited to seed that Christopher Columbus's son brought back around 1529. In Lima, the ombu at the Quinta de los Libertadores is said to have grown from seed José de San Martín carried up from Argentina in 1821.

species.name: Oriental Plane
species.intro: Before the London plane existed, its eastern parent was already the most storied shade tree in the world. Hippocrates is said to have taught medicine under an Oriental plane on Kos, Herodotus tells of a Persian king who halted an entire army to decorate one, and across Greece, Turkey and the Balkans the village square and the plane above it grew up as a single institution. The species hollows as it ages without weakening much, which lets individual trees pass five hundred years while whole communities hold meetings, weddings and cafes inside and beneath them. The Oriental planes mapped so far include spring-side giants that predate the towns around them, oldest first.

species.name: Osage Orange
species.intro: Every autumn these trees drop green spheres the size of a grapefruit that nothing alive wants to eat. The fruit of Maclura pomifera looks like a brain, weighs a kilo or more and seems to have been built for animals that vanished from North America thousands of years ago. The tree takes its name from the Osage nation, who made bows from the wood, which was traded far beyond their own territory. American farmers then found a second use: planted close and cut back, osage orange grows into a thorn hedge nothing can push through, and thousands of miles of it went in through the 1850s until barbed wire made it pointless. Abroad it is a curiosity: Caserta's has grown in a royal garden for about 200 years, and Melbourne's has stood beside the Yarra since the 1860s. Stand under one in November and watch your head.

species.name: Pecan
species.intro: A pecan is an odd thing to find towering over a European garden, and yet two of the tallest trees mapped here are exactly that: 38 metres in Bordeaux's Jardin Public, the tallest tree in the garden, and the tallest in the Real Alcazar of Seville, both outgrowing everything planted around them. The species belongs to the river bottoms of Texas and the lower Mississippi, and Dallas keeps its native range on show: a pecan that stood at the Trinity River crossing before the first bridge went up in 1855, a grove on Cedar Creek in Moore Park that predates the park's founding in 1938, and a marker tree whose trunk runs along the ground for about 25 feet. Austin's Mother Pecan, in Zilker Park, is a tree people mostly know from lying underneath it.

species.name: Pedunculate Oak
species.intro: Foresters used to say an oak spends three hundred years growing, three hundred resting, and three hundred slowly dying. The pedunculate oak, Quercus robur, is the tree that adage was built on: the classic broad English oak of parkland and legend, though it grows just as happily in Amsterdam or Berlin. Its trick for extreme age is to hollow out. As the heartwood rots away the tree keeps only its living outer sleeve, which lightens the load and can extend its life past a thousand years. That is why the oldest oaks are the fattest and most gnarled, not the tallest. Kings prized them enough to wall entire parks around them, and their timber built the navies and cathedrals of northern Europe. These are the ancient oaks mapped on the site so far, oldest first.

species.name: Pedunculate Oak, columnar form
species.intro: Bred to stay narrow instead of spreading, the columnar or fastigiate form of the pedunculate oak grows in a tight upright column that reads as a poplar until you look at the leaf. Nurseries have propagated Quercus robur 'Fastigiata' since the nineteenth century for that shape, which is why it usually turns up in pairs flanking a gate rather than standing alone. Krakow protected the oldest in 2008, a lone tree at a crossroads whose 288-centimetre girth puts its age at roughly 140 to 210 years, calculated rather than recorded. Warsaw has two matched pairs: one flanking the university botanical garden's observatory entrance, designated in 2024, the other on ul. Lowicka, protected in 2013 and visible from the street. Nobody has dated the Warsaw pairs; fastigiate oaks spread through European gardens over two centuries, which rules out a single planting year.

species.name: Peruvian Pepper
species.intro: The pink peppercorns sold in an expensive pepper grinder are not pepper. They come from this tree, an Andean member of the cashew family with no botanical relation to black pepper, carried out of South America by Spanish colonial trade in the sixteenth century and planted everywhere the climate allowed. Its weeping grey-green foliage moves in any wind at all, and a crushed leaf smells sharply of pepper, the family trait that earned it the name. In Melbourne it became the tree of colonial Australia, planted by the thousand along stock routes and rail sidings because it shrugged off drought and neglect; the one in Richmond's Madden Grove stands on ground set aside as a survey paddock in 1836, one of the city's earliest public reservations. Barcelona and Setubal took the opposite path, planting it singly as an ornamental curiosity, the softest tree in each garden it stands in.

species.name: Pin Oak
species.intro: Pin oak is a North American swamp species, native to wet bottomland from the Great Lakes down through the Mississippi valley, that reached European gardens at the start of the nineteenth century and became a Dutch park favourite decades later. The oldest here is an 1840s planting in Haarlem's Frederikspark; Apeldoorn's in the Oranjepark dates from the 1860s, Eindhoven's at Prinsenhof from around 1900, and Sittard's in the Stadspark from around 1910. It is easy to place once you have seen one. The lower branches sweep down toward the grass while the upper ones reach up, and the leaves are cut into narrow, bristle-tipped lobes far sharper than any native oak's. The name comes from the small pin-like stubs of dead branchlets along the trunk. It holds its scarlet October colour and its dead leaves well into winter, often the last oak in a park still dressed.

species.name: Plane
species.intro: These planes carry only their genus, Platanus, because whichever register or record named them stopped there or the sources disagree: planes hybridise readily and the parents can be hard to call from bark and leaf alone. The Platane de Préty went into a mound beside the village church in 1801, in place of an elm under which justice had been dispensed, to mark priests returning after the Revolution; never pollarded, it is 34 metres tall, and France protected it in 1909. In Pisa, two sources looked at the plane of the Scuola Botanica and named two different species. The Hague's Plane of Park Hoekenburg grows over Forum Hadriani, a Roman port town. Bratislava's is 6.11 metres round, and Budapest's at Jászai Mari Square kept growing after the bridge beside it was blown up in the war. If you can tell an Oriental from a London plane, tell us.

species.name: Pohutukawa
species.intro: New Zealand's Christmas tree does its flowering here in early summer. Metrosideros excelsa covers itself in scarlet brushes at the height of the southern summer, which in Cadiz, Lisbon, Porto, Sintra and Madeira falls half a year off its native schedule and a hemisphere from home. At home it grows on sea cliffs, gripping rock with aerial roots, which is close to what the Atlantic edge of Iberia offers it. The Monserrate tree in Sintra is the oldest here, though nobody will pin it closer than somewhere between 175 and 275 years. Porto's pair on the grass at Passeio Alegre stand eleven metres apart and are barely taller than a house. Lisbon's two, in the Jardim da Parada, are ten metres apart and protected as separate trees. Funchal's grows in the Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro, a garden that holds nine more listed trees.

species.name: Poplar
species.intro: Poplars grow fast and die young, which is exactly why the old ones here stand out: each has outlasted the ordinary run for the genus by decades. None of them is famous for its age. Ofunato's Dokonjo Poplar took the 2011 tsunami half underwater and kept standing, and the city built a memorial plaza around it. Biei's Ken and Mary Tree was just a farm boundary marker until a 1972 car commercial made it one of the most photographed trees in Hokkaido. Arnhem's Wagnerlaan Poplar has an official monument listing and nothing else, not even a settled species, and Warsaw's in Park Wielkopolski got a two-line designation in 2019 that does not say which poplar it is either. The sources cannot say which poplar any of them is, only that each is a Populus. If you know one on sight, tell us.

species.name: Queensland Kauri
species.intro: Queensland kauri grows wild only in a strip of eastern Australia, but the species travelled well. Sydney's, in the Royal Botanic Garden's Palm Grove, grew from a seed picked on New Year's Day 1849 by the garden's first director. Hobart's, in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, is rare enough to carry four separate significance ratings on the city's tree register, aesthetic, dimensions, age and rarity, where most trees earn one or two. Los Angeles has two. The Huntington's was planted in 1890; in 1908 a gardener cut through its taproot to move it out of the way of the mansion and sealed the wound with a blowtorch, and in 2021 it was named California's biggest Queensland kauri, 34 metres tall. The one in Chavez Ravine Arboretum, above Dodger Stadium's parking lots, has long been called the largest in the country on reputation alone.

species.name: Rain Tree
species.intro: The rain tree gets its name from what it does at the end of the day: the leaflets fold shut at dusk and again when a storm is coming, so the rain falls straight through a canopy that looked solid an hour earlier. In Hawaii nobody calls it that. There it is the monkeypod, and it only arrived around 1847, which is why the Gulick-Rowell tree in Waimea cannot be the 200 years old that local tradition insists on, however good the story about the Indian prince is. Kauai's other one was put in by the shopkeeper whose store it still shades. Oahu's is on Japanese television most weeks as Hitachi's emblem, and almost nobody watching knows it stands in Honolulu. Singapore's spreads over a public stairway out of Fort Canning Park, so everyone taking those steps walks under it whether they look up or not.

species.name: Red Horse Chestnut
species.intro: The red horse chestnut is a cross bred deliberately, joining the white-flowered chestnut of every European avenue with a red-flowered American buckeye, first recorded in Germany around 1820. The result flowers pink in May instead of white, sets almost no spiny conkers, and largely escapes the leaf miner moth that browns out its white parent by late summer. It was planted for gardens, not found in the wild, which shows in where the old ones stand. Amersfoort's, from the 1880s, grows between the Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren and the old Varkensmarkt. In Leeuwarden one survived the redevelopment of a former hospital garden with crown anchors and a trunk wound to show for it. The one on the Wilhelminaplein has nothing written down about it at all, and in the Bronx family tradition says a Van Cortlandt planted the one on the lawn of their 1748 house.

species.name: River Red Gum
species.intro: Seville and the province of Valencia each have a record holder for height, and both are the same Australian tree, growing thousands of kilometres from where it belongs. Eucalyptus camaldulensis follows the seasonal rivers of inland Australia across almost the whole continent, surviving drought by dropping whole limbs and resprouting from the base, which is a habit that makes municipal arborists nervous. Seville pruned its 50 metre specimen in 2025 specifically to reduce the risk of falling branches, and Valencia's crews need aerial platforms and help from the fire service to reach the top of theirs, 41 metres in a park in Benimamet. Barcelona's grew up inside the walled grounds of a charity house in the Raval, which is the only reason there was open soil for it in the densest neighbourhood in the city.

species.name: Rubber Fig
species.intro: Most people know Ficus elastica as the thing in the corner of the living room that stops when it hits the ceiling. On Drosopoulou Street in Athens it is 26.55 metres tall, higher than the apartment blocks either side of it. Seville's began as one of those: a containerised specimen the city kept for dressing squares during celebrations, put into the ground in 1972 beside a monument to a bullfighter and left there. Fifty four years later its trunk is 5.86 metres round and its crown covers the whole of the Plaza del Altozano, the only shade on it. Lisbon's got out of a cracked pot in Mouraria and drove its roots into the street between two building fronts, and nobody can say who put the pot there or when. Three cities, three trees, and two of them were once in a pot.

species.name: Ryukyu Pine
species.intro: A Ryukyu pine grows along the coasts and hillsides of the Ryukyu archipelago and southern Kyushu, and the three the site maps show three different reasons a community kept one standing. Iheya's Nento Hiramatsu is the second tree on its spot: the first was felled around 1716 and, the story goes, whoever cut it down fell ill soon after, so the replacement has stood untouched for two to three centuries since. Taipei's Common Three Pines predate their own building; National Taiwan University recessed the floor plan of its teaching block rather than remove them, and laid a wooden deck around their roots. Kagoshima's coastal pine takes its name from the Ryukyu trading ships that once steered by it, a landmark from the centuries after Satsuma conquered the Ryukyu kingdom in 1609.

species.name: Sago Palm
species.intro: A sago palm is not a palm at all. Cycas revoluta belongs to the cycads, a lineage that predates flowering plants, largely unchanged since before the dinosaurs, and it grows to match, sometimes a centimetre or two of height a year. Old ones sprawl into colonies of many trunks from one base. Japan names three great cycads. Myokoku-ji's in Sakai is put at over 1,100 years by tradition and Nomanji's at about a thousand, and both carry the same legend: a warlord took the plant to his castle and sent it home after it wept every night for its temple. Ryuge-ji's in Shimizu is one plant with fifty-eight trunks rising from a single base. One beside a museum in Kagoshima carries the name of a discovery: in 1896 a botanist found this species' sperm swimming inside an ovule, the first motile sperm ever seen in a seed plant.

species.name: Saw-leaf Zelkova
species.intro: In Japan this tree is keyaki, the timber temple carpenters and taiko drum makers reach for first, and the giants that survive tend to stand where nobody could cut them. Japan's largest grows in the playground of Higashine Elementary, on the site of a 1347 castle keep: 16 metres round at chest height, a Special Natural Monument, and the children are taught that catching three falling leaves earns a wish. In Haramachi traffic goes around another of the country's three great zelkovas in the middle of a junction. A Korean queen is recorded resting under the zelkova at Hwayang-dong in Seoul in 1882, in disguise, fleeing soldiers who had stormed the palace; it is about 700 years old. Leiden's are the first zelkovas ever to leave Japan, and Florence's has been measured three times in forty years, growing from 3.30 metres round to 4.40.

species.name: Scots Pine
species.intro: Scots pine is the plainest tree here and one of the toughest: the only pine native to nearly all of Europe, from Spain to Siberia, growing wherever the soil is too thin or sandy for anything grander. Estonia's largest tree by volume is one, the King's Pine in the Järvselja training forest, more than 33 metres tall and put at about 380 years. Poland's oldest, Wszebora, has stood roughly 370 years above the Srebrna river and was named by schoolchildren in 2016. Helsinki's grows on a rocky shore beside a Bronze Age burial cairn built around 2000 BC, itself around 340 years old and barely 10 metres tall, stunted by three centuries in bare granite. Strasbourg's did the opposite, twisting up into a crown flattened into a parasol. In 2004 Slovakia's very first Tree of the Year was a wild Scots pine above Veľké Borové.

species.name: Sea Fig
species.intro: Ficus superba is a strangler fig from the edge of the subtropics. Its range runs up from Taiwan and the Ryukyus and gives out around southern Kyushu, which is why nobody further north has heard of one and why Kagoshima alone protects four by name. The oldest sits on the side of an active volcano: the city's own signboard puts it near a thousand years, a figure three times the next-oldest tree on the register and resting on no published method, so take it as an official estimate rather than a measurement. At Nojima Shrine on the Nichinan coast, akou figs pour their roots over walls and rock through the whole precinct, and almost every visitor assumes the entire grove is protected; only one tree there carries the 1941 national designation. In Okinawa, the akou of Amaku is 19.5 metres round on a tree ten metres tall.

species.name: Service Tree
species.intro:
The service tree is the rowan's overlooked relative: the same family, but a proper timber tree that grows far larger and far slower, and rare enough north of the Alps that a healthy one gets written up. The fruit is what people planted it for, miniature apples and pears a couple of centimetres long, hard and mouth-drying until frost turns them soft and brown, and then eaten or fermented.

The Slovak one has a medal: about 250 years old at Uzovská Panica, planted to mark where one person's land stopped and the next began, 2.95 metres round, and winner of the national tree of the year vote in 2019. Copenhagen's stands in J.C. Jacobsens Have at 3.18 metres round and 16 metres tall, and the Danish register, which does not deal in compliments, calls it a large and beautiful tree. Geneva's is the youngest by a long way, planted in April 1966 beside the Route de Pregny.

species.name: Sessile Oak
species.intro: Sessile oak, Quercus petraea, is the pedunculate oak's straighter-trunked cousin: its acorns sit directly on the twig with no stalk, while its leaves carry the longer stalk the other species' acorns lack. In the Netherlands it is a genuine rarity, over 95 percent of the country's oaks are pedunculate, which is what made a single tree in Groningen's Zuiderplantsoen worth a public campaign when the city nearly felled it for a footpath in 2025. Germany's royal gardens kept better company: on Pfaueninsel, the private island a Prussian king filled with peacocks and follies, sessile oaks were already a century old when the landscaping began in 1793, and three still stand there, one carrying a door cut clean through its trunk since some forgotten fit of eighteenth century theatre. These are the sessile oaks mapped on the site so far.

species.name: Silk Floss Tree
species.intro: In Spanish it is the palo borracho, the drunken stick, and the trunk is the reason: green, swollen through the middle, tapering at both ends and studded with fat conical thorns. Ceiba speciosa comes from Argentina and Brazil, stores water in that belly and flowers pink in October, when the branches are half bare and the flowers are all there is to see. The one in the small Jardim Alfredo Keil turns a whole Lisbon garden pink for a few weeks. Naples' has the widest trunk of the 53 entries the national monumental register holds for that city. Malaga's survived the remodelling of the streets around the cathedral by being built into the result. Valencia's, in the university's botanic garden, has reached 32 metres. Cadiz's, in the Parque Genoves, is undated, which is normal for a tree that puts on girth this quickly.

species.name: Silky Oak
species.intro: Grevillea robusta is not an oak, and it is not related to any tree that uses the name. It belongs to the protea family alongside banksias and macadamias, native to the subtropical forests of eastern Australia. Brisbane's, in the species' own homeland, is 32 metres tall and roughly a century old, taller than almost any grevillea gets. Setubal's flowers in spring with dense one-sided combs of orange, more like a bottlebrush than anything most people picture when they hear silky oak. Measuring them is another matter. Barcelona's has a municipal girth of 4.1 metres and an independent 2017 measurement of barely half that, and in Alicante two standing eleven metres apart at either end of the Canalejas fig avenue agree on their height and disagree on their waistline by a factor of three. The wood was once prized by cabinetmakers for a silvery figure in the grain.

species.name: Silver Fir
species.intro: A silver fir this old is rare precisely because the species is not: Abies alba covers mountain slopes across central Europe by the million, so a single named, individually remarkable specimen stands out against a background of forestry. The Waldhaustanne in the Bayerischer Wald is Germany's tallest, thickest and oldest documented silver fir, unrecorded until a family out walking reported it in 2020: about 53 metres tall, 6.93 metres round and roughly 605 years old, reached by a boardwalk built to keep boots off its roots. In Romania's Southern Carpathians the Guardian of Cibin, about 500 years old, takes eight men with outstretched arms to circle. On Velebit, Croatian foresters call Jela Car, the emperor fir, the largest silver fir left in Europe. Aarhus's stands forty and a half metres over a family graveyard moved into Moesgård's park in 1926.

species.name: Silver Lime
species.intro: Silver lime carries its identifying trick on the underside of every leaf: a coat of fine white felt that flickers the whole crown between green and silver on a windy day, readable from thirty metres away. It is the last lime to flower, in July. Tilburg's oldest tree, standing off the main square where nobody thinks to look, grows in a town that may take its own name from the species. A second Tilburg lime, in a small park on the Fokkerpad, stood in a private garden laid out by Leonard Springer before the estate opened to the public. Bruges planted three at the Gentpoort in 1928 as peace trees, ten years after the peace; they are now 35 metres tall. Amersfoort's is grafted, a weeping 'Petiolaris' crown joined onto an ordinary lime rootstock, its long leaf stalks letting each leaf swivel independently in the wind.

species.name: Silver Maple
species.intro: Silver maple grows fast, splits easily in a storm, and is usually gone before it turns a hundred, which makes every old one on this list an exception to its own species. Acer saccharinum comes from the flooded river bottoms of eastern North America, where it is built to take a spring deluge that would kill less flexible trees. Montreal's McKenna maple was an ornamental on a florist's grounds before Notre-Dame-des-Neiges laid out its burial sections around the trunk; it is 5.8 metres round and about 150 years old. In Madrid's walled Cecilio Rodriguez garden one gave up on a single trunk early and grew four. Hoorn's by the Veliusbrug is the survivor of a pair. Warsaw declared one on Jazdów a protected tree four months after an expressway opened thirty metres away. Bruges planted its Canada Tree in 1947, possibly the wrong maple for the flag.

species.name: Sitka Spruce
species.intro: Sitka spruce grows taller than almost any other conifer on Earth, and this map holds three very different arguments for why that matters. Near Lake Quinault in Olympic National Park, the Quinault Big Spruce is a world-record specimen, roughly 58 metres tall and about 18 metres round, a straightforward giant on flat ground beside a resort. A short walk away at Kalaloch, the Tree of Life keeps almost none of the usual shape: an eroding creek has undercut its roots until the trunk hangs suspended over open air, alive and, by recent reports, still losing ground. On the Oregon coast, in Tillamook, wind rather than water has done the shaping: the Octopus Tree is a Sitka spruce whose trunk splits low into several huge limbs that arc out and back down like a candelabra, a form nobody planted and nobody can fully explain.

species.name: Small-leaved Lime
species.intro: For centuries in this part of Europe you were tried under one of these. The Gerichtslinde, the court lime, was a real institution: a broad tree on the village square with benches beneath it, where the local court sat in the open because everybody could then see and hear what had been decided. Small-leaved lime was usually the species chosen, since it lives long, takes heavy pruning and builds exactly that kind of wide low crown. Aachen's Forster Linde, put at roughly a thousand years, hosted a manorial court until 1390, death sentences included. The habit of gathering under them outlasted the courts. Carters running between Vienna and Trieste stopped under Ljubljana's Furmanska lipa to buy hay for their horses, and that tree, planted in 1626, turns 400 in 2026. In 2011 a lime before a village church in Transylvania was voted European Tree of the Year.

species.name: Southern Catalpa
species.intro: Old catalpas rarely grow straight, and Dutch gardeners have learned to let them. In April 1973 a storm knocked one flat in the grounds of Paleis Soestdijk in Baarn, and Queen Juliana told her gardener to leave it where it fell; new trunks have risen along its length since. Deventer's at De Lathmer has gone horizontal with age and lies across the grass, still flowering every summer. Breda's leans so far out over the pond in Wilhelminapark that the municipality props its lowest limbs on columns, and Milan's has spent about 136 years twisting behind a baroque fish pond in the Giardini della Guastalla. The species comes from a small pocket of the southeastern United States and is far commoner in European gardens than at home. It is bare well into May, then hangs out speckled cream trumpets in July and long thin pods after.

species.name: Southern Live Oak
species.intro: Southern live oak is the evergreen oak of the humid coastal South, hung with Spanish moss and rarely far from salt air, and its old ones spread wider than they grow tall. The Middleton Oak in Charleston, put at 900 to 1,000 years, was long described as the largest tree in the eastern United States. Brunswick built Albany Street around Lover's Oak rather than through it. In New Orleans the McDonogh Oak rests its heavy branches on wooden crutches, and the Live Oak Society, whose members are the trees themselves, lists the Middleton Oak as its First Vice President. The Emancipation Proclamation got its first public reading in the South under a live oak in Hampton, Virginia, in 1863. In Dealey Plaza the shots at President Kennedy passed through a live oak's canopy, and Pisa has grown one since 1829.

species.name: Southern Magnolia
species.intro: For a few weeks in early summer this tree opens cream white flowers the width of a dinner plate, lemon scented and finished within a couple of days. Magnolia grandiflora comes from the warm swamp forests of the American southeast and only reached Europe in the middle of the eighteenth century, which puts a hard ceiling on how old any of the European ones can be. The oldest here is Rome's, roughly 275 years, and it does not stand in a garden at all: it grows on the pavement of Via Corsini, outside the wall of the palace whose garden it was planted for. Padua's went in during 1786, the year Goethe came through the gate. Frederick Douglass planted two at Cedar Hill for his wife, on family testimony rather than a receipt. The leaves stay glossy and green all winter.

species.name: Spanish Fir
species.intro: The Spanish fir survives wild in only three small patches of mountain behind Ronda and Grazalema, left behind when the ice age retreated and the climate around it dried out everywhere else in Europe. Botanists did not describe Abies pinsapo until the 1830s, and within decades it was already in gardens across the continent, which is how one now stands in the royal parterres of La Granja de San Ildefonso, 700 kilometres from the nearest wild tree. The Sierra de las Nieves trees mapped here show how strange the species gets at home: Las Escaleretas has its own natural monument decree, La Perra forks into a candelabrum instead of a single spire, and the Solitary Pinsapo stands completely alone on bare rock. Four so far, three wild and one transplanted.

species.name: St Lucie Cherry
species.intro: Prunus mahaleb is usually a shrub, six metres tall on a good day, grown mostly as rootstock for other cherries rather than as a specimen in its own right. Three trees on this site ignore that description entirely. Budapest's, in the ELTE Fuveszkert botanical garden, stands 11.2 metres tall with a trunk 339 centimetres round, already growing on a nobleman's private estate before the university bought the ground around it in 1847. Den Bosch's, rooted for roughly a century against the medieval city wall on Parklaan, was nominated for the Dutch national Bomen Top 50 in 2022. Matera's, the thinnest evidenced of the three, has given its name to the city's Lanera district even though this pass could not confirm whether it still stands. Hungarians call the species sajmeggy, the Dutch call it Weichselboom; both names describe a fruit few gardeners plant a tree this size to get.

species.name: Stone Pine
species.intro: The stone pine is the tree that gives the Mediterranean skyline its flat topped silhouette, and it normally does that from a bare trunk ten or fifteen metres up, spreading wider than it grows tall. The one on Florence's Bobolino hillside ignores the rule and stands 31.5 metres. Two on a Setubal street are older than the street and are left over from the woodland it was cut through. Istanbul's Ata Fistik Cami, about 400 years old, gave a whole hill its name and was brought there from the Aegean rather than growing there naturally. On Mallorca the road between Valldemossa and Deià was widened around one rather than through it. Naples has the odd one out: the pine above Mergellina was arguably the most photographed tree on earth for a century, and the tree on that hillside now was planted in 1995 in place of the original.

species.name: Strawberry Tree
species.intro: Madrid put one of these on its coat of arms, a bear reaching up into the branches, and the tree on the Plaza de la Lealtad is the closest thing the city has to the original. The species is normally a shrub you can see over the top of, which makes the one on Via alla Rocca in Bergamo peculiar: 16 metres tall, with a trunk 355 centimetres around. Catalonia declared one near Can Genoer, in the hill country of the Baix Emporda, a monumental tree in 2000, at 8.5 metres about as large as the species is known to get. Autumn is the moment to go. Arbutus unedo flowers and ripens fruit at the same time, so a single branch carries white bells and red fruit at once. Florence's grows in the Giardino dell'Iris, and another stands on a wine estate above Nice at the Chateau de Cremat.

species.name: Sweet Chestnut
species.intro: On the slope of Etna above Sant'Alfio, what looks like three enormous chestnuts is one tree: the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, named for a queen said to have sheltered under it with a hundred mounted knights, and put at about 2,200 years by Italy's agricultural research council in 2022. Sweet chestnut collects stories because it stays around long enough. Corsica's Bread Tree at Pianello is so called because for centuries its nuts were the bread. In January 1949 a runaway bus above Trento was stopped by a chestnut, and local accounts still argue about which one. The trunk gives the age away better than any plaque, because as a chestnut ages its bark starts to spiral around the stem, and on the oldest the whole trunk looks wrung out like a towel.
