Charles II is behind the Greenwich Park tree, planted for the formal avenues he ordered after 1660.

species.name: Sweet Osmanthus
species.intro: Osmanthus fragrans is grown for one thing: for a few weeks each autumn, a mature tree's small flowers put out one of the strongest scents any hardy plant makes, apricot and ripe peach carried well past the tree itself. It rarely receives official protection of its own, which makes Japan's National Natural Monument osmanthus unusual. The Kinmokusei of Mishima Taisha, over 1,200 years by shrine tradition, flowers twice in the same month, early September and again two weeks later, and a 1985 assessment that gave it three years to live has been wrong for forty. At Eimeiji in Ora a typhoon felled the original in 1966, and the tree there now grew back from its stump. Kezoji's in Maebashi is the child of a famous tree that died. Caserta's, in the royal palace's English Garden, has a 6.5-metre girth made of several stems bundled together.

species.name: Swiss Pine
species.intro: Pinus cembra belongs at the Alpine and Carpathian treeline, in the last thin soil before rock takes over, which makes every specimen at street level or in a city park a transplant rather than a native. The oldest by story is Re Leone in Trentino's Passo Manghen, a cirmolo a forestry worker was sent to fell in the 1970s and refused, telling his supervisor it was a monument rather than timber. Berlin's grows on flat Dahlem sand, part of a 1903 teaching-garden planting nowhere near the two thousand metres of altitude this species normally needs. Vilnius keeps one three kilometres from its centre in the Antakalnis district, carrying the same edible seeds and dense, long needles as its wild Alpine cousins. Three cities so far.

species.name: Sycamore
species.intro: Nobody plants a sycamore on purpose any more. It seeds itself into gutters, railway banks and any gap it can find across northern Europe, grows fast, and gets cut down long before it becomes anything, which is precisely what makes an old one worth looking up at. Glasgow's Darnley Sycamore is put at 450 to 500 years, exceptional for a species that rarely passes 400, and it carries the name of Mary, Queen of Scots' husband on a story from 1565. On the village green at Tolpuddle in Dorset, six farm labourers met under a sycamore in 1833 to form a union and were transported to Australia for it; the tree is about 340 years old and 6.06 metres round. Copenhagen's is the thickest tree inside Assistens cemetery and the least exotic species in it. Edinburgh's grows sideways out of solid rock at the start of a riverside walkway.

species.name: Tasmanian Blue Gum
species.intro: A trunk 5.2 metres around on a tree planted in 1904 is what a blue gum does when nothing gets in its way. Eucalyptus globulus comes from Tasmania and southeastern Australia and puts on size faster than almost anything else that grows this big, which is why nineteenth century Europe planted it everywhere: for timber, for drying out marshland, and on the belief that its oils cleaned bad air. The tree on the hotel road at Bucaco is 7.15 metres around at about 150 years old, thicker than anything else on that walk, and Guimaraes has one of 7.05 metres on Monte da Penha. Naples' reaches 30 metres, the tallest tree the registers record inside the botanical garden. Madrid's stands north of the Estanque in the Retiro and is over a century old. Every one of them is younger than it looks.

species.name: Texas Live Oak
species.intro: Texas Live Oak is the tougher inland cousin of the coastal live oak, built to survive Hill Country droughts and freezes that would kill its Gulf Coast relative. The old ones carry more history than botanical fame. Austin's Treaty Oak, reckoned at about 500 years old and known locally as the father of the forest, survived a 1989 poisoning that killed two thirds of it, then set acorns again eight years later. The Battle Oaks nearly fell in 1923 to make room for a university building, until a classics professor talked the committee out of it. In 1872 a priest is said to have chosen the site of St. Edward's University by standing under the Sorin Oak, already about a century old. Fort Worth's Turner Oak kept a farmer's gold buried in its roots through the Civil War, dug up afterward to help pay off the young town's debts.

species.name: Tipu Tree
species.intro: None of the Lisbon tipus stands anywhere a gardener would have chosen. One holds down a traffic circle, where a crown 34 metres across had become the city's problem by 2018. One stands in the middle of a bus terminal. One occupies the triangle of grass outside parliament, which has kept a South American tree on its doorstep for about ninety years. The fourth grows in the garden named for the Portuguese defeat at La Lys in 1918. Tipuana tipu comes from the foothills of Bolivia and Argentina, a legume with feathery leaves and single winged pods that spin down like sycamore keys, and it puts up with pavement, drought and hard pruning better than most things. The Barcelona tree, about 101 years old, is the specimen the city measures its other tipus against, and there are plenty to measure: it is one of the commonest street trees in the city.

species.name: Tree of Heaven
species.intro: Ailanthus altissima is the tree cities spend the most money getting rid of, and the old ones here are protected or plaqued instead. The one in Ravenscourt Park in London has a green plaque at its foot. Zaragoza lists the specimen in its botanical garden as a singular tree. Dublin's is the largest in Ireland, framed between two Victorian glasshouses, and its age is a real argument: the register says 120 to 165 years, the way this species grows suggests closer to 70 or 100. That growth rate is the whole problem with it. Tree of heaven seeds into any crack, sends suckers under pavement and shades out whatever stood there first, fast enough to reach a serious size within one lifetime. The Danish name says what that looks like: skyraekker, sky reacher. Copenhagen's, in Assistens, is 15.5 metres.

species.name: Tulip Tree
species.intro: You can identify it from the pavement: the leaf looks as though someone snipped the tip off with scissors, four lobes and a flat end where the point should be. Liriodendron tulipifera is a tree of the eastern United States, and there it grows wild and tall. The Queens Giant came up on its own in a stretch of Alley Pond Park's forest that was never cleared; New York dates it to at least 368 years, and it is the tallest carefully measured tree in the city. In Chapel Hill, campus legend says the University of North Carolina stands where General Davie fell asleep under one in 1792. Europe's oldest exist because of the post. On 1 October 1716 a London apothecary sent seed to Leiden, and Herman Boerhaave sowed it in the botanical garden where it still stands. Braga's, planted under João V, is called the largest in Portugal.

species.name: Turkey Oak
species.intro: Quercus cerris is an oak of southern and southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, and north of its range every one was planted on purpose: gardeners liked how fast it grows and how large it gets while the person who planted it is still around to see it. Genoa's, in the English-style grounds of Villa Serra above the city, is the surprise: 41 metres, taller than the Californian redwood sixty metres away. Caserta's grows in the royal park's English Garden among trees collected from Australia and California, while the species grows wild in the hills a few kilometres away. Utrecht's four stand together on an old city-wall bastion, close enough that the Dutch register counts them as one entry. The leaves give it away: stiffer and more deeply cut than a pedunculate oak's, with whiskery bud scales and mossy, curl-wrapped acorn cups.

species.name: Turkish Hazel
species.intro: A hazel is supposed to be a shrub you can see over. The Turkish hazel puts up a single straight trunk instead and keeps going: the one in the Square du Temple in Paris stands sixteen metres tall with a trunk 235 centimetres around. The Amsterdam tree, planted in the Hortus in 1795, is called the oldest and thickest of its kind in the Netherlands by the Dutch tree foundation. Romania has only two officially protected specimens of Corylus colurna and one of them grows in Cismigiu in Bucharest. Vienna protected a pair in the Resselpark in 1972 for the way they match, though they went in seventeen years apart, in 1900 and 1917. The best line about any of them belongs to French regional television, which ran a news piece written in the voice of the hazel in Square Maurice-Gardette: I am 145, stop cracking my hazelnuts.

species.name: Turkish Pine
species.intro: Pinus brutia goes by three different names depending on where you stand in front of it: Turkish pine in English, pino bruzio or pin de Calabre on the ground in Italy and France, pino de Creta in Spain, describing a pine from Turkey, Cyprus, Crete and the Levant that colonises burnt ground first and produces a honey beekeepers actively seek. Botanists still argue whether it deserves its own species or belongs folded into the Aleppo pine; the national register in Florence files its specimen under Pinus halepensis regardless. Three cities map one each, and each shows a different way an old pine stands: Florence's has grown a lopsided, storm-prone flag crown after a century squeezed into a crowded botanical collection, Rouen's needed a support structure built under it in 2021, and Valencia's went straight up for thirty metres without leaning, forking or flattening at all.

species.name: Turner's Oak
species.intro: Turner's oak is a garden invention, not a wild species: an English nursery crossed the evergreen Mediterranean holm oak with the northern pedunculate oak in the late eighteenth century, and the hybrid kept the holm oak's leathery leaves through winter, only dropping them in spring when new growth pushes the old ones off. Amsterdam's, in the Hortus Botanicus, still carries its graft union thirty centimetres above the ground and a disputed planting year, 1865 by the city's own register or 1895 by the Bomenstichting's, thirty years apart on the same tree. Brussels has two, a few minutes' walk apart on the same lawns of Parc d'Egmont: the one entered into the region's tree register in 1999, and a taller, thicker neighbour registered separately nearby. None of the three is old by oak standards. All three are odd enough to be worth the detour.

species.name: Weeping Beech
species.intro: A weeping beech makes a room. The branches drop from the top of the trunk to the ground in a closed curtain, and the space inside is dark, hollow and tall enough to stand up in, which is most of the reason cities hold on to them. Munich's ordinance is unusually frank about that: the reason recorded for protecting the beech by the Schwanenbrucke is that people are fond of it. The same city protects a second one on Situlistrasse on the grounds that it is the largest weeping beech standing in Munich, and says so in its own paperwork. The Leiden tree, about 185 years old in the Hortus, has the longest paper trail, running back to the London nurseryman George Loddiges. Copenhagen's grows in Assistens, the cemetery the city treats as a park.

species.name: Weeping Fig
species.intro: The genuinely large, old weeping figs people go to see split into two very different stories. In Miriam Vale, Queensland, on the coast road to Agnes Water, one fig has grown to roughly 12 metres round and 35 metres across, doing duty since around the 1890s as the town's milk depot, its war memorial shelter and an impromptu vet's surgery, all under one crown. Brisbane's stands at the Alice Street gate of the City Botanic Gardens, about 155 years old, planted not long after the gardens themselves were founded, native ground for a species that grows wild across northern Australia and South and Southeast Asia. Lisbon's is the odd one out, five metres round in the Campo de Santana park, doing the same unlikely, enormous work eight thousand kilometres from where the species grows on its own. All three keep their leaves year-round and none has ever stopped spreading wider rather than taller, which is the whole trick of the tree.

species.name: Weeping Higan Cherry
species.intro: Shidarezakura hang their flowering branches straight down, so the tree makes a curtain you walk under rather than a canopy you look up into, and they open before the ordinary somei-yoshino. The greatest is the Miharu Takizakura in Fukushima, the waterfall cherry, put at over a thousand years by tradition, its crown 22 metres across; around 300,000 people a year come to stand under it. In the hills of Yamanashi, Shinden no Oitozakura told Kobuchisawa's farmers when to plant rice before calendars did. Kyoto's famous ones are often stand-ins, and nobody minds. The weeping cherry everyone photographs at Maruyama Park is the second one on the spot. The Taiko cherry at Daigo-ji is not the tree Toyotomi Hideyoshi saw at his enormous blossom party of 1598, but it stands where the party happened. In Nara, the local spring is dated from the cherry beside the approach to Himuro Shrine.

species.name: Weeping Silver Lime
species.intro: A weeping silver lime is a grafted cultivar of Tilia tomentosa, its branches trained to arch back toward the ground, and every leaf carries a coat of white felt on its underside that flickers the whole crown pale in the wind. Park designers planted it for exactly that shimmer. Ghent's grew from an 1851 planting laid out for a private zoo whose grounds became Muinkpark once the animals left. Maastricht's stand in a group along the moated bank of Haet ende Nijt, planted in the 1860s. Tilburg's has an actual date, 1898, in Leonard Springer's original layout of the Wilhelminapark. Alkmaar's is younger, from the 1930s, on the old rampart earthworks the city turned into parkland. Copenhagen's in J.C. Jacobsens Have is 27.5 metres tall, its main branches held together with wire.

species.name: Weeping Willow
species.intro: The weeping willow is not built to last. It is fast-growing and soft-wooded, the sort of tree that usually falls to storm or age long before it earns a place beside the oaks and yews this site otherwise maps. That makes its exceptions worth naming. In Hiroshima, one stood 370 metres from the point the atomic bomb detonated in 1945 and is still alive today, the closest registered survivor the city has. In Leiden, one has wept over the statue of Pieter van der Werf for more than a century, its own history otherwise unrecorded by any source found so far. In Alkmaar, a third bends over an 1876 victory monument in a park laid out by the Zocher family, who also reshaped the city's old bastions. None of these three are ancient by this site's usual standards. They earn their place by surviving what a short-lived species rarely manages.

species.name: Western Red Cedar
species.intro: Western red cedar grows to enormous size in the rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, and its wood resists rot so well that a tree can stay alive on a strip of bark. The Duncan Cedar, near Olympic National Park, is the largest known in the world and the largest tree of any species in Washington: over a thousand years old, 54 metres tall, and mostly dead wood. Planted abroad, it does something else. Its lowest branches bend under their own weight, touch the ground, root where they land and thicken into trunks of their own. Sintra's has been heading toward the lake below Pena Palace for about 150 years, and forestry students have used it as a teaching example since at least 1916. Strasbourg's is doing the same in the Parc de l'Orangerie. Cork's, at Blarney, sends out limbs each thicker than most full grown trees.

species.name: White Mulberry
species.intro: These trees were planted as machinery. White mulberry leaf is the only thing a silkworm will eat, so every ruler who fancied a silk industry ordered mulberries into the ground, and the trees stayed long after the venture folded. At the Krka falls in Croatia, the Green Lady stands below the ruins of a mill, about 400 years old by the national park's account; in the 1830s nearby Skradin was the largest silkworm-breeding centre in Dalmatia. Maria Theresa's push put orchards across Taban in Buda, which is most likely where Budapest's oldest mulberry comes from, whatever the Ottoman legend says. Around Bergamo the leaves fed trays of larvae in farmhouse lofts, and three of those trees still stand in a public garden. Split's, in the courtyard of Hajduk's first ground, was DNA sampled in 2015 and cloned 105 times, once per year of the club.

species.name: White Oak
species.intro: White oak is eastern North America's slow, wide-crowned oak, tougher and longer-lived than red oak. The oldest, on the edge of Old Logan Cemetery in Ohio, is put at roughly six hundred years; the town sells saplings raised from its acorns to keep the line going. In Baltimore the Ruxton Liberty Tree was a seedling around 1646 and marked a boundary between two land grants by 1694; the family whose lawn it stands on pays for 5,000 gallons of water a week to keep it alive. At Gettysburg, the Devil's Den witness tree was a sapling when Longstreet's assault opened around it in July 1863. Boston's grows wild on the Arnold Arboretum's Peters Hill, uncatalogued until 2010 and cored in 2018 to roughly two centuries old. Athens, Georgia's is the son of an oak an 1890 newspaper story said legally owned itself.

species.name: White Poplar
species.intro: White poplars rarely get the chance to grow old. The species spreads fast by root suckers and gets cleared as a nuisance long before it reaches any real size, which is why an old one stands out. Every leaf is covered underneath in white felt, so a gust turns the crown from green to silver. Lithuania's Vainiai Poplar is 6.85 metres round, still standing in a former manor park that has otherwise reverted to scrub. Warsaw's, nearly five metres round, stands in a small Rakowiec park with a playground and a pond. Krakow's, on Plac Emila Serkowskiego across the river in Podgorze, has been a natural monument since 1997. Amsterdam's is the odd one out: its own protection register admits it is no longer an impressive specimen and keeps it listed anyway, on the strength of being, most likely, the oldest living thing in its park.

species.name: White Willow
species.intro: White willow is a river tree that rarely gets old. It roots fast on a gravel bar scoured clean by a flood, grows up in crowded thickets, and by forty or fifty years is usually splitting apart under its own soft, fast-grown wood. The ones that reach two centuries are almost always the ones that were pollarded, cut back hard to the same point on the trunk every few years, which is the history behind Alkmaar's willow in the old Veenbos polder, closing in on two hundred years old. Munich's stands alone on the Isar's northern floodplain, unusual enough on its own that the city's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it for that solitude. Gdansk's, beside a pond in Oliwa, survived an arson attack on 29 December 2025 that burned out its core before firefighters arrived in time to save the second protected willow growing next to it.

species.name: Wild Olive
species.intro: A wild olive hollows out as it ages, which is what makes every age on this page an estimate rather than a measurement: no ring count survives in a trunk that has lost its heartwood. All three grow in Sardinia, in the granite hills of Gallura and the coast of Ogliastra, and together they are the closest thing Italy has to an age record. S'Ozzastru, at Santu Baltolu di Carana near Luras, is Italy's oldest living tree by most estimates: the University of Sassari puts it at 2,500 to 4,000 years, its trunk 11.5 metres round, and Sardinians call it su babbu mannu, the great father. A second, unnamed olivastro grows a few metres along the same path, half the girth at 5.4 metres and overshadowed by its neighbour, though nowhere else on the island would it go unnoticed. The third stands alone in the village square of Santa Maria Navarrese, beside a church five centuries its junior, its trunk scarred by an arson attempt in the early 1960s that it survived. All three were declared natural monuments by the region, in 1991 and 1994, and all three are free to visit.

species.name: Willowleaf Podocarp
species.intro: Three of these stand on this site, two in Rome and one in Singapore, and each is protected for a different reason. Podocarps are a mostly southern conifer family that split off before pines existed and never adopted the cone: the seed sits instead on a swollen, fleshy stalk that turns purple and gets eaten by birds, which is how the species spread from the Himalayan foothills to New Guinea and why Buddhist communities planted it around temples across that range. Rome's Villa Sciarra specimen made Italy's national monumental register for a single reason, botanical rarity, with no claim to age or size at all; the city calls it splendid and enormous anyway. A second Rome tree, in Piazza Vittorio's garden, is one of the largest in the city and was listed in 2025. Singapore's grows on a lawn in the Botanic Gardens, its own age never recorded.

species.name: Wych Elm
species.intro: On the night of 12 May 1971 a crowd of Stockholmers climbed into the elms of Kungstradgarden and refused to come down, and the city workers went home. Those trees are still standing, between 160 and 205 years old. Any wych elm of size is worth a detour now, because a fungus carried tree to tree by bark beetles cleared out most of the big ones within two generations. One of the oldest in the Netherlands, put at roughly 275 years, stands on a lawn behind an office building in The Hague that was a manor house first. Brighton's, in a dog exercise area above a playground, is the widest recorded in Sussex. Munich protects the elm on Maximiliansplatz precisely because almost every elm that size in the city has gone. Trento's stands in the garden facing the station, under two minutes from the platform.

species.name: Wych Elm 'Exoniensis'
species.intro: This is the feather elm, pluimiep in Dutch, also called the Exeter Elm: a cultivar of wych elm bred narrow and upright where the wild species spreads wide, grafted on a rootstock to keep that shape. Old wych elms of any kind are a rare sight after a century of Dutch elm disease took most of them out, which is reason enough to go looking for these. In Leeuwarden, two grow in the small Vosseparkje at the edge of the old town, told apart mainly by which one stands nearer the pond. A third is a street planting on Molenstraat, where the graft union has swollen into a collar of scar tissue over five metres round, wider at that point than the trunk beneath it. Alkmaar's, on the rampart behind the cultural centre, has survived about 130 years and is filed in one register as an ordinary Dutch elm.
